path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.1 The Fourier Transform.md
title: Symmetric Fourier Transform on the Real Line
body:
> [!definition|848a83d1-1f06-5ed3-8618-355d7855c621.local at=300bf9a5-9b50-534e-a926-8869a2be77d0] Symmetric Fourier Transform on the Real Line
> Here integrable means $\int_{\mathbb R}|f(x)|\,dx<\infty$.
>
> Suppose that $f$ is integrable on the real line, the Fourier transform of $f$, denoted by $\mathcal{F}(f)$ or $\widehat{f}$, is defined by
>
> $$
> \widehat{f}(\omega)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) e^{-i \omega x} d x \quad(-\infty<\omega<\infty)
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.1 The Fourier Transform.md
title: Symmetric Inverse Fourier Transform
body:
> [!definition|9eb08051-45eb-51f2-9755-ab827dd4ca90.local at=c59c2eec-aca3-56b8-ba97-909a068daf57] Symmetric Inverse Fourier Transform
> For $g\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, the following integral converges absolutely. More generally, when the symmetric principal value exists, it defines the inverse transform by the limit of integrals over $[-a,a]$ as $a\to\infty$.
>
> The inverse Fourier transform of $g(\omega)$ is
>
> $$
> \mathcal{F}^{-1}(g)(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(\omega) e^{i \omega x} d \omega \quad(-\infty<x<\infty)
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.1 The Fourier Transform.md
title: Fourier Inversion for an Integrable Piecewise Smooth Function
body:
> [!theorem|2ed5979b-d489-5724-bd76-1c83fd3dd815.local at=c88ef409-bda2-5f09-8ea9-bd195bb6319a] Fourier Inversion for an Integrable Piecewise Smooth Function
> Use the symmetric Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$. The inverse integral is a symmetric principal value; $f(x\pm)$ denote one-sided limits.
>
> Suppose that $f$ is piecewise smooth and integrable on the real line. Then, for all $x$, we have
>
> $$
> \frac{f(x+)+f(x-)}{2}=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\hat{f})(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \widehat{f}(\omega) e^{i \omega x} d \omega
> $$
>
> In particular, if $f$ is piecewise smooth and continuous at $x$, then
>
> $$
> f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \widehat{f}(\omega) e^{i \omega x} d \omega
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.1 The Fourier Transform.md
title: Conjugate Symmetry of the Fourier Transform of a Real Function
body:
> [!theorem|f05b6b1c-863e-565d-b503-17da680993ae.local at=97758786-f9ad-5c2f-8e46-1a861d40c2ac] Conjugate Symmetry of the Fourier Transform of a Real Function
> Use the symmetric Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$.
>
> Suppose that $f$ is real-valued and integrable and let $g(x)=f(-x)$. Then
>
> $$
> \widehat{f}(-\omega)=\overline{\widehat{f}(\omega)}=\widehat{g}(\omega), \quad \text { for all } \omega
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.1 The Fourier Transform.md
title: Linearity of the Symmetric Fourier Transform
body:
> [!theorem|26facabc-35ce-5616-a0db-7fb753cd4439.local at=14256709-18d0-5fc8-ab99-f127c16fd580] Linearity of the Symmetric Fourier Transform
> Use the symmetric Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$.
>
> The Fourier transform is a linear operation; that is, for any integrable functions $f$ and $g$ and any real numbers $a$ and $b$,
>
> $$
> \mathcal{F}(a f+b g)=a \mathcal{F}(f)+b \mathcal{F}(g)
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.1 The Fourier Transform.md
title: Fourier Transform Parity for Real Integrable Functions
body:
> [!theorem|fbaee10e-5824-5e09-b674-46758f55ed36.local at=e017a07b-899c-513b-abec-5bade5e30679] Fourier Transform Parity for Real Integrable Functions
> Use the symmetric Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$. Parity of an integrable function is understood up to equality almost everywhere; if $f$ is continuous, it is pointwise parity.
>
> Suppose that $f$ is real-valued and integrable. Then
> (i) $\hat{f}$ is real-valued if and only if $f$ is even;
> (ii) $\hat{f}$ is purely imaginary if and only if $f$ is odd.

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.1 The Fourier Transform.md
title: Fourier Reciprocity and Reflection
body:
> [!theorem|6dc6aa94-7a43-5053-8497-683d923db4e0.local at=56f0fe32-b398-522d-ac55-60c0a4a6f00b] Fourier Reciprocity and Reflection
> Use the symmetric Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$.
>
> For $g\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, $\mathcal Fg(\omega)=\mathcal F^{-1}g(-\omega)$. If $f$ and $\widehat f$ are integrable, then $\mathcal F(\mathcal Ff)(\omega)=f(-\omega)$ almost everywhere; the equality is pointwise wherever the inversion formula recovers $f$.

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.1 The Fourier Transform.md
title: Truncated Fourier Inversion as a Sine-Kernel Convolution
body:
> [!lemma|0b7769e9-2b04-5a1d-8591-269040ff5f2d.local at=efd6509c-54e7-5222-bb1a-5ab7e682286e] Truncated Fourier Inversion as a Sine-Kernel Convolution
> Use the symmetric Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$.
>
> Suppose that $f$ is integrable on the real line and $a>0$. Then
>
> $$
> \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-a}^{a} \widehat{f}(\omega) e^{i x \omega} d \omega=\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x-y) \frac{\sin a y}{y} d y
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.1 The Fourier Transform.md
title: Riemann–Lebesgue Lemma for Sine and Cosine Integrals
body:
> [!lemma|43b9f535-b68f-5c4d-a712-bf5a8b3edec2.local at=1d5ca281-6948-599a-8154-da2a0e7526d8] Riemann–Lebesgue Lemma for Sine and Cosine Integrals
> Suppose that $\int_{A}^{B}|g(x)| d x<\infty$, where $-\infty \leq A<B \leq \infty$. Then
> $\lim _{\omega \rightarrow \infty} \int_{A}^{B} g(y) \sin \omega y d y=0$ and $\lim _{\omega \rightarrow \infty} \int_{A}^{B} g(y) \cos \omega y d y=0$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.2 Operational Properties.md
title: Fourier Transforms of Derivatives
body:
> [!theorem|919c9527-2e40-5f7d-ba42-5547a0c14265.local at=b3c9a3ae-fac1-52da-a9b6-b751b60879ca] Fourier Transforms of Derivatives
> Use the symmetric Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$. For each stated derivative order, assume the lower derivatives are locally absolutely continuous, so integration by parts applies. In the general formula also assume $f(x)\to0$ at both infinities.
>
> (i) Suppose $f(x)$ and $f^{\prime}(x)$ are integrable and $f(x) \rightarrow 0$ as $|x| \rightarrow \infty$; then
>
> $$
> \mathcal{F}\left(f^{\prime}\right)=i \omega \mathcal{F}(f) .
> $$
>
> (ii) If, in addition, $f^{\prime \prime}(x)$ is integrable and $f^{\prime}(x) \rightarrow 0$ as $|x| \rightarrow \infty$, then
>
> $$
> \mathcal{F}\left(f^{\prime \prime}\right)=i \omega \mathcal{F}\left(f^{\prime}\right)=-\omega^{2} \mathcal{F}(f) .
> $$
>
> (iii) In general, if $f^{(k)}(x) \rightarrow 0(k=1,2, \ldots, n-1)$ as $|x| \rightarrow \infty$, and $f$ and its derivatives of order up to $n$ are integrable, then
>
> $$
> \mathcal{F}\left(f^{(n)}\right)=(i \omega)^{n} \mathcal{F}(f) .
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.2 Operational Properties.md
title: Differentiation of the Fourier Transform by Multiplication in Position
body:
> [!theorem|4a7c260a-75bb-5fd4-a015-fab7b9a6dd83.local at=b1010265-7403-51b5-ae36-f6dc2845b989] Differentiation of the Fourier Transform by Multiplication in Position
> Use the symmetric Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$. Integrability means absolute integrability on $\mathbb R$; $n$ is a positive integer.
>
> (i) Suppose $f(x)$ and $x f(x)$ are integrable, then
>
> $$
> \mathcal{F}(x f(x))(\omega)=i[\hat{f}]^{\prime}(\omega)=i \frac{d}{d \omega} \mathcal{F}(f)(\omega)
> $$
>
> (ii) In general, if $f(x)$ and $x^{n} f(x)$ are integrable, then
>
> $$
> \mathcal{F}\left(x^{n} f(x)\right)=i^{n}[\hat{f}]^{(n)}(\omega)
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.2 Operational Properties.md
title: Fourier Translation and Modulation Laws
body:
> [!theorem|85044e8d-43b2-51c9-aee8-d04f90d3bc7a.local at=bb222b73-e8e9-5a43-9877-468d1d7a46a1] Fourier Translation and Modulation Laws
> Use the symmetric Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$. Assume $f\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb R$.
>
> (i) Shifting on the $x$-axis: Let $\alpha$ be arbitrary, then
>
> $$
> \mathcal{F}(f(x-\alpha))(\omega)=e^{-i \alpha \omega} \widehat{f}(\omega)
> $$
>
> (ii) Shifting on the $\omega$-axis:
>
> $$
> \mathcal{F}\left(e^{i \alpha x} f(x)\right)(\omega)=\widehat{f}(\omega-\alpha)
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.2 Operational Properties.md
title: Normalized Convolution on the Real Line
body:
> [!definition|ce251f7e-b24d-5894-8522-2dcb7d623bb8.local at=d28aeba4-2e47-537e-b4af-cb188e55c241] Normalized Convolution on the Real Line
> For $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, their normalized convolution, defined for almost every $x$, is
>
> $$
> (f*g)(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x-t)g(t)\,dt.
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.2 Operational Properties.md
title: Fourier Transform of Normalized Convolution
body:
> [!theorem|5ba4babe-0c07-5fea-9706-d4fe75d4b43d.local at=0f47916c-7204-54dd-a8df-0279e735f670] Fourier Transform of Normalized Convolution
> Use the symmetric Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$. The normalized convolution is $(f*g)(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x-t)g(t)\,dt$.
>
> Suppose that $f$ and $g$ are integrable, then
>
> $$
> \mathcal{F}(f * g)=\mathcal{F}(f) \mathcal{F}(g)
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.2 Operational Properties.md
title: Differentiation of Normalized Convolution
body:
> [!theorem|e0b81521-076b-50b7-bd89-d9e140d49885.local at=0df90327-94ea-5e96-92d5-eaa81476caa3] Differentiation of Normalized Convolution
> The normalized convolution is $(f*g)(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x-t)g(t)\,dt$. Assume the derivatives used below are absolutely integrable, the lower derivatives are locally absolutely continuous, and the boundary terms vanish at infinity.
>
> Let $n, \alpha$ and $\beta$ denote nonnegative integers, such that $n=\alpha+\beta$. Then
>
> $$
> \frac{d^{n}}{d x^{n}}(f * g)=\frac{d^{\alpha} f}{d x^{\alpha}} * \frac{d^{\beta} g}{d x^{\beta}}
> $$
>
> In particular, taking $\alpha=n$ and $\beta=0$, then $\alpha=0$ and $\beta=n$, we obtain
>
> $$
> \frac{d^{n}}{d x^{n}}(f * g)=\frac{d^{n} f}{d x^{n}} * g=f * \frac{d^{n} g}{d x^{n}}
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.2 Operational Properties.md
title: Parseval Inner-Product Identity for the Symmetric Fourier Transform
body:
> [!theorem|5db59350-e816-5761-afd3-ebfd705154a9.local at=c5f01410-f1d2-58c8-bacb-57ebd0e73de1] Parseval Inner-Product Identity for the Symmetric Fourier Transform
> Use the symmetric Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$. For general $L^2(\mathbb R)$ functions, use the continuous $L^2$ extension of this transform.
>
> Suppose that $f$ and $g$ are square integrable functions on the real line. Then
>
> $$
> \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \overline{g(x)} d x=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \hat{f}(\omega) \overline{\widehat{g}(\omega)} d \omega
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.2 Operational Properties.md
title: Plancherel Norm Identity for the Symmetric Fourier Transform
body:
> [!theorem|3f25af67-aeed-5cdf-bee7-fc7c23b552f2.local at=6b543933-5925-5d1e-a8c6-8bfc8fad1be2] Plancherel Norm Identity for the Symmetric Fourier Transform
> Use the symmetric Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$. For general $L^2(\mathbb R)$ functions, use the continuous $L^2$ extension of this transform.
>
> Suppose that $f$ is a square integrable function on the real line. Then
>
> $$
> \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|f(x)|^{2} d x=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|\hat{f}(\omega)|^{2} d \omega
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.2 Operational Properties.md
title: Fourier Transforms of Dirac Deltas and Heaviside Steps
body:
> [!identity|839a2472-b06d-52a8-832f-b9177a0ffe32.local at=baa330f9-19e6-5f7f-b503-9d9ab9c2587b] Fourier Transforms of Dirac Deltas and Heaviside Steps
> The following identities hold in the sense of tempered distributions, with the symmetric negative-exponent Fourier convention:
>
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> \mathcal{F}\left(\delta_{0}(x)\right)(\omega) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \\
> \mathcal{F}\left(\delta_{\alpha}(x)\right)(\omega) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{-i \alpha \omega} \\
> \mathcal{F}\left(\mathcal{U}_{0}(x)\right)(\omega) & =\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,\delta_0(\omega)-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\operatorname{pv}\frac1\omega \\
> \mathcal{F}\left(\mathcal{U}_{\alpha}(x)\right)(\omega) & =\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,\delta_0(\omega)-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-i\alpha\omega}\operatorname{pv}\frac1\omega
> \end{aligned}
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.3 The Fourier Transform Method.md
title: Partial Fourier Transform in a Spatial Variable
body:
> [!definition|1653a0ab-d562-511f-85b3-ba5f9382150a.local at=22643d4d-413e-5f9d-bd0e-4af8b4507a18] Partial Fourier Transform in a Spatial Variable
> For fixed $t$, assume $u(\cdot,t)\in L^1(\mathbb R)$. The symmetric Fourier transform in $x$ is
>
> $$
> \mathcal{F}(u(x, t))(\omega)=\widehat{u}(\omega, t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} u(x, t) e^{-i \omega x} d x
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.3 The Fourier Transform Method.md
title: Partial Fourier Transform of Spatial and Temporal Derivatives
body:
> [!property|97b9dc34-4b51-57c7-b9e3-84b06b5f6678.local at=a8f0c715-691f-5f43-a76f-48c118d60861] Partial Fourier Transform of Spatial and Temporal Derivatives
> Use $\widehat u(\omega,t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}u(x,t)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$. Assume spatial derivatives used below are integrable, lower spatial derivatives are locally absolutely continuous and vanish at infinity, and temporal differentiation under the integral is justified by an integrable dominating function on compact time intervals.
>
> Given $u(x, t)$ with $-\infty<x<\infty$ and $t>0$, we have
>
> $$
> \begin{gathered}
> \mathcal{F}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial t} u(x, t)\right)(\omega)=\frac{d}{d t} \widehat{u}(\omega, t) \\
> \mathcal{F}\left(\frac{\partial^{n}}{\partial t^{n}} u(x, t)\right)(\omega)=\frac{d^{n}}{d t^{n}} \widehat{u}(\omega, t), \quad n=1,2, \ldots \\
> \mathcal{F}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x} u(x, t)\right)(\omega)=i \omega \widehat{u}(\omega, t) \\
> \mathcal{F}\left(\frac{\partial^{n}}{\partial x^{n}} u(x, t)\right)(\omega)=(i \omega)^{n} \widehat{u}(\omega, t), \quad n=1,2, \ldots
> \end{gathered}
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.3 The Fourier Transform Method.md
title: Fourier Transform Method for Linear PDEs on the Real Line
body:
> [!procedure|e85f4f15-0f7b-5cae-8ae7-18e0e5ae8450.local at=86a54b81-3664-5e4c-8ded-fa7d75eeea51] Fourier Transform Method for Linear PDEs on the Real Line
> When a PDE has an unbounded spatial variable and its data and derivatives admit Fourier transforms (classically or in a suitable generalized sense), proceed as follows. Retain the transformed initial or boundary conditions and any explicitly required growth or boundedness conditions.
>
> Step 1: Fourier transform the given boundary value problem in $u(x, t)$ and get an ordinary differential equation in $\widehat{u}(\omega, t)$ in the variable $t$.
> Step 2: Solve the ordinary differential equation and find $\widehat{u}(\omega, t)$.
> Step 3: Inverse Fourier transform $\widehat{u}(\omega, t)$ to get $u(x, t)$.

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.4 The Heat Equation and Gauss's Kernel.md
title: Gaussian Convolution Solution of the Heat Equation on the Real Line
body:
> [!theorem] Gaussian Convolution Solution of the Heat Equation on the Real Line
> The normalized convolution is $(f*g)(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x-t)g(t)\,dt$. Let $c>0$, $t>0$, and let the initial data $f$ be bounded and piecewise continuous. For $u_t=c^2u_{xx}$ on $\mathbb R$, the formula below gives a bounded solution tending to $f(x)$ at its continuity points as $t\downarrow0$.
>
> The solution with initial temperature distribution $f$ is the convolution of $f$ with the heat kernel. More explicitly,
>
> $$
> u(x, t)=\frac{1}{c \sqrt{2 t}} e^{-x^{2} / 4 c^{2} t} * f=\frac{1}{2 c \sqrt{\pi t}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(s) e^{-(x-s)^{2} / 4 c^{2} t} d s
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.4 The Heat Equation and Gauss's Kernel.md
title: Real Error Function
body:
> [!definition] Real Error Function
> For a real argument $w$, the error function is
>
> $$
> \operatorname{erf}(w)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{0}^{w} e^{-z^{2}} d z, \quad \text { for all } w
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.5 The Poisson Integral and the Hilbert Transform.md
title: Harmonicity of the Poisson and Conjugate Poisson Kernels
body:
> [!theorem|c9653b03-a8be-50a6-8d4a-fc679e8eb1b3.local at=cdae0e75-8f1f-5a0b-bf07-c56fdcc3c8d8] Harmonicity of the Poisson and Conjugate Poisson Kernels
> The Poisson kernel $P_{y}(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{y}{x^{2}+y^{2}}$ is harmonic for all $(x, y) \neq(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{0})$. Moreover, it has a harmonic conjugate (called the conjugate Poisson kernel) given by
> $$
> Q_{y}(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{x}{x^{2}+y^{2}}, \quad(x, y) \neq(0,0)
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.5 The Poisson Integral and the Hilbert Transform.md
title: Harmonic Conjugate from the Conjugate Poisson Integral
body:
> [!theorem|4e77a596-e099-541d-9212-2bc5c7d7313d.local at=ba61bf31-c7d4-5f99-96a2-5c6548fd787e] Harmonic Conjugate from the Conjugate Poisson Integral
> The normalized convolution is $(f*g)(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x-t)g(t)\,dt$. Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ be real-valued, $y>0$, $P_y(x)=\sqrt{2/\pi}\,y/(x^2+y^2)$, and $Q_y(x)=\sqrt{2/\pi}\,x/(x^2+y^2)$.
>
> Let $u(x, y)=P_{y} * f(x)$ denote the Poisson extension in the upper half-plane. Then a harmonic conjugate of $u(x, y)$ is given by
>
> $$
> v(x, y)=Q_{y} * f(x)=\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x-s) \frac{s}{s^{2}+y^{2}} d s \quad(y>0)
> $$
>
> where $Q_{y}$ is the conjugate Poisson kernel.

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.5 The Poisson Integral and the Hilbert Transform.md
title: Hilbert Transform as a Fourier Multiplier
body:
> [!theorem|5b01e8f8-1d6e-5c6e-9e53-9cd1284d08ae.local at=f16eb417-cc12-518f-badd-0c4bd357cf56] Hilbert Transform as a Fourier Multiplier
> Use the symmetric Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$. Use $Hf(x)=\pi^{-1}\operatorname{pv}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x-s)/s\,ds$. For $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ this is interpreted as the $L^2$ Hilbert transform.
>
> Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb R)\cap L^2(\mathbb R)$, and let $H(f)(x)$ denote its Hilbert transform. Then
>
> $$
> \widehat{H f}(\omega)=-i \operatorname{sgn}(\omega) \widehat{f}(\omega) \quad\text{for almost every }\omega .
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.5 The Poisson Integral and the Hilbert Transform.md
title: Poisson Extension of a Hilbert Transform
body:
> [!theorem|d08bc374-420b-5e61-a58f-9304451f71a5.local at=e5aa6ccd-bc7d-52a0-b7b3-ed4c4c0fca0a] Poisson Extension of a Hilbert Transform
> The normalized convolution is $(f*g)(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x-t)g(t)\,dt$. Use $Hf(x)=\pi^{-1}\operatorname{pv}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x-s)/s\,ds$. For $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ this is interpreted as the $L^2$ Hilbert transform. For $y>0$, write $P_y(x)=\sqrt{2/\pi}\,y/(x^2+y^2)$ and $Q_y(x)=\sqrt{2/\pi}\,x/(x^2+y^2)$.
>
> Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb R)\cap L^2(\mathbb R)$, and let $H(f)(x)$ denote its Hilbert transform. Then
>
> $$
> v(x, y)=Q_{y} * f(x)=P_{y} *(H f)(x) .
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.6 The Fourier Cosine and Sine Transforms.md
title: Fourier Cosine Transform on the Positive Half-Line
body:
> [!definition|2ad4ca4b-47d6-514c-b10a-c8cdfb816eb3.local at=f28d16b5-f6b1-590a-bbbd-15e3d1f9f1cb] Fourier Cosine Transform on the Positive Half-Line
> For $f\in L^1(0,\infty)$, define
>
> $$
> \hat{f}_{c}(\omega)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \int_{0}^{\infty} f(t) \cos \omega t d t \quad(\omega \geq 0)
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.6 The Fourier Cosine and Sine Transforms.md
title: Fourier Sine Transform on the Positive Half-Line
body:
> [!definition|70dd3d22-12c7-56a4-aaa6-b7706d1447ca.local at=177baa3f-63c7-5dac-9443-a9dacada64c8] Fourier Sine Transform on the Positive Half-Line
> For $f\in L^1(0,\infty)$, define
>
> $$
> \widehat{f}_{s}(\omega)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \int_{0}^{\infty} f(t) \sin \omega t d t \quad(\omega \geq 0)
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.6 The Fourier Cosine and Sine Transforms.md
title: Fourier Cosine and Sine Transforms via Even and Odd Extensions
body:
> [!rule|3b1da59a-e83c-5039-b2f7-931204f0fdd6.local at=07470adf-3ef2-5b52-a30c-36ea42ea443a] Fourier Cosine and Sine Transforms via Even and Odd Extensions
> Let $f\in L^1(0,\infty)$ and use the symmetric Fourier convention $\mathcal Fg(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}g(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$, with $\mathcal F_c f=\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_0^\infty f(x)\cos(\omega x)\,dx$ and the analogous sine integral for $\mathcal F_s$.
>
> If $f(x)(x \geq 0)$ is the restriction of an even function $f_{e}$, then
>
> $$
> \mathcal{F}_{c}(f)(\omega)=\mathcal{F}\left(f_{e}\right)(\omega) \text { for all } \omega \geq 0
> $$
>
> If $f(x)(x \geq 0)$ is the restriction of an odd function $f_{o}$, then
>
> $$
> \mathcal{F}_{s}(f)(\omega)=i \mathcal{F}\left(f_{o}\right)(\omega) \text { for all } \omega \geq 0
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.6 The Fourier Cosine and Sine Transforms.md
title: Linearity of Fourier Cosine and Sine Transforms
body:
> [!theorem|479b74a3-faee-5858-b132-1649beebffb5.local at=3492ceca-619d-574b-a8f9-b8d293550e6b] Linearity of Fourier Cosine and Sine Transforms
> For $\omega\geq0$, use $\mathcal F_c f(\omega)=\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_0^\infty f(x)\cos(\omega x)\,dx$ and $\mathcal F_s f(\omega)=\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_0^\infty f(x)\sin(\omega x)\,dx$. Assume $f,g\in L^1(0,\infty)$.
>
> If $f$ and $g$ are functions and $a$ and $b$ are numbers, then
>
> $$
> \mathcal{F}_{c}(a f+b g)=a \mathcal{F}_{c}(f)+b \mathcal{F}_{c}(g),
> $$
>
> and
>
> $$
> \mathcal{F}_{s}(a f+b g)=a \mathcal{F}_{s}(f)+b \mathcal{F}_{s}(g) .
> $$

path: Chapter 08 The Fourier Transform and Its Applications/8.6 The Fourier Cosine and Sine Transforms.md
title: Fourier Cosine and Sine Transforms of Derivatives
body:
> [!theorem|61e4b0c7-57c0-551a-8159-0fc24202de92.local at=610f5238-f155-589b-98f4-c03685deb301] Fourier Cosine and Sine Transforms of Derivatives
> For $\omega\geq0$, use $\mathcal F_c f(\omega)=\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_0^\infty f(x)\cos(\omega x)\,dx$ and $\mathcal F_s f(\omega)=\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_0^\infty f(x)\sin(\omega x)\,dx$. Assume the functions and derivatives used below are integrable on $(0,\infty)$, the lower derivatives are locally absolutely continuous, and the displayed endpoint values exist.
>
> Suppose that $f(x) \rightarrow 0$ as $x \rightarrow \infty$; then
>
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> & \mathcal{F}_{c}\left(f^{\prime}\right)=\omega \mathcal{F}_{s}(f)-\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} f(0), \\
> & \mathcal{F}_{s}\left(f^{\prime}\right)=-\omega \mathcal{F}_{c}(f) .
> \end{aligned}
> $$
>
> If in addition $f^{\prime}(x) \rightarrow 0$ as $x \rightarrow \infty$, then
>
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> & \mathcal{F}_{c}\left(f^{\prime \prime}\right)=-\omega^{2} \mathcal{F}_{c}(f)-\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} f^{\prime}(0) \\
> & \mathcal{F}_{s}\left(f^{\prime \prime}\right)=-\omega^{2} \mathcal{F}_{s}(f)+\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \omega f(0)
> \end{aligned}
> $$

title: Frequency Derivatives of Fourier Cosine and Sine Transforms
body:
> [!theorem|23d86484-a477-5269-825f-188cf3802e31.local at=7769b35b-5c0d-5cfa-86f2-28d3c3aaedcd] Frequency Derivatives of Fourier Cosine and Sine Transforms
> For $\omega\geq0$, use $\mathcal F_c f(\omega)=\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_0^\infty f(x)\cos(\omega x)\,dx$ and $\mathcal F_s f(\omega)=\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_0^\infty f(x)\sin(\omega x)\,dx$. Assume $f$ and $xf$ are integrable on $(0,\infty)$.
>
> We have
>
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> & \mathcal{F}_{c}(x f(x))=\frac{d}{d \omega} \mathcal{F}_{s}(f(x)) \\
> & \mathcal{F}_{s}(x f(x))=-\frac{d}{d \omega} \mathcal{F}_{c}(f(x))
> \end{aligned}
> $$

path: Chapter 09 The Laplace and Hankel Transforms with Applications/9.1 The Laplace Transform.md
title: One-Sided Laplace Transform
body:
> [!definition|b9229dbe-41fd-56e8-be6f-4f260e3f4008.local at=6daf84c8-5a7e-5cae-afd2-aa1343710d2b] One-Sided Laplace Transform
> For a locally integrable function $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb C$, its one-sided Laplace transform is
>
> $$
> F(s)=\mathcal Lf(s)=\int_0^\infty f(t)e^{-st}\,dt
> $$
>
> where the improper integral converges. The parameter $s$ may be real or complex; absolute convergence holds in the right half-plane specified by an exponential growth bound.

path: Chapter 09 The Laplace and Hankel Transforms with Applications/9.1 The Laplace Transform.md
title: Global Exponential Bound on the Positive Half-Line
body:
> [!definition|9f1b84c9-6029-5529-bca1-cb463addb25a.local at=abe4fc0d-2f18-5027-9c50-28ca06c1962a] Global Exponential Bound on the Positive Half-Line
> A function $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb C$ satisfies a global exponential bound if there are constants $M>0$ and $a>0$ such that $|f(t)|\leq Me^{at}$ for every $t\geq0$.

path: Chapter 09 The Laplace and Hankel Transforms with Applications/9.1 The Laplace Transform.md
title: Existence of the Laplace Transform under an Exponential Bound
body:
> [!theorem|e4f15047-1a89-56ba-a366-4da977816f96.local at=6abac71b-f0a9-5637-9140-8754976c1d5d] Existence of the Laplace Transform under an Exponential Bound
> Write $\mathcal Lf(s)=\int_0^\infty f(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ for the one-sided Laplace transform.
>
> If $f$ is piecewise continuous on every bounded subinterval of $[0,\infty)$ and $|f(t)|\leq Me^{at}$ for constants $M>0$ and real $a$, then $\mathcal Lf(s)$ converges absolutely for every complex $s$ with $\operatorname{Re}s>a$.

path: Chapter 09 The Laplace and Hankel Transforms with Applications/9.1 The Laplace Transform.md
title: Linearity of the One-Sided Laplace Transform
body:
> [!theorem|c06973b1-0111-5f40-ac1e-b83269e28a8a.local at=a6e0737b-3255-5f46-aa18-76c15ffbea45] Linearity of the One-Sided Laplace Transform
> Write $\mathcal Lf(s)=\int_0^\infty f(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ for the one-sided Laplace transform.
>
> For constants $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$ and functions $f,g$ whose transforms converge at $s$,
>
> $$
> \mathcal L(\alpha f+\beta g)(s)=\alpha\mathcal Lf(s)+\beta\mathcal Lg(s).
> $$

path: Chapter 09 The Laplace and Hankel Transforms with Applications/9.1 The Laplace Transform.md
title: Laplace Transforms of Ordinary Derivatives
body:
> [!theorem|f525c8b5-a9ac-5106-9edb-4c1f124074f4.local at=fe4d9a46-eb30-5c99-a5a8-0f69a8cfa2eb] Laplace Transforms of Ordinary Derivatives
> Write $\mathcal Lf(s)=\int_0^\infty f(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ for the one-sided Laplace transform.
>
> Let $n\geq1$ be an integer. Evaluate all transforms at real $s$ larger than the exponential growth rates of the functions involved. Derivatives at zero are right derivatives.
>
> (i) Suppose that $f$ is continuous on $[0, \infty)$ and of exponential order with a common bound $Me^{at}$. Suppose further that $f^{\prime}$ is piecewise continuous on $[0, \infty)$ and of exponential order. Then
>
> $$
> \mathcal{L}\left(f^{\prime}\right)=s \mathcal{L}(f)-f(0)
> $$
>
> (ii) More generally, if $f, f^{\prime}, \ldots, f^{(n-1)}$ are continuous on $[0, \infty)$ and of exponential order with a common bound $Me^{at}$, and $f^{(n)}$ is piecewise continuous on $[0, \infty)$ and of exponential order, then
>
> $$
> \mathcal{L}\left(f^{(n)}\right)=s^{n} \mathcal{L}(f)-s^{n-1} f(0)-s^{n-2} f^{\prime}(0)-\cdots-f^{(n-1)}(0)
> $$

path: Chapter 09 The Laplace and Hankel Transforms with Applications/9.1 The Laplace Transform.md
title: Differentiating a Laplace Transform by Multiplying by Powers of Time
body:
> [!theorem|13aabdbc-dba9-531a-9b23-053cce0dc9ce.local at=9480f161-e76f-52eb-911c-1531dd405b21] Differentiating a Laplace Transform by Multiplying by Powers of Time
> Write $\mathcal Lf(s)=\int_0^\infty f(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ for the one-sided Laplace transform.
>
> Assume $|f(t)|\leq Me^{at}$ on $[0,\infty)$, take $s>a$, and let $n$ be a nonnegative integer.
>
> (i) Suppose $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous and of exponential order. Then
>
> $$
> \mathcal{L}(t f(t))(s)=-\frac{d}{d s} \mathcal{L}(f)(s)
> $$
>
> (ii) In general, if $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous and of exponential order, then
>
> $$
> \mathcal{L}\left(t^{n} f(t)\right)=(-1)^{n} \frac{d^{n}}{d s^{n}} \mathcal{L}(f)(s)
> $$

path: Chapter 09 The Laplace and Hankel Transforms with Applications/9.1 The Laplace Transform.md
title: Exponential Multiplication and Frequency Shifts of the Laplace Transform
body:
> [!theorem|675e2821-a2b3-5efe-92ec-83d7bd866f90.local at=92279ffe-1f63-5248-a326-a14e135421db] Exponential Multiplication and Frequency Shifts of the Laplace Transform
> Write $\mathcal Lf(s)=\int_0^\infty f(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ for the one-sided Laplace transform.
>
> Let $f$ be piecewise continuous on bounded intervals of $[0,\infty)$, with $|f(t)|\leq Me^{at}$. For real $\alpha$ and $s>a+\alpha$,
>
> $$
> \mathcal L(e^{\alpha t}f(t))(s)=F(s-\alpha),\qquad F(s)=\mathcal Lf(s).
> $$

path: Chapter 09 The Laplace and Hankel Transforms with Applications/9.1 The Laplace Transform.md
title: Bromwich Inversion Formula for the One-Sided Laplace Transform
body:
> [!equation|4c56c8f4-d1a7-5497-b916-2b44976dad76.local at=63100233-c082-54d0-a352-0c7721ac3cf8] Bromwich Inversion Formula for the One-Sided Laplace Transform
> Let $f$ be piecewise smooth on bounded subintervals of $[0,\infty)$ and satisfy $|f(t)|\leq Me^{at}$. Define $\mathcal Lf(z)=\int_0^\infty f(t)e^{-zt}\,dt$ for $\operatorname{Re}z>a$. For $t>0$ and any real $b>a$,
>
> $$
> \frac{f(t+)+f(t-)}{2}=\lim _{R \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{2 \pi i} \int_{b-i R}^{b+i R} \mathcal{L}(f)(z) e^{z t} d z
> $$

path: Chapter 09 The Laplace and Hankel Transforms with Applications/9.2 Further Properties of the Laplace Transform.md
title: Causal Time Delay in the One-Sided Laplace Transform
body:
> [!theorem|63bfac33-dcc2-5db8-8768-4c1b04c5fcd5.local at=02ea2f7f-2e27-57f8-9be9-30593f719031] Causal Time Delay in the One-Sided Laplace Transform
> Write $\mathcal Lf(s)=\int_0^\infty f(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ for the one-sided Laplace transform.
>
> Let $a>0$, let $\mathcal U_0(t)=0$ for $t<0$ and $1$ for $t\geq0$, and suppose $F(s)=\mathcal Lf(s)$ converges. Define the delayed function to be zero for $t<a$. Then
>
> $$
> \mathcal L\!\left(\mathcal U_0(t-a)f(t-a)\right)(s)=e^{-as}F(s).
> $$

path: Chapter 09 The Laplace and Hankel Transforms with Applications/9.2 Further Properties of the Laplace Transform.md
title: Causal Convolution on the Positive Half-Line
body:
> [!definition|8f9d61fa-5533-5e73-9f56-a19583ce2300.local at=25d71684-89c7-59ba-a2fb-af40888316c9] Causal Convolution on the Positive Half-Line
> For piecewise continuous functions $f,g:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb C$, their causal convolution is
>
> $$
> (f*g)(t)=\int_0^t f(t-\tau)g(\tau)\,d\tau,\qquad t\geq0.
> $$

path: Chapter 09 The Laplace and Hankel Transforms with Applications/9.2 Further Properties of the Laplace Transform.md
title: Laplace Transform of a Causal Convolution
body:
> [!theorem|a8a05283-149f-5ec1-b9df-f1a4eb92aee1.local at=616ada6f-378a-5753-8ddf-a2f3fca4f1e6] Laplace Transform of a Causal Convolution
> Write $\mathcal Lf(s)=\int_0^\infty f(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ for the one-sided Laplace transform.
>
> Let $f,g$ be piecewise continuous on bounded intervals, with exponential bounds $|f(t)|\leq M_fe^{at}$ and $|g(t)|\leq M_ge^{bt}$. For $s>\max(a,b)$ and $(f*g)(t)=\int_0^t f(t-\tau)g(\tau)\,d\tau$,
>
> $$
> \mathcal L(f*g)(s)=\mathcal Lf(s)\,\mathcal Lg(s).
> $$

path: Chapter 09 The Laplace and Hankel Transforms with Applications/9.3 The Laplace Transform Method.md
title: Partial Laplace Transform in Time
body:
> [!definition|514faa66-dea5-5c0e-b4d9-b0a4b5a7ea32.local at=a5854b0d-e10b-54ca-8d7d-f28911c47c91] Partial Laplace Transform in Time
> The Laplace transform of $u(x, t)$ with respect to the variable $t$ is
>
> $$
> \mathcal{L}(u(x, t))(s)=U(x, s)=\int_{0}^{\infty} u(x, t) e^{-s t} d t
> $$
>
>
>
> The integral is evaluated where it converges, with $x$ held fixed.

path: Chapter 09 The Laplace and Hankel Transforms with Applications/9.3 The Laplace Transform Method.md
title: Time and Spatial Derivatives under the Partial Laplace Transform
body:
> [!property|399e8cfd-e2cb-5f85-b518-583e2608850d.local at=788ab6be-77eb-5c0c-a1b1-9eaf7019bab3] Time and Spatial Derivatives under the Partial Laplace Transform
> Let $U(x,s)=\int_0^\infty u(x,t)e^{-st}\,dt$. Assume the required time derivatives are piecewise continuous, $u$ and $u_t$ are continuous at the time endpoint, and the functions have exponential bounds below $s$. For spatial differentiation, assume the derivatives exist and have an integrable dominating function after multiplication by $e^{-st}$ locally in $x$. Then
>
> $$
> \mathcal{L}\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\right)=s U(x, s)-u(x, 0)
> $$
>
> and
>
> $$
> \mathcal{L}\left(\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial t^{2}}\right)=s^{2} U(x, s)-s u(x, 0)-\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}(x, 0)
> $$
>
> Keeping in mind that we are taking the Laplace transform with respect to $t$, we also have
>
> $$
> \mathcal{L}\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)=\frac{d U}{d x}(x, s),
> $$
>
> and
>
> $$
> \mathcal{L}\left(\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial x^{2}}\right)=\frac{d^{2} U}{d x^{2}}(x, s)
> $$

path: Chapter 09 The Laplace and Hankel Transforms with Applications/9.4 The Hankel Transform with Applications.md
title: Hankel Transform of Nonnegative Order
body:
> [!definition|b48a9f4a-3400-57df-8ff2-3eeb92b83146.local at=ee41df9f-d485-5be9-8726-a8ea110b03e7] Hankel Transform of Nonnegative Order
> Suppose that $f(x)$ is defined for all $x \geq 0$. The Hankel transform of order $\nu \geq 0$ of $f(x)$ is given by
>
> $$
> \mathcal{H}_{\nu}(f)(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) J_{\nu}(s x) x d x, \quad s \geq 0
> $$
>
> where $J_{\nu}$ is the Bessel function of the first kind of order $\nu$. 
>
> The integral is understood wherever it converges.

path: Chapter 09 The Laplace and Hankel Transforms with Applications/9.4 The Hankel Transform with Applications.md
title: Self-Inversion of the Hankel Transform
body:
> [!property|2169c6d6-8158-5aea-bb2e-9d3208b02910.local at=f2b86664-9a3f-5ec0-be6d-aa9e60b84377] Self-Inversion of the Hankel Transform
> For $\nu\geq0$, the transform $\mathcal H_\nu f(s)=\int_0^\infty f(x)J_\nu(sx)x\,dx$ extends to a unitary involution on $L^2((0,\infty),x\,dx)$:
>
> $$
> \mathcal H_\nu(\mathcal H_\nu f)=f.
> $$
>
> The equality is in the weighted $L^2$ sense; pointwise use of the iterated integrals requires additional convergence hypotheses.

path: Chapter 09 The Laplace and Hankel Transforms with Applications/9.4 The Hankel Transform with Applications.md
title: Hankel Transforms of First Derivatives and the Radial Laplacian
body:
> [!property|47710a13-e85e-55f2-9bad-b11d1a5c74c7.local at=f7827811-0a71-51e2-9ae5-721560f0f038] Hankel Transforms of First Derivatives and the Radial Laplacian
> Write $\mathcal H_\nu f(s)=\int_0^\infty f(x)J_\nu(sx)x\,dx$. For $s>0$, assume the displayed integrals converge and integration by parts is valid. The boundary terms $xf(x)J_1(sx)$ vanish at both endpoints for the first formula; $xf(x)J_0(sx)$ vanish for the second; and $xf\,J_1(sx)$ and $xf^{\prime}(x)J_0(sx)$ vanish for the third. For example, smooth functions compactly supported inside $(0,\infty)$ satisfy these requirements.
>
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> -s \mathcal{H}_{0}(f)(s) & =\mathcal{H}_{1}\left(f^{\prime}\right)(s) \\
> \mathcal{H}_{0}\left(f^{\prime}+\frac{1}{x} f\right)(s) & =s \mathcal{H}_{1}(f)(s) \\
> \mathcal{H}_{0}\left(f^{\prime \prime}+\frac{1}{x} f^{\prime}\right)(s) & =-s^{2} \mathcal{H}_{0}(f)(s)
> \end{aligned}
> $$

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.1 Linear Ordinary Differential Equations.md
title: Linear Ordinary Differential Equation in Standard Form
body:
> [!definition|7db2073f-ab58-5437-aca4-16c500070e9a.local at=2f81238a-9d7d-51d8-8141-31dc3cf7aefe] Linear Ordinary Differential Equation in Standard Form
> An ordinary differential equation is an equation that involves an unknown function $y$ and its derivatives $y^{(j)}$ of order $j$. A linear ordinary differential equation in standard form is an equation
>
> $$
> y^{(n)}+p_{n-1}(x) y^{(n-1)}+\cdots+p_{1}(x) y^{\prime}+p_{0}(x) y=g(x)
> $$
>
> where $n$ is called the order of the equation and $p_j(x)$ and $g(x)$ are given functions of $x$. The expression standard form refers to the fact that the leading coefficient is 1 . A solution of this equation on an interval $I$ is any $n$ times differentiable function $y=y(x)$ satisfying the equation on $I$. The equation is homogeneous if $g(x) \equiv 0$, otherwise it is nonhomogeneous.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.1 Linear Ordinary Differential Equations.md
title: Integrating-Factor Formula for a First-Order Linear ODE
body:
> [!theorem|1fd50e80-c6dd-5663-b76f-62cb76946c6f.local at=fa13fb7f-b377-52f0-b6cd-4b7416cd4085] Integrating-Factor Formula for a First-Order Linear ODE
> Suppose that $p(x)$ and $g(x)$ are continuous on the interval $I$. Then any solution of the first-order linear differential equation
>
> $$
> y^{\prime}+p(x) y=g(x), \quad x \text { in } I,
> $$
>
> is of the form
>
> $$
> y=e^{-\int p(x) d x}\left[C+\int g(x) e^{\int p(x) d x} d x\right]
> $$
>
> where $\int p(x) d x$ represents the same antiderivative of $p(x)$ in both occurrences.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.1 Linear Ordinary Differential Equations.md
title: Wronskian of a Finite Family of Functions
body:
> [!definition|18a292cd-fb05-5a7f-8487-87369bb7350e.local at=f610b10d-92a0-5cb5-9fd7-22daf3013e0b] Wronskian of a Finite Family of Functions
> Let $y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n}$ be $n$ functions with derivatives through order $n-1$ on an interval. The Wronskian $W\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n}\right)$ of these functions is given by the following $n \times n$ determinant:
>
> $$
> W\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n}\right)=\left|\begin{array}{cccc}
> y_{1} & y_{2} & \ldots & y_{n} \\
> y_{1}^{\prime} & y_{2}^{\prime} & \ldots & y_{n}^{\prime} \\
> \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
> y_{1}^{(n-1)} & y_{2}^{(n-1)} & \ldots & y_{n}^{(n-1)}
> \end{array}\right| .
> $$

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.1 Linear Ordinary Differential Equations.md
title: Abel’s Formula for the Wronskian of Linear ODE Solutions
body:
> [!theorem|58d36e0f-23d5-5fc2-a7af-d48845743392.local at=ae61bbfd-6cf0-5838-a0b1-c687acef90cc] Abel’s Formula for the Wronskian of Linear ODE Solutions
> On an interval $I$, consider $L[y]=y^{(n)}+p_{n-1}(x)y^{(n-1)}+\cdots+p_1(x)y^{\prime}+p_0(x)y$, where $n\geq1$ and every coefficient $p_j$ is continuous.
>
> Let $y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n}$ be any $n$ solutions to $L[y]=0$. Then the Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies the first-order differential equation
>
> $$
> W^{\prime}(x)+p_{n-1}(x) W(x)=0 . \quad \text { for } x \text { in } I,
> $$
>
> and hence
>
> $$
> W(x)=C e^{-\int p_{n-1}(x) d x}
> $$
>
> Consequently, either $W(x) \neq 0$ for all $x$ in $I$, or $W(x) \equiv 0$ on $I$.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.1 Linear Ordinary Differential Equations.md
title: Fundamental Solution Sets for Homogeneous Linear ODEs
body:
> [!theorem|db15dfe7-346c-58c1-8951-18bd923b981e.local at=82d9c1c5-dacf-5fa9-9199-7e7854129d88] Fundamental Solution Sets for Homogeneous Linear ODEs
> The homogeneous equation
>
> $$
> y^{(n)}+p_{n-1}(x) y^{(n-1)}+\cdots+p_{1}(x) y^{\prime}+p_{0}(x) y=0 .
> $$
>
> where the coefficient functions $p_{j}(x)$ are all continuous on an interval $I$, has $n$ solutions $y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n}$ with nonvanishing Wronskian on $I$. Furthermore, given any such set $y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots y_{n}$ and any solution $y$, then $y=c_{1} y_{1}+c_{2} y_{2}+ \cdots+c_{n} y_{n}$ for a unique choice of constants $c_{1}, c_{2}, \ldots \ldots c_{n}$. The set of solutions $y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n}$ with nonvanishing Wronskian is called a fundamental set of solutions.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.1 Linear Ordinary Differential Equations.md
title: Superposition of Homogeneous Linear ODE Solutions
body:
> [!theorem|cb200824-c353-579a-9ff0-cd179f9d6e12.local at=7d6b0cc2-3654-54e2-9af8-eac5712a0bcd] Superposition of Homogeneous Linear ODE Solutions
> On an interval $I$, consider $L[y]=y^{(n)}+p_{n-1}(x)y^{(n-1)}+\cdots+p_1(x)y^{\prime}+p_0(x)y$, where $n\geq1$ and every coefficient $p_j$ is continuous.
>
> If $L[u]=L[v]=0$, then $L[cu+dv]=0$ for arbitrary constants $c,d$.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.1 Linear Ordinary Differential Equations.md
title: General Solution of a Nonhomogeneous Linear ODE
body:
> [!theorem|c4e81fe4-f52b-5477-83a1-df188c8bcf6a.local at=fd3850cc-d23a-5891-a840-635cb32dfc87] General Solution of a Nonhomogeneous Linear ODE
> On an interval $I$, consider $L[y]=y^{(n)}+p_{n-1}(x)y^{(n-1)}+\cdots+p_1(x)y^{\prime}+p_0(x)y$, where $n\geq1$ and every coefficient $p_j$ is continuous.
>
> Let $g$ be continuous on $I$ and let $y_p$ be any particular solution of $L[y]=g$. Every solution has the form $y=y_h+y_p$, where $y_h$ is a solution of $L[y_h]=0$. If $y_1,\ldots,y_n$ is a fundamental set for the homogeneous equation, then $y=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jy_j+y_p$ with arbitrary constants $c_j$.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.1 Linear Ordinary Differential Equations.md
title: Existence and Uniqueness for Linear ODE Initial Value Problems
body:
> [!theorem|12d47e51-786c-53e9-a14b-1272ed834ece.local at=f9afdc7a-c723-5527-b50e-5a177b36c12a] Existence and Uniqueness for Linear ODE Initial Value Problems
> On an interval $I$, consider $L[y]=y^{(n)}+p_{n-1}(x)y^{(n-1)}+\cdots+p_1(x)y^{\prime}+p_0(x)y$, where $n\geq1$ and every coefficient $p_j$ is continuous.
>
> If $g$ is continuous on $I$, $x_0\in I$, and $b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1}$ are prescribed constants, then $L[y]=g$ has exactly one solution on $I$ satisfying $y^{(j)}(x_0)=b_j$ for $j=0,\ldots,n-1$.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.1 Linear Ordinary Differential Equations.md
title: Linear Independence of Functions on an Interval
body:
> [!definition|30633ae5-b6c2-5e89-a843-405b3ac75152.local at=9d6c51b1-76b0-5769-85b1-b8cd19af9c8b] Linear Independence of Functions on an Interval
> The functions $f_{1}, f_{2}, \ldots, f_{n}$ defined on an interval $[a, b]$ are said to be linearly independent on $[a, b]$ if the only choice of the constants $c_{1}, c_{2}, \ldots$, $c_{n}$ for which the linear combination $c_{1} f_{1}+c_{2} f_{2}+\cdots+c_{n} f_{n}$ vanishes identically on $[a, b]$ is $c_{1}=c_{2}=\cdots=c_{n}=0$. Otherwise, the functions are said to be linearly dependent.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.1 Linear Ordinary Differential Equations.md
title: Wronskian Criterion for a Fundamental Set of Linear ODE Solutions
body:
> [!theorem|e9b1c9b6-7a98-5fe0-a9b9-a4669d1e18ef.local at=a97cae01-9f6e-56a3-bfed-06e078e1c08f] Wronskian Criterion for a Fundamental Set of Linear ODE Solutions
> On an interval $I$, consider $L[y]=y^{(n)}+p_{n-1}(x)y^{(n-1)}+\cdots+p_1(x)y^{\prime}+p_0(x)y$, where $n\geq1$ and every coefficient $p_j$ is continuous.
>
> Let $y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots y_{n}$ be any $n$ solutions to $L[y]=0$ with coefficients continuous on an interval $I$. The following are equivalent:
> (i) $y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n}$ are linearly independent on $I$;
> (ii) $y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots y_{n}$ form a fundamental set of solutions of $L[y]=0$:
> (iii) $W\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n}\right)\left(x_{0}\right) \neq 0$ for some $x_{0}$ in $I$;
> (iv) $W\left(y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n}\right)(x) \neq 0$ for all $x$ in $I$.

> For $a_ny^{(n)}+\cdots+a_1y^{\prime}+a_0y=0$ with constant coefficients and $a_n\ne0$,
>
> The roots of this equation are called the characteristic roots. For future use, we define the characteristic polynomial
>
> $$
> p(\lambda)=a_{n} \lambda^{n}+a_{n-1} \lambda^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{1} \lambda+a_{0} .
> $$

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.2 Linear Ordinary Differential Equations with Constant Coefficients.md
title: Characteristic-Root Construction for Constant-Coefficient Homogeneous Linear ODEs
body:
> [!rule|d20db426-76e0-56ae-a30c-c4dd6a5f292d.local at=dec31ecc-135b-5e87-983e-541fa27dba48] Characteristic-Root Construction for Constant-Coefficient Homogeneous Linear ODEs
> Let all coefficients $a_j$ be real constants, with $a_n\ne0$. Multiplicities are algebraic multiplicities, and constants in different root contributions are independent.
>
> Consider the equation
>
> $$
> a_{n} y^{(n)}+a_{n-1} y^{(n-1)}+\cdots+a_{1} y^{\prime}+a_{0} y=0
> $$
>
> with characteristic equation
>
> $$
> a_{n} \lambda^{n}+a_{n-1} \lambda^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{1} \lambda+a_{0}=0
> $$
>
> The general real solution of the differential equation is constructed according to the nature of the roots of the characteristic equation as follows.
>
> Case I For each real root $\mu$ of multiplicity $m \geq 1$, we include a linear combination of the form
>
> $$
> c_{1} e^{\mu x}+c_{2} x e^{\mu x}+\cdots+c_{m} x^{m-1}e^{\mu x}
> $$
>
> Case II For each nonreal root $\mu=\alpha+i \beta$ and its complex conjugate $\bar{\mu}=\alpha-i \beta$ of multiplicity $m \geq 1$, we include a linear combination of the form
>
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> & c_{1} e^{\alpha x} \cos \beta x+c_{2} x e^{\alpha x} \cos \beta x+\cdots+c_{m} x^{m-1} e^{\alpha x} \cos \beta x \\
> & \quad+d_{1} e^{\alpha x} \sin \beta x+d_{2} x e^{\alpha x} \sin \beta x+\cdots+d_{m} x^{m-1} e^{\alpha x} \sin \beta x
> \end{aligned}
> $$

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.2 Linear Ordinary Differential Equations with Constant Coefficients.md
title: Real General Solutions of Second-Order Constant-Coefficient Homogeneous ODEs
body:
> [!rule|82e7bb10-ee1c-58b9-a1b4-179d76a3554d.local at=80cec4ea-5d4d-5671-b00d-2a975958e9e0] Real General Solutions of Second-Order Constant-Coefficient Homogeneous ODEs
> Let $a,b,c$ be real constants with $a\ne0$. The constants $c_1,c_2$ below are arbitrary.
>
> Consider the equation
>
> $$
> a y^{\prime \prime}+b y^{\prime}+c y=0
> $$
>
> with characteristic equation
>
> $$
> a \lambda^{2}+b \lambda+c=0
> $$
>
> Let $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ denote the characteristic roots. The general solution y of this differential equation is given by one of the following cases.
> Case I If $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ are distinct real roots, then
>
> $$
> y=c_{1} e^{\lambda_{1} x}+c_{2} e^{\lambda_{2} x}
> $$
>
> Equivalently, write $\lambda_{1}=\frac{-b}{2 a}+\frac{\sqrt{b^{2}-4 a c}}{2 a}=\alpha+\beta$ and $\lambda_{2}=\alpha-\beta$, then
>
> $$
> y=e^{\alpha x}\left(c_{1} \cosh \beta x+c_{2} \sinh \beta x\right) .
> $$
>
> Case II If $\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}$, then
>
> $$
> y=c_{1} e^{\lambda_{1} x}+c_{2} x e^{\lambda_{1} x}
> $$
>
> Case III If $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ are complex conjugate roots with $\lambda_{1}=\alpha+i \beta$, then
>
> $$
> y=c_{1} e^{\alpha x} \cos \beta x+c_{2} e^{\alpha x} \sin \beta x .
> $$

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.2 Linear Ordinary Differential Equations with Constant Coefficients.md
title: Undetermined Coefficients for Second-Order Constant-Coefficient ODEs
body:
> [!procedure|8ee66310-8c6c-5b69-87bb-fd2965628cac.local at=151d6798-685e-5922-8104-417e052e6120] Undetermined Coefficients for Second-Order Constant-Coefficient ODEs
> To find a particular solution of $ay^{\prime\prime}+by^{\prime}+cy=g(x)$, where $a,b,c$ are real constants and $a\ne0$, when
>
> $$
> g(x)=\left(a_{n} x^{n}+a_{n-1} x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{0}\right) e^{\alpha x}\left\{\begin{array}{l}
> \cos \beta x \\
> \sin \beta x
> \end{array}\right.
> $$
>
> we use
>
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> y_{p}= & \left(A_{n} x^{n}+A_{n-1} x^{n-1}+\cdots+A_{0}\right) e^{\alpha x} \cos \beta x \\
> & +\left(B_{n} x^{n}+B_{n-1} x^{n-1}+\cdots+B_{0}\right) e^{\alpha x} \sin \beta x
> \end{aligned}
> $$
>
> provided that no term in the expression of $y_{p}$ is a solution of the associated homogeneous equation. If not, we modify this expression by multiplying by $x$ or $x^{2}$. We use $x$ if the characteristic polynomial of the associated homogeneous equation has distinct roots, and $x^{2}$ if it has a double root.
> Superposition rule If the right side of $ay^{\prime\prime}+by^{\prime}+cy=g(x)$, where $a,b,c$ are real constants and $a\ne0$, is a sum of several different functions of the stated polynomial–exponential–trigonometric form, we use a corresponding sum of terms of the corresponding trial form.

title: Vandermonde Determinant
body:
> [!definition|0fe6cb98-c376-572e-834c-cef1f298e4ac.local at=f9c6be4e-8cae-526b-98b0-c2ae162f781e] Vandermonde Determinant
> Given $n$ numbers $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}, \ldots, \lambda_{n}$, we define the Vandermonde determinant $V\left(\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}, \ldots, \lambda_{n}\right)$ to be
>
> $$
> \left|\begin{array}{cccc}
> 1 & 1 & \ldots & 1 \\
> \lambda_{1} & \lambda_{2} & \ldots & \lambda_{n} \\
> \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
> \lambda_{1}^{n-1} & \lambda_{2}^{n-1} & \ldots & \lambda_{n}^{n-1}
> \end{array}\right|
> $$

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.3 Linear Ordinary Differential Equations with Nonconstant Coefficients.md
title: Reduction of Order for a Second-Order Homogeneous Linear ODE
body:
> [!rule|f272087c-bbd0-5309-a2f3-ce52cf655a7a.local at=ca9cb3db-25df-58e8-b879-5ec5e7e621a5] Reduction of Order for a Second-Order Homogeneous Linear ODE
> Let $p,q$ be continuous on an interval $I$ and let $y_1$ be a solution of $y^{\prime\prime}+p(x)y^{\prime}+q(x)y=0$ that has no zeros on $I$. A linearly independent second solution is
>
> $$
> y_2(x)=y_1(x)\int\frac{e^{-\int p(x)\,dx}}{y_1(x)^2}\,dx.
> $$
>
> Use a fixed antiderivative in the exponential. The formula applies on intervals where $y_1
> e0$; extension across a zero requires a separate argument.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.3 Linear Ordinary Differential Equations with Nonconstant Coefficients.md
title: Variation of Parameters for a Second-Order Linear ODE
body:
> [!rule|8581a96b-e43e-5712-883a-446d14e9edc5.local at=79e898a5-d4a0-5a18-9dc1-7ffbb0360372] Variation of Parameters for a Second-Order Linear ODE
> Assume $p,q,g$ are continuous on an interval $I$, and take a fundamental pair $y_1,y_2$ of the associated homogeneous equation, so their Wronskian is nowhere zero on $I$.
>
> A particular solution of $y^{\prime\prime}+p(x)y^{\prime}+q(x)y=g(x)$ is given by
>
> $$
> y_{p}=y_{1} \int \frac{-y_{2} g(x)}{W\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)} d x+y_{2} \int \frac{y_{1} g(x)}{W\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)} d x
> $$
>
> where $y_{1}$ and $y_{2}$ are linearly independent solutions of $y^{\prime\prime}+p(x)y^{\prime}+q(x)y=0$, and $W\left(y_{1}, y_{2}\right)= y_{1} y_{2}^{\prime}-y_{1}^{\prime} y_{2}$ is the Wronskian of $y_{1}$ and $y_{2}$.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.3 Linear Ordinary Differential Equations with Nonconstant Coefficients.md
title: General Solutions of the Second-Order Cauchy–Euler Equation
body:
> [!rule|ddb62b20-b6b9-5464-af10-4b6d045eb481.local at=eb679021-cd50-5280-861b-e10948fd15ec] General Solutions of the Second-Order Cauchy–Euler Equation
> Work on a connected interval contained in $x>0$ or $x<0$. Constants on the two sides of zero are independent.
>
> Consider $x^2y^{\prime\prime}+\alpha xy^{\prime}+\beta y=0$ with real constants $\alpha,\beta$ and its indicial equation, which we write as
>
> $$
> r^{2}+(\alpha-1) r+\beta=0
> $$
>
> Let $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ denote the indicial roots. The general solution $y$ of this equation is given by the following cases.
> Case I If $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ are distinct real roots, then
>
> $$
> y=c_{1}|x|^{r_{1}}+c_{2}|x|^{r_{2}}
> $$
>
> Case II If $r_{1}=r_{2}$, then
>
> $$
> y=\left(c_{1}+c_{2} \ln |x|\right)|x|^{r_{1}}
> $$
>
> Case III If $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ are complex conjugate roots with $r_{1}=a+i b$, then
>
> $$
> y=|x|^{a}\left[c_{1} \cos (b \ln |x|)+c_{2} \sin (b \ln |x|)\right]
> $$
>
> Clearly when $x>0$ we may drop the absolute values.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.4 The Power Series Method, Part I.md
title: Power Series Centered at a Real Point
body:
> [!definition|cbf289c6-b5df-518b-b621-db258f675bd6.local at=9fe1ef30-cc04-588a-abc1-919ccafce5b5] Power Series Centered at a Real Point
> A power series is a series of the form
>
> $$
> \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} a_{m}(x-a)^{m}=a_{0}+a_{1}(x-a)+a_{2}(x-a)^{2}+\cdots,
> $$
>
> where $a, a_{0}, a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ are constants and $x$ is a variable. The series is said to be centered at $a$. If the series is centered at $a=0$, it takes on the simpler form
>
> $$
> \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} a_{m} x^{m}=a_{0}+a_{1} x+a_{2} x^{2}+\cdots
> $$

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.4 The Power Series Method, Part I.md
title: Linear Combinations of Power Series with a Common Center
body:
> [!property|f3a33803-a80f-5388-85fa-9b47a1cf80aa.local at=ec80d941-813c-53a4-a67e-cb433b51a3c6] Linear Combinations of Power Series with a Common Center
> Consider the power series representations
>
> $$
> f(x)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty} a_{m}(x-a)^{m} \quad \text { and } \quad g(x)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty} b_{m}(x-a)^{m},
> $$
>
> with common center at $a$ and radii of convergence $R_{1}>0$ and $R_{2}>0$, respectively. Then it is not difficult to show that for any real numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$, we have
>
> $$
> \alpha f(x)+\beta g(x)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\left(\alpha a_{m}+\beta b_{m}\right)(x-a)^{m}
> $$
>
>
>
> The equality holds for $|x-a|<\min(R_1,R_2)$.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.4 The Power Series Method, Part I.md
title: Uniqueness of Coefficients in a Convergent Power Series
body:
> [!property|55d973e6-e5a8-5f66-9ddd-46efc46e43f7.local at=ff821645-d23f-5da1-a423-585c58853692] Uniqueness of Coefficients in a Convergent Power Series
> Suppose $f(x)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty} a_{m}(x-a)^{m}$ and $g(x)= \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} b_{m}(x-a)^{m}$, where both series have positive radii of convergence. If $f(x)=g(x)$ for all $x$ in an open interval containing $a$, then $a_{m}=b_{m}$ for all $m$. In other words, a power series representation is unique.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.4 The Power Series Method, Part I.md
title: Quotients of Real Analytic Functions with Nonzero Denominator

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.5 The Power Series Method, Part II.md
title: Analytic Solutions of a Linear ODE at an Ordinary Point
body:
> [!theorem] Analytic Solutions of a Linear ODE at an Ordinary Point
> Suppose that the functions $p(x), q(x)$, and $g(x)$ have power series expansions at $x=a$ with positive radii of convergence; then any solution of
>
> $$
> y^{\prime \prime}+p(x) y^{\prime}+q(x) y=g(x)
> $$
>
> has a power series expansion at $x=a$. Thus any solution $y$ can be expressed as a power series centered at $a$,
>
> $$
> y=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty} a_{m}(x-a)^{m}
> $$
>
> Moreover, the radius of convergence of this power series is at least as large as the minimum of the radii of convergence of $p, q$, and $g$.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.5 The Power Series Method, Part II.md
title: Ordinary Point of an Analytic Linear ODE
body:
> [!definition] Ordinary Point of an Analytic Linear ODE
> When $p(x), q(x)$, and $g(x)$ have power series expansions with positive radius of convergence at $x=a$, the point $a$ is called an ordinary point for the normalized equation $y^{\prime\prime}+p(x)y^{\prime}+q(x)y=g(x)$.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.6 The Method of Frobenius.md
title: Regular Singular Point of a Second-Order Linear ODE
body:
> [!definition|4310fc90-62ef-5896-a361-26ea63c28f90.local at=21cf724c-a744-50f3-a019-c9fa29c80ce8] Regular Singular Point of a Second-Order Linear ODE
> Suppose that $x=0$ is a singular point of the equation
>
> $$
> y^{\prime \prime}+p(x) y^{\prime}+q(x) y=0
> $$
>
> We say that $x=0$ is a regular singular point of the equation if both of the functions $x p(x)$ and $x^{2} q(x)$ have power series expansions at $x=0$.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.6 The Method of Frobenius.md
title: Frobenius Series about the Origin
body:
> [!definition|fe802857-e36c-5f71-a6c2-6811da025301.local at=2f51e866-9c22-53d2-abfd-ab33ef363c92] Frobenius Series about the Origin
> For $x>0$ and exponent $r$,
>
> $$
> y=x^{r}\left(a_{0}+a_{1} x+a_{2} x^{2}+\cdots\right)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty} a_{m} x^{r+m}
> $$
>
> with $a_{0} \neq 0$. The analytic power-series factor is required to have positive radius of convergence.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.6 The Method of Frobenius.md
title: First Frobenius Solution at a Regular Singular Point
body:
> [!theorem|4c10f688-34c5-5087-9fb3-d3a4eb8115f3.local at=0df8f924-a00e-566d-b7a8-9531941750cf] First Frobenius Solution at a Regular Singular Point
> Let $P(x)=xp(x)$ and $Q(x)=x^2q(x)$ extend analytically to $x=0$, with power series converging for $|x|<R$, $R>0$. Write $p_0=P(0)$ and $q_0=Q(0)$. Treat the intervals $0<x<R$ and $-R<x<0$ separately; for complex exponents use $|x|^r=e^{r\ln|x|}$.
>
> If $x=0$ is a regular singular point of the equation
>
> $$
> y^{\prime \prime}+p(x) y^{\prime}+q(x) y=0 .
> $$
>
> then one solution is of the form
>
> $$
> y_{1}=|x|^{r_{1}}\left(a_{0}+a_{1} x+a_{2} x^{2}+\cdots\right) . \quad a_{0} \neq 0
> $$
>
> where $r_{1}$ is a root of $r(r-1)+p_0r+q_0=0$. with the convention that $r_{1}$ is the larger of the two roots when both roots are real.
>
>
>
> The analytic factor converges for $|x|<R$.

path: Chapter 10 Ordinary Differential Equations Review of Concepts and Methods/10.6 The Method of Frobenius.md
title: Frobenius Fundamental Solutions and Logarithmic Resonance
body:
> [!theorem|a6cbc45d-0dc2-5f2c-abd7-3b407939e739.local at=006d8e52-423a-5e14-afc1-429cb581b13c] Frobenius Fundamental Solutions and Logarithmic Resonance
> Let $P(x)=xp(x)$ and $Q(x)=x^2q(x)$ be analytic for $|x|<R$, with $R>0$. Set $p_0=P(0)$, $q_0=Q(0)$, and let $r_1,r_2$ solve $r(r-1)+p_0r+q_0=0$, ordered $r_1\geq r_2$ if real. Work separately on either side of zero; interpret complex powers as $|x|^r=e^{r\ln|x|}$. All analytic series factors below converge for $|x|<R$.
>
> Suppose that $x=0$ is a regular singular point of the differential equation
>
> $$
> y^{\prime \prime}+p(x) y^{\prime}+q(x) y=0 .
> $$
>
> and let $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ denote the indicial roots. The differential equation has two linearly independent solutions $y_{1}$ and $y_{2}$, as we now describe.
> Case 1. If $r_{1}-r_{2}$ is not an integer. then
>
> $$
> y_{1}=|x|^{r_{1}} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} a_{m} x^{m} . \quad y_{2}=|x|^{r_{2}} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} b_{m} x^{m} . \quad a_{0} \neq 0 \text { and } b_{0} \neq 0 .
> $$
>
> Case 2. If $r=r_{1}=r_{2}$, then
>
> $$
> y_{1}=|x|^{r} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} a_{m} x^{m}, \quad y_{2}=y_{1} \ln |x|+|x|^{r} \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} b_{m} x^{m} . \quad a_{0} \neq 0 .
> $$
>
> Case 3. If $r_{1}-r_{2}$ is a positive integer, with $r_{1} \geq r_{2}$, then
>
> $$
> y_{1}=|x|^{r_{1}} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} a_{m} x^{m}, \quad y_{2}=k y_{1} \ln |x|+|x|^{r_{2}} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} b_{m} x^{m} .
> $$
>
> where $a_{0} \neq 0, b_{0} \neq 0$ ( $k$ may or may not be 0 ).

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.1 Partial Differential Equations in Physics and Engineering.md
title: Laplacian in Euclidean coordinates
body:
> [!definition] Laplacian in Euclidean coordinates
> For a twice continuously differentiable scalar function $u$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$, its Laplacian is
> $$
> \Delta u=\nabla^2u=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x_j^2}.
> $$

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.1 Partial Differential Equations in Physics and Engineering.md
title: Order and linearity of a partial differential equation
body:
> [!definition] Order and linearity of a partial differential equation
> The order of a partial differential equation is the highest derivative order appearing in it. A PDE is linear if the unknown function and its partial derivatives occur only to the first degree, with at most one such factor in each term; their coefficients may depend on the independent variables but not on the unknown function. Otherwise the equation is nonlinear.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.1 Partial Differential Equations in Physics and Engineering.md
title: Superposition principle for homogeneous linear partial differential equations
body:
> [!theorem] Superposition principle for homogeneous linear partial differential equations
> If $u_1$ and $u_2$ solve the same homogeneous linear partial differential equation on a common domain, then $c_1u_1+c_2u_2$ also solves it for any constants $c_1,c_2$. If both solutions satisfy the same homogeneous linear boundary or initial condition, their linear combination satisfies that condition as well.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.10 Neumann and Robin Conditions.md
title: Separated harmonic functions in a rectangle with zero values on opposite sides
body:
> [!proposition|69421399-4f98-5528-9247-fac030cee062.local at=9b6c5129-a47d-56f3-9124-4ea89a4c631b] Separated harmonic functions in a rectangle with zero values on opposite sides
> If a nonzero function $\phi(x, y)=X(x) Y(y)$ is a product solution of $\phi_{xx}+\phi_{yy}=0$ on $0<x<a$, $0<y<b$, where $a,b>0$, with $\phi(0,y)=\phi(a,y)=0$, then
>
> $$
> \phi(x, y)=\phi_{m}(x, y)=\sin \frac{m \pi}{a} x\left(A_{m} \cosh \frac{m \pi}{a} y+B_{m} \sinh \frac{m \pi}{a} y\right)
> $$
>
> where $m=1,2, \ldots$, and $A_{m}$ and $B_{m}$ are arbitrary constants.
> In some applications, it will be convenient to write the same solution in the form
>
> $$
> \phi_{m}(x, y)=\sin \frac{m \pi}{a} x\left(\alpha_{m} \cosh \frac{m \pi}{a}(\beta-y)+\beta_{m} \sinh \frac{m \pi}{a}(\beta-y)\right),
> $$
>
> where $\beta$ is a fixed number. The two displayed forms are equivalent, as can be verified by expressing the hyperbolic cosine and sine in terms of the exponential function.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.10 Neumann and Robin Conditions.md
title: Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin boundary conditions
body:
> [!definition|a4e32151-7186-55cb-85c7-7222899d6f7b.local at=235d7f1f-5602-5e71-8a86-808ae828807c] Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin boundary conditions
> For a scalar field $u$ and the outward unit normal $n$ to a boundary:
>
> A Dirichlet condition specifies $u=h$.
>
> A Neumann condition specifies $\partial u/\partial n=h$.
>
> A generalized Robin condition specifies $\alpha u+\beta\,\partial u/\partial n=h$, with prescribed coefficients $\alpha,\beta$ not both zero. It includes the Dirichlet case $\beta=0$ and the Neumann case $\alpha=0$. When $\beta\ne0$, it can be normalized to $\partial u/\partial n+(\alpha/\beta)u=h/\beta$.
>
> For a rectangle, the outward normal derivatives on the left, right, bottom, and top sides are respectively $-u_x$, $u_x$, $-u_y$, and $u_y$.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.11 The Maximum Principle.md
title: Maximum–minimum principle for the one-dimensional heat equation
body:
> [!theorem|e3151e58-4abe-51b8-994f-5bf8715928e5.local at=3ed9a45d-0de1-5b88-855b-c847ceddd982] Maximum–minimum principle for the one-dimensional heat equation
> Let $L,c,T>0$ and let $u$ be continuous on $[0,L]\times[0,T]$, with $u_t,u_x,u_{xx}$ continuous where $0<x<L$ and $0<t\le T$. Suppose $u_t=c^2u_{xx}$ there. If constants $m,M$ bound the initial and endpoint data,
> $$
> m\le u(x,0)\le M,\qquad m\le u(0,t),u(L,t)\le M,
> $$
> for $0\le x\le L$ and $0\le t\le T$, then
> $$
> m\le u(x,t)\le M\qquad(0\le x\le L,\ 0\le t\le T).
> $$
> If the same hypotheses and bounds hold on every finite time interval, the conclusion holds for all $t\ge0$.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.11 The Maximum Principle.md
title: Maximum–minimum principle for harmonic functions on a rectangle
body:
> [!theorem|886b3dfe-9e5b-5024-a65a-175b637d5e91.local at=103584d6-0646-5778-bbb8-550810cc13e5] Maximum–minimum principle for harmonic functions on a rectangle
> Let $a,b>0$, $R=(0,a)\times(0,b)$, and let $u\in C^2(R)\cap C(\overline R)$ satisfy $u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0$ in $R$. If $m\le u\le M$ on the boundary $\partial R$, then $m\le u\le M$ throughout $\overline R$.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.11 The Maximum Principle.md
title: Quadratic perturbation for the heat-equation maximum principle
body:
> [!lemma|6bb9824e-3ee6-5902-8dab-a1b393dc42ed.local at=e415ff92-81fa-5027-802b-2b56f8bd944e] Quadratic perturbation for the heat-equation maximum principle
> Let $L,c,T>0$ and $R_T=[0,L]\times[0,T]$. Let $u$ be continuous on $R_T$, solve $u_t=c^2u_{xx}$ classically for $0<x<L$, $0<t\le T$, and satisfy $u\le M$ on $x=0$, $x=L$ and $t=0$. For any positive integer $n$, set $v(x,t)=u(x,t)+x^2/n$. Then:
>
> (i) $v_t<c^2v_{xx}$ for $0<x<L$, $0<t\le T$.
>
> (ii) The maximum of $v$ on $R_T$ occurs on the initial or lateral boundary.
>
> (iii) $v(x,t)\le M+L^2/n$ everywhere on $R_T$.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.2 Modeling: Vibrating Strings and the Wave Equation.md
title: Wave equation for small transverse vibrations of a taut string
body:
> [!equation] Wave equation for small transverse vibrations of a taut string
> For a perfectly elastic homogeneous string with constant tension $\tau>0$ and mass per unit length $\rho>0$, small transverse displacement $u(x,t)$ and small slope satisfy, when external forces and bending resistance are neglected,
> $$
> u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx},\qquad c^2=\frac{\tau}{\rho}.
> $$

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.2 Modeling: Vibrating Strings and the Wave Equation.md
title: Forced transverse wave equation for a taut string
body:
> [!equation] Forced transverse wave equation for a taut string
> For a homogeneous string under constant tension $\tau>0$, with mass per unit length $\rho>0$, negligible bending resistance and small transverse displacement and slope, an applied transverse force per unit length $F(x,t)$ gives
> $$
> u_{tt}=\frac{\tau}{\rho}u_{xx}+\frac{F(x,t)}{\rho}.
> $$
> Here $u$ is the transverse displacement and $F$ is positive in the positive $u$ direction.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.3 Solution of the One Dimensional Wave Equation: The Method of Separation of Variables.md
title: Fourier sine series solution of the fixed-end wave equation
body:
> [!equation|42a9293d-9ab5-5a0a-9e9d-58f153c669c5.local at=bf1ea29d-8e6a-5e79-800a-03c4a311111e] Fourier sine series solution of the fixed-end wave equation
> Let $L,c>0$. With initial data whose odd $2L$-periodic extensions satisfy $f^*\in C^2$ and $g^*\in C^1$, the solution of the one dimensional wave equation
>
> $$
> \frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial t^{2}}=c^{2} \frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial x^{2}}, \quad 0<x<L, t>0
> $$
>
> with boundary conditions
>
> $$
> u(0, t)=0 \quad \text { and } \quad u(L, t)=0 \text { for all } t>0
> $$
>
> and initial conditions
>
> $$
> u(x, 0)=f(x) \text { and } \frac{\partial u}{\partial t}(x, 0)=g(x) \text { for } 0<x<L
> $$
>
> is
>
> $$
> u(x, t)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \sin \frac{n \pi}{L} x\left(b_{n} \cos \lambda_{n} t+b_{n}^{*} \sin \lambda_{n} t\right)
> $$
>
> where
> $\quad b_{n}=\frac{2}{L} \int_{0}^{L} f(x) \sin \frac{n \pi}{L} x d x, \quad b_{n}^{*}=\frac{2}{c n \pi} \int_{0}^{L} g(x) \sin \frac{n \pi}{L} x d x$, and
>
> $$
> \lambda_{n}=c \frac{n \pi}{L}, \quad n=1,2, \ldots
> $$

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.3 Solution of the One Dimensional Wave Equation: The Method of Separation of Variables.md
title: Normal modes and fundamental frequency of a fixed-end string
body:
> [!definition|18460707-322c-5ff2-851e-d581c88c0460.local at=65199ab8-13a2-5639-949a-fb7e406644f2] Normal modes and fundamental frequency of a fixed-end string
> For $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ on $0<x<L$ with $u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0$ and $L,c>0$, the $n$th normal mode is a motion of the form
> $$
> u_n(x,t)=\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\left(b_n\cos\omega_nt+b_n^*\sin\omega_nt\right),\qquad\omega_n=\frac{n\pi c}{L},\quad n=1,2,\ldots.
> $$
> The constants $b_n,b_n^*$ set the amplitude and phase. The first mode is the fundamental mode; modes with $n>1$ are overtones. The angular frequency is $\omega_n$, and the ordinary frequency is $\omega_n/(2\pi)$.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.4 D'Alembert's Method.md
title: D’Alembert formula for a finite string with fixed ends
body:
> [!equation|d8a7686f-1ae4-55fa-b8d7-b401ae3561a5.local at=c87e6df6-8372-5a11-b888-5cb0e2dda84e] D’Alembert formula for a finite string with fixed ends
> Let $c,L>0$ and let $f^*,g^*$ be the odd, $2L$-periodic extensions of initial displacement $f$ and velocity $g$ on $(0,L)$. If $f^*\in C^2$ and $g^*\in C^1$, the solution of
> $$
> u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx},\quad 0<x<L,\quad t>0,\qquad u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0,
> $$
> with $u(x,0)=f(x)$ and $u_t(x,0)=g(x)$ is
> $$
> u(x,t)=\frac12\left[f^*(x-ct)+f^*(x+ct)\right]+\frac{1}{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}g^*(s)\,ds.
> $$
> For piecewise smooth data, the formula is used piecewise or in the generalized sense at propagating corners.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.4 D'Alembert's Method.md
title: Characteristic parallelogram identity for the one-dimensional wave equation
body:
> [!proposition|72fef828-6f1d-553b-8c08-b58f0744bf69.local at=5adbd0d1-cd6e-594a-9822-33e4a96b1401] Characteristic parallelogram identity for the one-dimensional wave equation
> Let $u$ be a classical solution of $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$, $c>0$, on a neighborhood of a characteristic parallelogram: its sides lie on lines $x-ct=\text{constant}$ and $x+ct=\text{constant}$. If $P_1,P_2$ are opposite vertices and $Q_1,Q_2$ the other opposite pair, then
> $$
> u(P_1)+u(P_2)=u(Q_1)+u(Q_2).
> $$

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.5 The One Dimensional Heat Equation.md
title: Fourier sine solution of the heat equation with zero endpoint temperatures
body:
> [!equation|e4fe2eeb-5cb3-505e-b82b-6e6e72f16ad6.local at=67bcbebb-0f84-5694-a221-cdcce1200bc1] Fourier sine solution of the heat equation with zero endpoint temperatures
> Let $c,L>0$ and let $f$ be piecewise smooth on $[0,L]$. The solution of the one dimensional heat boundary value problem
>
> $$
> \frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=c^{2} \frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial x^{2}} \quad 0<x<L, \quad t>0,
> $$
>
> $$
> u(0, t)=0 \quad \text { and } \quad u(L, t)=0 \quad \text { for all } t>0,
> $$
>
> $$
> u(x, 0)=f(x) \quad \text { for } 0<x<L,
> $$
>
> is
>
> $$
> u(x, t)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_{n} e^{-\lambda_{n}^{2} t} \sin \frac{n \pi}{L} x
> $$
>
> where
> $\quad b_{n}=\frac{2}{L} \int_{0}^{L} f(x) \sin \frac{n \pi}{L} x d x \quad$ and $\quad \lambda_{n}=c \frac{n \pi}{L}, \quad n=1,2, \ldots$
>
>
>
> For $t>0$ the series is smooth and satisfies the equation and endpoint conditions. As $t\downarrow0$ it approaches $f(x)$ at interior continuity points and the mean of the one-sided limits at jumps. Continuity at the initial corners additionally requires $f(0)=f(L)=0$.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.5 The One Dimensional Heat Equation.md
title: Fourier law of one-dimensional heat conduction
body:
> [!equation|d9a0dfd1-efe8-53fa-a318-6435d873e437.local at=4ffe94e8-ded7-5cc1-afc9-ea90f0eb0c1a] Fourier law of one-dimensional heat conduction
> For temperature $u(x,t)$ and positive thermal conductivity $K_0$, the heat flux in the positive $x$ direction, measured as energy per unit area per unit time, is
> $$
> \phi(x,t)=-K_0\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}(x,t).
> $$

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.6 Heat Conduction in Bars: Varying the Boundary Conditions.md
title: Robin boundary condition for a scalar field
body:
> [!definition] Robin boundary condition for a scalar field
> A Robin boundary condition is a linear relation between a scalar field and its outward normal derivative on the boundary:
> $$
> \alpha u+\beta\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}=h.
> $$
> The prescribed coefficients $\alpha,\beta$ are not both zero. In one dimension it may be written $c_1u(x_0,t)+c_2u_x(x_0,t)=h(t)$, with the endpoint orientation absorbed into $c_2$.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.7 The Two Dimensional Wave and Heat Equations.md
title: Double sine series solution for a rectangular membrane with fixed edges
body:
> [!equation|c7aedb00-3e43-5e30-a0c8-8df3b6883019.local at=44160e7e-a39e-530b-8253-84cfc783831e] Double sine series solution for a rectangular membrane with fixed edges
> Let $a,b,c>0$. On $0<x<a$, $0<y<b$, consider $u_{tt}=c^2(u_{xx}+u_{yy})$, with $u=0$ on all four edges, $u(x,y,0)=f(x,y)$ and $u_t(x,y,0)=g(x,y)$. Its eigenfunction expansion is
> $$
> u(x,y,t)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\left(B_{mn}\cos\lambda_{mn}t+B^*_{mn}\sin\lambda_{mn}t\right)\sin\frac{m\pi x}{a}\sin\frac{n\pi y}{b},
> $$
> where
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> \lambda_{mn}&=c\pi\sqrt{m^2/a^2+n^2/b^2},\\
> B_{mn}&=\frac4{ab}\int_0^b\int_0^a f(x,y)\sin\frac{m\pi x}{a}\sin\frac{n\pi y}{b}\,dx\,dy,\\
> B^*_{mn}&=\frac4{ab\lambda_{mn}}\int_0^b\int_0^a g(x,y)\sin\frac{m\pi x}{a}\sin\frac{n\pi y}{b}\,dx\,dy.
> \end{aligned}
> $$
> For a classical solution, the initial data must satisfy the boundary compatibility conditions and the series must permit the required differentiations. For square-integrable data the expansion is understood in the spectral, generalized sense rather than as an assertion of pointwise second differentiability.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.7 The Two Dimensional Wave and Heat Equations.md
title: Double Fourier sine series representation on a rectangle
body:
> [!theorem|fd168324-0286-5644-8537-4b299510d6bb.local at=33b94323-398f-5887-bbb2-160e06024e5c] Double Fourier sine series representation on a rectangle
> Let $a,b>0$ and let $f$ and its first and second partial derivatives be continuous on $[0,a]\times[0,b]$. At interior points $0<x<a$, $0<y<b$,
> $$
> f(x,y)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}B_{mn}\sin\frac{m\pi x}{a}\sin\frac{n\pi y}{b},
> $$
> where
> $$
> B_{mn}=\frac4{ab}\int_0^b\int_0^a f(x,y)\sin\frac{m\pi x}{a}\sin\frac{n\pi y}{b}\,dx\,dy,\qquad m,n\ge1.
> $$
> The sine series is zero on the edges; matching nonzero edge values is not asserted.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.7 The Two Dimensional Wave and Heat Equations.md
title: Double sine series solution of the heat equation on a rectangle with zero edge temperatures
body:
> [!equation|266f946b-4282-5c79-87dc-ec1a646cc15e.local at=c731967c-40af-5851-84f1-cbdfeb170fba] Double sine series solution of the heat equation on a rectangle with zero edge temperatures
> Let $a,b,c>0$ and $f\in L^2((0,a)\times(0,b))$. The solution of the two dimensional heat equation
>
> $$
> \frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=c^{2}\left(\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial x^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial y^{2}}\right), \quad 0<x<a, \quad 0<y<b, \quad t>0
> $$
>
> with boundary conditions
>
> $$
> u(0, y, t)=u(a, y, t)=0, \quad 0<y<b, \quad t>0
> $$
>
>
> $$
> u(x, 0, t)=u(x, b, t)=0, \quad 0<x<a, \quad t>0
> $$
>
> and initial condition
>
> $$
> u(x, y, 0)=f(x, y), \quad 0<x<a, \quad 0<y<b
> $$
>
> is
>
> $$
> u(x, y, t)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} A_{m n} \sin \frac{m \pi}{a} x \sin \frac{n \pi}{b} y e^{-\lambda_{m n}^{2} t},
> $$
>
> where
>
> $$
> \lambda_{m n}=c \pi \sqrt{\frac{m^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{n^{2}}{b^{2}}}
> $$
>
> and
>
> $$
> \begin{gathered}
> A_{m n}=\frac{4}{a b} \int_{0}^{b} \int_{0}^{a} f(x, y) \sin \frac{m \pi}{a} x \sin \frac{n \pi}{b} y d x d y \\
> m, n=1,2, \ldots
> \end{gathered}
> $$
>
>
>
> The initial condition is attained in $L^2$ as $t\downarrow0$. For positive time the exponential factors regularize the series; at interior continuity points of bounded piecewise smooth data the initial limit is pointwise.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.8 Laplace's Equation in Rectangular Coordinates.md
title: Dirichlet problem for Laplace’s equation
body:
> [!definition] Dirichlet problem for Laplace’s equation
> Given a domain $\Omega$ and prescribed boundary values $h$, the Dirichlet problem for Laplace’s equation asks for a harmonic function $u$ in $\Omega$ satisfying $u=h$ on $\partial\Omega$. For the classical continuous-boundary formulation, $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.8 Laplace's Equation in Rectangular Coordinates.md
title: Fourier series solution of the Dirichlet problem for a rectangle
body:
> [!equation] Fourier series solution of the Dirichlet problem for a rectangle
> Let $a,b>0$. For Laplace’s equation $u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0$ on $0<x<a$, $0<y<b$, prescribe piecewise smooth boundary data
> $$
> u(x,0)=f_1(x),\quad u(x,b)=f_2(x),\quad u(0,y)=g_1(y),\quad u(a,y)=g_2(y).
> $$
> The solution in the rectangle is
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> u(x,y)={}&\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left[A_n\sinh\frac{n\pi(b-y)}a+B_n\sinh\frac{n\pi y}a\right]\sin\frac{n\pi x}a\\
> &+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left[C_n\sinh\frac{n\pi(a-x)}b+D_n\sinh\frac{n\pi x}b\right]\sin\frac{n\pi y}b,
> \end{aligned}
> $$
> with
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> A_n&=\frac{2}{a\sinh(n\pi b/a)}\int_0^a f_1(x)\sin\frac{n\pi x}a\,dx,&
> B_n&=\frac{2}{a\sinh(n\pi b/a)}\int_0^a f_2(x)\sin\frac{n\pi x}a\,dx,\\
> C_n&=\frac{2}{b\sinh(n\pi a/b)}\int_0^b g_1(y)\sin\frac{n\pi y}b\,dy,&
> D_n&=\frac{2}{b\sinh(n\pi a/b)}\int_0^b g_2(y)\sin\frac{n\pi y}b\,dy.
> \end{aligned}
> $$
