> Boundary data are attained at continuity points on the open sides. Continuity on the closed rectangle additionally requires compatible values at the corners.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.9 Poisson's Equation: The Method of Eigenfunction Expansions.md
title: Eigenfunction solution of the rectangular Poisson problem with Dirichlet data
body:
> [!equation|930aae7c-1ac9-5c9f-be40-285f192fbff5.local at=5ebb093c-bf33-5e97-ad7e-952ab63cd4bb] Eigenfunction solution of the rectangular Poisson problem with Dirichlet data
> Let $a,b>0$, $\Omega=(0,a)\times(0,b)$, and consider $\Delta u=f$ with prescribed Dirichlet boundary values $h$. Write $u=u_0+v$, where $v$ solves $\Delta v=0$ with boundary values $h$. The zero-boundary part is
> $$
> u_0(x,y)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}E_{mn}\sin\frac{m\pi x}{a}\sin\frac{n\pi y}{b},
> $$
> where
> $$
> \lambda_{mn}=\left(\frac{m\pi}{a}\right)^2+\left(\frac{n\pi}{b}\right)^2,\qquad
> E_{mn}=-\frac4{ab\lambda_{mn}}\int_0^b\int_0^a f(x,y)\sin\frac{m\pi x}{a}\sin\frac{n\pi y}{b}\,dx\,dy.
> $$
> For $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ the series gives the weak zero-Dirichlet solution; use classical differentiations only when the data and convergence justify them. The harmonic part $v$ must have the prescribed boundary trace, with corner compatibility required for continuity on the closed rectangle.

path: Chapter 11 Partial Differential Equations in Rectangular Coordinates/11.9 Poisson's Equation: The Method of Eigenfunction Expansions.md
title: Helmholtz equation and the negative Laplacian eigenvalue convention
body:
> [!equation|0e3cc99c-6c2e-55ee-a48d-19e148c954f5.local at=4d6f6877-7109-5c46-8929-86d0cef0a304] Helmholtz equation and the negative Laplacian eigenvalue convention
> For a scalar field $\phi$ on a spatial domain and a constant spectral parameter $\lambda$, the Helmholtz equation is
> $$
> \Delta\phi+\lambda\phi=0.
> $$
> A nonzero solution satisfying specified homogeneous boundary conditions is an eigenfunction of $-\Delta$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$. Its eigenvalue for $\Delta$ is $-\lambda$.

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.1 The Laplacian in Various Coordinate Systems.md
title: Laplacian in plane polar coordinates
body:
> [!equation|8450766e-50ec-5f20-b45c-783e65c84f3d.local at=61614e69-06f9-58c2-9391-d0833053a16d] Laplacian in plane polar coordinates
> For a $C^2$ scalar field expressed with $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$ and $r>0$,
> $$
> \Delta u=\nabla^{2} u=\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial r^{2}}+\frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial u}{\partial r}+\frac{1}{r^{2}} \frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial \theta^{2}}
> $$

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.1 The Laplacian in Various Coordinate Systems.md
title: Laplacian in cylindrical coordinates
body:
> [!equation|0ce2f75f-7132-54f9-ba34-ff5147e94ea3.local at=7108db11-fdb5-55ed-a364-9b0fe766a26b] Laplacian in cylindrical coordinates
> For a $C^2$ scalar field with $x=\rho\cos\phi$, $y=\rho\sin\phi$, $z=z$ and $\rho>0$,
> $$
> \Delta u=\nabla^{2} u=\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial \rho^{2}}+\frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial u}{\partial \rho}+\frac{1}{\rho^{2}} \frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial \phi^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial z^{2}}
> $$

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.1 The Laplacian in Various Coordinate Systems.md
title: Laplacian in spherical coordinates with polar angle measured from the positive z-axis
body:
> [!equation|8d333aa3-8fdf-559b-b0f5-a285d5c75c35.local at=6ded986c-f19e-5eeb-91dd-f91f8e602c07] Laplacian in spherical coordinates with polar angle measured from the positive z-axis
> For a $C^2$ scalar field, use $x=r\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $y=r\sin\theta\sin\phi$, $z=r\cos\theta$. Here $r>0$, $0<\theta<\pi$ is colatitude and $\phi$ is azimuth. Then
> $$
> \Delta u=\nabla^{2} u=\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial r^{2}}+\frac{2}{r} \frac{\partial u}{\partial r}+\frac{1}{r^{2}}\left(\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial \theta^{2}}+\cot \theta \frac{\partial u}{\partial \theta}+\csc ^{2} \theta \frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial \phi^{2}}\right)
> $$
> The coordinate expression is singular on the axis and at the origin; for a smooth Cartesian field, values there are obtained by appropriate limits.

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.2 Vibrations of a Circular Membrane: Symmetric Case.md
title: Fourier–Bessel solution for axisymmetric vibrations of a clamped circular membrane
body:
> [!theorem] Fourier–Bessel solution for axisymmetric vibrations of a clamped circular membrane
> Let $a,c>0$. For the radially symmetric wave equation $u_{tt}=c^2(u_{rr}+r^{-1}u_r)$ on $0<r<a$, require regularity at the center, $u(a,t)=0$, $u(r,0)=f(r)$ and $u_t(r,0)=g(r)$. Its solution is
>
> $$
> u(r, t)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(A_{n} \cos c \lambda_{n} t+B_{n} \sin c \lambda_{n} t\right) J_{0}\left(\lambda_{n} r\right)
> $$
>
> where
>
> $$
> \begin{gathered}
> A_{n}=\frac{2}{a^{2} J_{1}^{2}\left(\alpha_{n}\right)} \int_{0}^{a} f(r) J_{0}\left(\lambda_{n} r\right) r d r \\
> B_{n}=\frac{2}{c \alpha_{n} a J_{1}^{2}\left(\alpha_{n}\right)} \int_{0}^{a} g(r) J_{0}\left(\lambda_{n} r\right) r d r \\
> \lambda_{n}=\frac{\alpha_{n}}{a}, \quad \text { and } \quad \alpha_{n}=n \text {th positive zero of } J_{0}
> \end{gathered}
> $$
>
>
>
> Here $J_0,J_1$ are Bessel functions of the first kind. This is an eigenfunction expansion for data in the weighted space $L^2((0,a),r\,dr)$. Classical pointwise use requires enough regularity and compatibility to justify differentiation; a smooth radial field also has $u_r(0,t)=0$.

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.2 Vibrations of a Circular Membrane: Symmetric Case.md
title: Definite integral of a power times a Bessel function of the first kind
body:
> [!identity] Definite integral of a power times a Bessel function of the first kind
> For $a>0$, $\alpha>0$, $p\ge0$, and the Bessel functions of the first kind $J_p$ and $J_{p+1}$,
> $$
> \int_{0}^{a} x^{p+1} J_{p}\left(\frac{\alpha}{a} x\right) d x=\frac{a^{p+2}}{\alpha} J_{p+1}(\alpha)
> $$

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.3 Vibrations of a Circular Membrane: General Case.md
title: Definite Bessel integral with a quadratic radial weight
body:
> [!identity|af8d9359-9d57-580d-97d9-457e815c37d6.local at=c9cc37cd-01bf-5bf0-aded-7a850779c2ae] Definite Bessel integral with a quadratic radial weight
> For the Bessel functions of the first kind $J_k,J_{k+2}$ and any $k \geq 0, a>0$, and $\alpha>0$, we have
>
> $$
> \int_{0}^{a}\left(a^{2}-r^{2}\right) r^{k+1} J_{k}\left(\frac{\alpha}{a} r\right) d r=2 \frac{a^{k+4}}{\alpha^{2}} J_{k+2}(\alpha)
> $$

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.3 Vibrations of a Circular Membrane: General Case.md
title: Fourier–Bessel solution for a clamped circular membrane with general initial data
body:
> [!equation|862493e4-3880-5679-882b-4991975f7421.local at=c892da15-c887-5400-a40f-75f44457dec3] Fourier–Bessel solution for a clamped circular membrane with general initial data
> Let $a,c>0$. Consider $u_{tt}=c^2(u_{rr}+r^{-1}u_r+r^{-2}u_{\theta\theta})$ on the disk $0<r<a$, with $u(a,\theta,t)=0$, angular $2\pi$-periodicity, regularity at the center, and initial data $u(r,\theta,0)=f(r,\theta)$, $u_t(r,\theta,0)=g(r,\theta)$. The solution has the Fourier–Bessel expansion
>
> $$
> u(r, \theta, t)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} J_{m}\left(\lambda_{m n} r\right)\left(a_{m n} \cos m \theta+b_{m n} \sin m \theta\right) \cos c \lambda_{m n} t
> $$
>
> $$
> +\sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} J_{m}\left(\lambda_{m n} r\right)\left(a_{m n}^{*} \cos m \theta+b_{m n}^{*} \sin m \theta\right) \sin c \lambda_{m n} t
> $$
>
> where $\lambda_{m n}=\frac{\alpha_{m n}}{a} ; \alpha_{m n}$ is the $n$th positive zero of $J_{m} ; a_{mn},b_{mn}$ are the displacement coefficients defined below; and
>
> $$
> a_{0 n}^{*}=\frac{1}{\pi c \alpha_{0 n} a J_{1}^{2}\left(\alpha_{0 n}\right)} \int_{0}^{a} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} g(r, \theta) J_{0}\left(\lambda_{0 n} r\right) r d \theta d r
> $$
>
> $$
> a_{m n}^{*}=\frac{2}{\pi c \alpha_{m n} a J_{m+1}^{2}\left(\alpha_{m n}\right)} \int_{0}^{a} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} g(r, \theta) \cos m \theta J_{m}\left(\lambda_{m n} r\right) r d \theta d r
> $$
>
> $$
> b_{m n}^{*}=\frac{2}{\pi c \alpha_{m n} a \cdot J_{m+1}^{2}\left(\alpha_{m n}\right)} \int_{0}^{a} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} g(r, \theta) \sin m \theta \cdot J_{m}\left(\lambda_{m n} r\right) r d \theta d r
> $$
>
> Here $n\ge1$ throughout, and $m\ge1$ in the formulas involving $a^*_{mn}$ and $b^*_{mn}$. Set $b_{0n}=b^*_{0n}=0$.
>
>
>
> The displacement coefficients are
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> a_{0n}&=\frac{1}{\pi a^2J_1(\alpha_{0n})^2}\int_0^a\int_0^{2\pi}f(r,\theta)J_0(\lambda_{0n}r)r\,d\theta\,dr,\\
> a_{mn}&=\frac{2}{\pi a^2J_{m+1}(\alpha_{mn})^2}\int_0^a\int_0^{2\pi}f(r,\theta)\cos(m\theta)J_m(\lambda_{mn}r)r\,d\theta\,dr,\\
> b_{mn}&=\frac{2}{\pi a^2J_{m+1}(\alpha_{mn})^2}\int_0^a\int_0^{2\pi}f(r,\theta)\sin(m\theta)J_m(\lambda_{mn}r)r\,d\theta\,dr,
> \end{aligned}
> $$
> with $m,n\ge1$ in the last two lines. The functions $J_m$ are Bessel functions of the first kind. For square-integrable initial data on the disk the formula is interpreted as an eigenfunction expansion; pointwise differentiation requires additional smoothness and compatibility with the clamped edge and center regularity.

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.4 Laplace's Equation in Circular Regions.md
title: Fourier solution of the Dirichlet problem inside a disk
body:
> [!equation|bfa1439a-6563-50d7-90f7-54e64982e2cf.local at=67cde9ca-2bbf-5926-ac53-d884c29fb835] Fourier solution of the Dirichlet problem inside a disk
> Let $a>0$ and let $f$ be a piecewise smooth $2\pi$-periodic boundary function. The bounded harmonic solution in the disk $0\le r<a$ with boundary data $u(a,\theta)=f(\theta)$ is
> $$
> u(r,\theta)=a_0+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(r/a)^n\left(a_n\cos n\theta+b_n\sin n\theta\right),
> $$
> where
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> a_0&=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(\theta)\,d\theta,\\
> a_n&=\frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi}f(\theta)\cos n\theta\,d\theta,\qquad
> b_n=\frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi}f(\theta)\sin n\theta\,d\theta\quad(n\ge1).
> \end{aligned}
> $$
> The radial boundary limit equals $f$ at continuity points and the mean of its one-sided limits at jumps. For continuous $f$, the solution extends continuously to the closed disk.

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.4 Laplace's Equation in Circular Regions.md
title: Arctangent sum of the damped Fourier sine series
body:
> [!identity|cc924af8-1c36-5a35-a968-caac85cfbb81.local at=5040ae46-199f-5a4c-b148-14a3c36e495f] Arctangent sum of the damped Fourier sine series
> For $0\le r<1$ and real $\theta$, with the principal real arctangent,
> $$
> \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} r^{n} \frac{\sin n \theta}{n}=\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{r \sin \theta}{1-r \cos \theta}\right)
> $$

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.5 Laplace's Equation in a Cylinder.md
title: Axisymmetric Dirichlet solution in a cylinder with zero lateral and bottom temperatures
body:
> [!equation|759e4cfd-19fb-55c3-9d13-1fc494493637.local at=989cdb39-f93c-5465-a81f-e6666e444d27] Axisymmetric Dirichlet solution in a cylinder with zero lateral and bottom temperatures
> Let $a,h>0$. The solution of $u_{\rho\rho}+\rho^{-1}u_\rho+u_{zz}=0$ in $0<\rho<a$, $0<z<h$, regular at the cylinder axis and independent of azimuth, with boundary conditions
>
> $$
> \begin{array}{r}
> u(\rho, 0)=0, \quad 0<\rho<a \\
> u(a, z)=0, \quad 0<z<h \\
> u(\rho, h)=f(\rho), \quad 0<\rho<a
> \end{array}
> $$
>
> is
>
> $$
> u(\rho, z)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} A_{n} J_{0}\left(\lambda_{n} \rho\right) \sinh \lambda_{n} z
> $$
>
> where
>
> $$
> A_{n}=\frac{2}{\sinh \left(\lambda_{n} h\right) a^{2} J_{1}^{2}\left(\alpha_{n}\right)} \int_{0}^{a} f(\rho) J_{0}\left(\lambda_{n} \rho\right) \rho d \rho, \quad \lambda_{n}=\frac{\alpha_{n}}{a}
> $$
>
> and $\alpha_{n}$ is the $n$th positive zero of $J_{0}$, the Bessel function of order 0 .
>
>
> Assume piecewise smooth prescribed temperature data. Boundary limits are taken on the open faces at continuity points; continuity across the circular edges requires matching data. The functions $J_0,J_1$ are Bessel functions of the first kind and $I_0$ is the modified Bessel function of the first kind.

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.5 Laplace's Equation in a Cylinder.md
title: Axisymmetric Dirichlet solution in a cylinder with zero base temperatures
body:
> [!equation|bf8bfac8-6676-537a-a7f2-11398f29b5e7.local at=8e9d1cca-bb7f-5992-8f06-67f8d96d1b5f] Axisymmetric Dirichlet solution in a cylinder with zero base temperatures
> Let $a,h>0$. The solution of $u_{\rho\rho}+\rho^{-1}u_\rho+u_{zz}=0$ in $0<\rho<a$, $0<z<h$, regular at the cylinder axis and independent of azimuth, with boundary conditions
>
> $$
> \begin{gathered}
> u(\rho, 0)=u(\rho, h)=0, \quad 0<\rho<a \\
> u(a, z)=f(z), \quad 0<z<h
> \end{gathered}
> $$
>
> is
>
> $$
> u(\rho, z)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} B_{n} I_{0}\left(\frac{n \pi}{h} \rho\right) \sin \frac{n \pi}{h} z,
> $$
>
> where $I_{0}$ is the modified Bessel function of the first kind of order 0, and
>
> $$
> B_{n}=\frac{2}{I_{0}\left(\frac{n \pi a}{h}\right) h} \int_{0}^{h} f(z) \sin \frac{n \pi}{h} z d z .
> $$
>
>
>
> Assume piecewise smooth prescribed temperature data. Boundary limits are taken on the open faces at continuity points; continuity across the circular edges requires matching data. The functions $J_0,J_1$ are Bessel functions of the first kind and $I_0$ is the modified Bessel function of the first kind.

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.6 The Helmholtz and Poisson Equations.md
title: Dirichlet eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the negative Laplacian on a disk
body:
> [!theorem|f1738541-0273-5e3e-b782-350615e9efd1.local at=ac537d24-9a90-531a-97d6-1bf73e9e89cb] Dirichlet eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the negative Laplacian on a disk
> Let $a>0$. For $-\Delta\phi=k\phi$ on the disk of radius $a$, with $\phi=0$ at $r=a$, angular $2\pi$-periodicity and regularity at the origin, the eigenvalues are
> $$
> k=\lambda_{mn}^2=(\alpha_{mn}/a)^2,\qquad m=0,1,2,\ldots,\quad n=1,2,\ldots,
> $$
> where $\alpha_{mn}$ is the $n$th positive zero of the Bessel function $J_m$ of the first kind. The associated eigenfunctions are
> $$
> J_m(\lambda_{mn}r)\cos m\theta\quad(m\ge0),\qquad
> J_m(\lambda_{mn}r)\sin m\theta\quad(m\ge1).
> $$
> For $m=0$ only the cosine function is nonzero; for $m\ge1$ the sine and cosine functions give two linearly independent modes.

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.6 The Helmholtz and Poisson Equations.md
title: Fourier–Bessel eigenfunction expansion of a square-integrable function on a disk
body:
> [!theorem|93faa464-9f3c-571a-b4bf-ff9f7ef2b938.local at=59461e7f-f1a0-5019-969f-69cc5c671c86] Fourier–Bessel eigenfunction expansion of a square-integrable function on a disk
> Let $a>0$, let $f\in L^2(D_a)$ with area measure $r\,dr\,d\theta$, and let $\alpha_{mn}$ be the $n$th positive zero of the Bessel function $J_m$ of the first kind. Set $\lambda_{mn}=\alpha_{mn}/a$. Then
> $$
> f(r,\theta)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}J_m(\lambda_{mn}r)\left(a_{mn}\cos m\theta+b_{mn}\sin m\theta\right)
> $$
> in the $L^2$ sense, where $b_{0n}=0$ and
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> a_{0n}&=\frac1{\pi a^2J_1(\alpha_{0n})^2}\int_0^a\int_0^{2\pi}f(r,\theta)J_0(\lambda_{0n}r)r\,d\theta\,dr,\\
> a_{mn}&=\frac2{\pi a^2J_{m+1}(\alpha_{mn})^2}\int_0^a\int_0^{2\pi}f(r,\theta)\cos m\theta\,J_m(\lambda_{mn}r)r\,d\theta\,dr,\\
> b_{mn}&=\frac2{\pi a^2J_{m+1}(\alpha_{mn})^2}\int_0^a\int_0^{2\pi}f(r,\theta)\sin m\theta\,J_m(\lambda_{mn}r)r\,d\theta\,dr.
> \end{aligned}
> $$
> Here $n\ge1$, and $m\ge1$ in the last two formulas. Pointwise convergence requires additional regularity; it is not asserted merely because $f$ is defined on the disk.

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.6 The Helmholtz and Poisson Equations.md
title: Eigenfunction solution of a Poisson–Dirichlet problem on a disk
body:
> [!procedure|ef333ef0-c62d-5624-8af6-a14de4c83bf7.local at=b9005dd7-d04c-5890-abef-5069ca7a91b6] Eigenfunction solution of a Poisson–Dirichlet problem on a disk
> To solve $\Delta u=f$ on a disk of radius $a>0$ with $u(a,\theta)=g(\theta)$, first find a harmonic function $v$ with boundary values $g$. Expand $f$ in the regular zero-Dirichlet eigenfunctions
> $$
> \phi_{mn}^{c}=J_m(\alpha_{mn}r/a)\cos m\theta,\qquad
> \phi_{mn}^{s}=J_m(\alpha_{mn}r/a)\sin m\theta,
> $$
> where $\alpha_{mn}$ is the $n$th positive zero of $J_m$, $m\ge0$, $n\ge1$, and the zero sine mode is omitted. Their positive eigenvalues for $-\Delta$ are $\lambda_{mn}^2=(\alpha_{mn}/a)^2$.
>
> For either nonzero mode $\phi$, its source coefficient is $F_\phi=\langle f,\phi\rangle/\langle\phi,\phi\rangle$, using disk area measure $r\,dr\,d\theta$. Set
> $$
> u=v-\sum_{\phi}\frac{F_\phi}{\lambda_\phi^2}\phi.
> $$
> For $f\in L^2$ this gives the weak zero-boundary correction to $v$. Pointwise differentiation and continuous boundary values require the corresponding regularity and boundary compatibility.

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.7 Bessel's Equation and Bessel Functions.md
title: Bessel function of the first kind
body:
> [!definition|8b252a49-ba06-58f7-8ee0-2ea2e2b6f5fb.local at=20a2e4df-9ff2-5ed7-a842-048160670720] Bessel function of the first kind
> For real order $p\ge0$ and $x>0$, the Bessel function of the first kind is
>
> $$
> J_{p}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{k}}{k!\Gamma(k+p+1)}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^{2 k+p} .
> $$
>
> Here $\Gamma$ denotes the gamma function. The value at $x=0$ is defined by the right-hand limit.

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.7 Bessel's Equation and Bessel Functions.md
title: Bessel function of the second kind
body:
> [!definition|3eb52e35-d2a0-5902-ab98-9f125f2a5d2a.local at=b2fd50e8-8398-5a9d-9334-bc1f95265c68] Bessel function of the second kind
> For $x>0$ and noninteger real order $p\ge0$, define
> $$
> Y_p(x)=\frac{J_p(x)\cos(\pi p)-J_{-p}(x)}{\sin(\pi p)},
> $$
> where $J_\nu$ is the Bessel function of the first kind. For a nonnegative integer $n$, define
> $$
> Y_n(x)=\lim_{\nu\to n}Y_\nu(x).
> $$
> The limit exists. These are the Bessel functions of the second kind; $J_p$ and $Y_p$ are linearly independent solutions of Bessel's equation on $(0,\infty)$.

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.7 Bessel's Equation and Bessel Functions.md
title: Bessel functions of the second kind diverge at the origin
body:
> [!property|e8592b84-46f2-501c-a88f-0d3577aa0a55.local at=1614d4e0-c6bd-56c0-9383-ac1a9102df62] Bessel functions of the second kind diverge at the origin
> For real order $p\ge0$, the Bessel function of the second kind satisfies
> $$
> \lim_{x\to0^+}Y_p(x)=-\infty.
> $$

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.7 Bessel's Equation and Bessel Functions.md
title: General solution of Bessel’s differential equation on the positive axis
body:
> [!equation|3f367ba5-7274-57c5-9f48-982e8ed1dfc3.local at=299d01d5-9a3e-50af-8a46-629dbeb9d5ed] General solution of Bessel’s differential equation on the positive axis
> For a fixed real order $p\ge0$, the general solution of
> $$
> x^2y''+xy'+(x^2-p^2)y=0,\qquad x>0,
> $$
> is
> $$
> y(x)=c_1J_p(x)+c_2Y_p(x),
> $$
> where $c_1,c_2$ are arbitrary constants and $J_p,Y_p$ are the Bessel functions of the first and second kinds. If $p$ is not an integer, an alternative fundamental pair is $J_p,J_{-p}$:
> $$
> y(x)=c_1J_p(x)+c_2J_{-p}(x).
> $$

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.7 Bessel's Equation and Bessel Functions.md
title: Euler gamma function on the positive real axis
body:
> [!definition|1e29771b-e89a-59e7-a628-b61ecfa915b8.local at=816109b3-eb31-5aa3-8e54-d94e615da8be] Euler gamma function on the positive real axis
> The gamma function is defined for $x>0$ by
>
> $$
> \Gamma(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty} t^{x-1} e^{-t} d t
> $$

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.7 Bessel's Equation and Bessel Functions.md
title: Recurrence relation for the gamma function
body:
> [!property|36db6dd5-e306-5bc8-af5c-34dc0fb418b4.local at=44e8b883-b973-5a2e-8211-6a2a95012654] Recurrence relation for the gamma function
> For $x>0$, the Euler gamma function satisfies
> $$
> \Gamma(x+1)=x\Gamma(x).
> $$

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.8 Bessel Series Expansions.md
title: Differentiation identities for powers times Bessel functions of the first kind
body:
> [!identity|526b6194-6aad-5d21-8f21-aeef31a91829.local at=eb82eefc-b051-5f42-8fc6-5542b40594d1] Differentiation identities for powers times Bessel functions of the first kind
> For real $p\ge0$ and $x>0$, the Bessel function $J_p$ of the first kind satisfies
>
> $$
> \frac{d}{d x}\left[x^{p} J_{p}(x)\right]=x^{p} J_{p-1}(x)
> $$
>
> $$
> \frac{d}{d x}\left[x^{-p} J_{p}(x)\right]=-x^{-p} J_{p+1}(x)
> $$

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.8 Bessel Series Expansions.md
title: Order recurrences for Bessel functions of the first kind
body:
> [!identity|e810a894-67c4-5fbd-83e2-71c7f99d063e.local at=4c06bf98-c6cc-5e29-a594-79257b2bf3b6] Order recurrences for Bessel functions of the first kind
> For real $p\ge0$ and $x>0$, the Bessel functions $J_\nu$ of the first kind satisfy
>
> $$
> \begin{gathered}
> x J_{p}^{\prime}(x)+p J_{p}(x)=x J_{p-1}(x) \\
> x J_{p}^{\prime}(x)-p J_{p}(x)=-x J_{p+1}(x) \\
> J_{p-1}(x)-J_{p+1}(x)=2 J_{p}^{\prime}(x) \\
> J_{p-1}(x)+J_{p+1}(x)=\frac{2 p}{x} J_{p}(x)
> \end{gathered}
> $$

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.8 Bessel Series Expansions.md
title: Antiderivatives of power-weighted Bessel functions of the first kind
body:
> [!identity|04e76fe2-b50e-54bb-a3b6-206f69783650.local at=4bb611bb-6d68-5eeb-8963-11918666e714] Antiderivatives of power-weighted Bessel functions of the first kind
> For real $p\ge0$ and $x>0$, with arbitrary integration constant $C$,
>
> $$
> \int x^{p+1} J_{p}(x) d x=x^{p+1} J_{p+1}(x)+C
> $$
>
> and
>
> $$
> \int x^{-p+1} J_{p}(x) d x=-x^{-p+1} J_{p-1}(x)+C
> $$

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.8 Bessel Series Expansions.md
title: Weighted orthogonality and squared norms of Dirichlet Bessel modes
body:
> [!theorem|0772d5b0-9a5c-5645-b3fe-75e1d07a2a86.local at=a36dcd1b-ef7a-57c9-9cba-6ee29634022b] Weighted orthogonality and squared norms of Dirichlet Bessel modes
> Fix $p\ge0$ and $a>0$. Let $J_p$ be the Bessel function of the first kind, let $\alpha_{pj}$ be its $j$th positive zero, and set $\lambda_{pj}=\alpha_{pj}/a$. Then
>
> $$
> \int_{0}^{a} J_{p}\left(\lambda_{p j} x\right) J_{p}\left(\lambda_{p k} x\right) x d x=0 \text { for } j \neq k
> $$
>
> and
>
> $$
> \int_{0}^{a} J_{p}^{2}\left(\lambda_{p j} x\right) x d x=\frac{a^{2}}{2} J_{p+1}^{2}\left(\alpha_{p j}\right) \text { for } j=1,2, \ldots
> $$

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.8 Bessel Series Expansions.md
title: Pointwise convergence of a Fourier–Bessel series on an open finite interval
body:
> [!theorem|cf3f6d2d-dc5a-555b-86e2-323ff9599805.local at=d93068ef-da1e-5cd8-a42e-9b6e1a1173ea] Pointwise convergence of a Fourier–Bessel series on an open finite interval
> Fix $a>0$ and real $p\ge0$. Suppose $f$ is piecewise smooth on $[0,a]$: it has a finite partition into continuously differentiable pieces with finite one-sided limits of the function and its derivative. Let $\alpha_{pj}$ be the $j$th positive zero of the Bessel function $J_p$ of the first kind, and put $\lambda_{pj}=\alpha_{pj}/a$. The Fourier–Bessel series
> $$
> \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}A_jJ_p(\lambda_{pj}x),\qquad
> A_j=\frac{2}{a^2J_{p+1}(\alpha_{pj})^2}\int_0^a f(t)J_p(\lambda_{pj}t)t\,dt,
> $$
> converges at every $0<x<a$ to
> $$
> \frac{f(x+)+f(x-)}2.
> $$
> At continuity points this equals $f(x)$. No endpoint-convergence assertion is included.

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.8 Bessel Series Expansions.md
title: Regular Dirichlet eigenmodes of the parametric Bessel equation
body:
> [!theorem|ab5e42d2-4be6-53d3-ad29-a2620bbff2c2.local at=12c592fe-9ce1-5ba9-9978-23abf0e09241] Regular Dirichlet eigenmodes of the parametric Bessel equation
> Let $a>0$, $p\ge0$, and $\lambda>0$. The boundary-value problem
> $$
> x^2y''+xy'+(\lambda^2x^2-p^2)y=0,\qquad 0<x<a,
> $$
> with $y$ bounded as $x\to0^+$ and $y(a)=0$ has a nonzero solution exactly when
> $$
> \lambda=\lambda_{pj}=\frac{\alpha_{pj}}a,\qquad j=1,2,\ldots,
> $$
> where $\alpha_{pj}$ is the $j$th positive zero of the Bessel function $J_p$ of the first kind. Each such solution is a scalar multiple of $J_p(\lambda_{pj}x)$. Distinct modes are orthogonal with weight $x$, and
> $$
> \int_0^a J_p(\lambda_{pj}x)J_p(\lambda_{pk}x)x\,dx=
> \begin{cases}0,&j\ne k,\\[2pt]\dfrac{a^2}2J_{p+1}(\alpha_{pj})^2,&j=k.\end{cases}
> $$

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.8 Bessel Series Expansions.md
title: Spherical Bessel functions of the first kind
body:
> [!definition|ea4affd5-e5a4-5891-a463-4ddc05cd5773.local at=6aaa9d07-2d96-5393-80c7-48608a7f872c] Spherical Bessel functions of the first kind
> For integers $n\ge0$ and $x>0$, the spherical Bessel function of the first kind is defined by
>
> $$
> j_{n}(x)=\left(\frac{\pi}{2 x}\right)^{1 / 2} J_{n+\frac{1}{2}}(x), \quad n=0,1,2, \ldots
> $$
>
> Here $J_{n+1/2}$ is the ordinary Bessel function of the first kind. Values at $x=0$ are defined by the right-hand limits.

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.9 Integral Formulas and Asymptotics for Bessel Functions.md
title: Integral representation of integer-order Bessel functions of the first kind
body:
> [!theorem] Integral representation of integer-order Bessel functions of the first kind
> For every integer $n$ and every real $x$, the Bessel function $J_n$ of the first kind satisfies
> $$
> J_n(x)=\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi\cos(n\theta-x\sin\theta)\,d\theta.
> $$

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.9 Integral Formulas and Asymptotics for Bessel Functions.md
title: Jacobi–Anger Fourier expansion of a sinusoidal complex exponential
body:
> [!theorem] Jacobi–Anger Fourier expansion of a sinusoidal complex exponential
> For real $x$ and $\theta$,
> $$
> e^{ix\sin\theta}=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}J_n(x)e^{in\theta},
> $$
> where $J_n$ denotes the Bessel function of the first kind of integer order $n$. For each fixed $x$, the series converges absolutely and uniformly in $\theta$.

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.9 Integral Formulas and Asymptotics for Bessel Functions.md
title: Large-argument asymptotic expansion of integer-order Bessel functions
body:
> [!theorem] Large-argument asymptotic expansion of integer-order Bessel functions
> For each fixed nonnegative integer $n$, as $x\to+\infty$,
> $$
> J_n(x)=\sqrt{\frac2{\pi x}}\cos\left(x-\frac\pi4-\frac{n\pi}2\right)+O(x^{-3/2}),
> $$
> where $J_n$ is the Bessel function of the first kind. Thus a constant $C_n$ bounds the absolute error by $C_nx^{-3/2}$ for all sufficiently large positive $x$. The error is additive; no ratio limit is asserted at the zeros of the oscillatory leading term.

path: Chapter 12 Partial Differential Equations in Polar and Cylindrical Coordinates/12.9 Integral Formulas and Asymptotics for Bessel Functions.md
title: Stationary-phase approximation at a single nondegenerate interior critical point
body:
> [!lemma] Stationary-phase approximation at a single nondegenerate interior critical point
> Let $a<b$, and let $f$ be real-valued and smooth on $[a,b]$, with a Taylor expansion near $t_0\in(a,b)$. Suppose $f'(t_0)=0$, $f''(t_0)\ne0$, and $f'(t)\ne0$ for $t\ne t_0$ in $[a,b]$. Let $g$ be a smooth complex-valued function on $[a,b]$. As $x\to+\infty$,
> $$
> \int_a^b e^{ixf(t)}g(t)\,dt=
> \sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{x}}\,\frac{g(t_0)}{\sqrt{|f''(t_0)|}}
>  e^{i\left(xf(t_0)+\frac\pi4\operatorname{sgn}f''(t_0)\right)}+O(x^{-1}).
> $$
> The phase shift is $+\pi/4$ when $f''(t_0)>0$ and $-\pi/4$ when $f''(t_0)<0$. If $g(t_0)\ne0$, the displayed leading term is an asymptotic equivalent. If $g(t_0)=0$, further terms and endpoint contributions must be examined to obtain the first nonzero approximation.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.1 Preview of Problems and Methods.md
title: Axisymmetric Laplace equation in spherical coordinates
body:
> [!equation|7c65c2f9-13c0-50ef-ac5c-c61c4139a2e9.local at=44d6584d-7551-5bbd-8ef1-ff5d1d330d76] Axisymmetric Laplace equation in spherical coordinates
> Use spherical coordinates $x=r\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $y=r\sin\theta\sin\phi$, $z=r\cos\theta$, with colatitude $\theta$ and azimuth $\phi$. For a twice differentiable function independent of $\phi$, Laplace's equation becomes
> $$
> u_{rr}+\frac2r u_r+\frac1{r^2}\left(u_{\theta\theta}+\cot\theta\,u_\theta\right)=0,\qquad r>0,\quad0<\theta<\pi.
> $$
> Axisymmetry means invariance under rotation about the $z$-axis; it permits dependence on $\theta$. A radially symmetric function depends only on $r$.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.2 Dirichlet Problems with Symmetry.md
title: Axisymmetric Dirichlet solution inside a ball by Legendre series
body:
> [!theorem|dc29d4e6-1aee-5a21-a63d-46b8e290d2e4.local at=efc6be32-e1e9-5111-9eee-d0464b9e30e5] Axisymmetric Dirichlet solution inside a ball by Legendre series
> Let $a>0$, with colatitude $0\le\theta\le\pi$ and azimuth $\phi$. Let the prescribed surface temperature $f(\theta)$ be independent of $\phi$ and piecewise smooth. The regular harmonic solution inside the ball $r<a$ is
> $$
> u(r,\theta)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}A_n\left(\frac ra\right)^nP_n(\cos\theta),
> \qquad
> A_n=\frac{2n+1}{2}\int_0^\pi f(\theta)P_n(\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\theta,
> $$
> where $P_n$ is the Legendre polynomial normalized by $P_n(1)=1$. The interior series solves $\Delta u=0$ and has radial boundary limit $f(\theta)$ at continuity points. If $f$ is continuous on $[0,\pi]$, it gives the unique harmonic solution continuous on the closed ball with $u(a,\theta)=f(\theta)$.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.3 Spherical Harmonics and the General Dirichlet Problem.md
title: Orthonormal complex spherical harmonics with the Condon–Shortley phase
body:
> [!definition|70c0c06d-0abd-5637-a985-60980824a550.local at=867a9f45-675e-5433-9650-fbbd0289b7a8] Orthonormal complex spherical harmonics with the Condon–Shortley phase
> On the unit sphere, let $\theta\in[0,\pi]$ denote colatitude and $\phi$ denote azimuth modulo $2\pi$. For integers $n\ge0$ and $-n\le m\le n$, define
> $$
> Y_{n,m}(\theta,\phi)=\sqrt{\frac{2n+1}{4\pi}\frac{(n-m)!}{(n+m)!}}\,P_n^m(\cos\theta)e^{im\phi}.
> $$
> Here $P_n$ is the Legendre polynomial normalized by $P_n(1)=1$. For $0\le m\le n$,
> $$
> P_n^m(s)=(-1)^m(1-s^2)^{m/2}\frac{d^m}{ds^m}P_n(s),
> $$
> and for $1\le m\le n$,
> $$
> P_n^{-m}(s)=(-1)^m\frac{(n-m)!}{(n+m)!}P_n^m(s).
> $$
> The factor $(-1)^m$ is the Condon–Shortley phase convention. The surface measure used for normalization is $d\Omega=\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi$.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.3 Spherical Harmonics and the General Dirichlet Problem.md
title: Orthonormality of complex spherical harmonics on the unit sphere
body:
> [!theorem|10694bbd-a986-5f2c-876f-69b68411a74e.local at=080ce504-87c9-5e15-8fd6-aaa180d59f5d] Orthonormality of complex spherical harmonics on the unit sphere
> Let $Y_{n,m}$ be the standard normalized complex spherical harmonics of degree $n\ge0$ and order $-n\le m\le n$, using colatitude $\theta$ and azimuth $\phi$. For any two admissible degree–order pairs,
> $$
> \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi Y_{n,m}(\theta,\phi)\overline{Y_{n',m'}(\theta,\phi)}\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi
> =\delta_{nn'}\delta_{mm'},
> $$
> where the overbar denotes complex conjugation and $\delta$ is the Kronecker delta. In particular, each harmonic has squared norm $1$ with respect to unit-sphere area measure.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.3 Spherical Harmonics and the General Dirichlet Problem.md
title: Mean-square expansion of a function on the sphere in spherical harmonics
body:
> [!theorem|97f3a242-dfd4-5495-a5fb-a4e2850d691f.local at=c2fd17f9-8f57-5537-837f-b30dad59cd4c] Mean-square expansion of a function on the sphere in spherical harmonics
> Let $f\in L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$, where $d\Omega=\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi$ is unit-sphere area measure, $\theta$ is colatitude, and $\phi$ is azimuth. Let $Y_{n,m}$ be the standard orthonormal complex spherical harmonics. Then
> $$
> f(\theta,\phi)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{m=-n}^{n}A_{nm}Y_{n,m}(\theta,\phi)
> $$
> with convergence in the $L^2$ norm, where
> $$
> A_{nm}=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi f(\theta,\phi)\overline{Y_{n,m}(\theta,\phi)}\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi.
> $$
> Square integrability alone does not assert pointwise convergence.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.3 Spherical Harmonics and the General Dirichlet Problem.md
title: Interior Dirichlet solution in a ball by spherical harmonics
body:
> [!theorem|dc75bd76-a3d7-5017-99e8-77e5238bed47.local at=b3ff9dc1-5b54-565e-a598-bd6d0a291469] Interior Dirichlet solution in a ball by spherical harmonics
> Let $a>0$, and prescribe a continuous function $f$ on the sphere of radius $a$. With colatitude $\theta$ and azimuth $\phi$, let
> $$
> A_{nm}=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi f(\theta,\phi)\overline{Y_{n,m}(\theta,\phi)}\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi,
> $$
> where $Y_{n,m}$ are the standard orthonormal complex spherical harmonics. The unique solution of $\Delta u=0$ in the ball, continuous on its closure and satisfying $u(a,\theta,\phi)=f(\theta,\phi)$, is
> $$
> u(r,\theta,\phi)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{m=-n}^{n}A_{nm}\left(\frac ra\right)^nY_{n,m}(\theta,\phi),\qquad0\le r<a.
> $$
> For square-integrable boundary data the same interior series gives the harmonic extension with boundary convergence in $L^2$. For bounded piecewise smooth data, the radial boundary limit equals the data at continuity points.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.3 Spherical Harmonics and the General Dirichlet Problem.md
title: Eigenvalues and eigenspaces of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on the unit sphere
body:
> [!theorem|44585a75-2600-5aa5-b0a5-51337f490e14.local at=ef29e080-d5f4-5424-8a53-a0dc8ede9de5] Eigenvalues and eigenspaces of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on the unit sphere
> In colatitude $\theta$ and azimuth $\phi$, consider functions smooth on the unit sphere and the equation
> $$
> \Delta_{S^2}Y+\mu Y=0,\qquad
> \Delta_{S^2}Y=Y_{\theta\theta}+\cot\theta\,Y_\theta+\csc^2\theta\,Y_{\phi\phi}.
> $$
> Nonzero solutions exist exactly for $\mu=n(n+1)$, $n=0,1,2,\ldots$. The corresponding eigenspace of $-\Delta_{S^2}$ has dimension $2n+1$ and an orthonormal basis
> $$
> Y_{n,m}(\theta,\phi),\qquad m=-n,-n+1,\ldots,n,
> $$
> given by the normalized complex spherical harmonics. Orthogonality uses surface measure $\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi$. The coordinate formula is used for $0<\theta<\pi$ with regularity at the poles and $2\pi$-periodicity in $\phi$.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.4 The Helmholtz Equation with Applications to the Poisson, Heat, and Wave Equations.md
title: Dirichlet eigenfunctions of the negative Laplacian in a ball
body:
> [!theorem|efc5ac01-2469-5568-8a2b-ec8c4e0b0503.local at=6e849eda-9451-5496-91cc-c8f567c7d2f9] Dirichlet eigenfunctions of the negative Laplacian in a ball
> Let $a>0$. Use spherical coordinates with colatitude $\theta$, azimuth $\phi$, and volume measure $dV=r^2\sin\theta\,dr\,d\theta\,d\phi$. Write $Y_{n,m}$ for the standard unit-sphere orthonormal complex spherical harmonics and $j_n$ for the spherical Bessel function of the first kind. Let $\alpha_{n+1/2,j}$ be the $j$th positive zero of the ordinary Bessel function $J_{n+1/2}$, and set $\lambda_{n,j}=\alpha_{n+1/2,j}/a$ and
> $$
> \Psi_{jnm}(r,\theta,\phi)=j_n(\lambda_{n,j}r)Y_{n,m}(\theta,\phi),
> \qquad j\ge1,\ n\ge0,\ -n\le m\le n.
> $$
>
> The problem $-\Delta\Psi=k\Psi$ in the ball $r<a$, with zero boundary value at $r=a$ and regularity throughout the ball, has positive eigenvalues $k=\lambda_{n,j}^2$. For each fixed pair $(n,j)$, the functions $\Psi_{jnm}$ with $-n\le m\le n$ give $2n+1$ linearly independent angular modes. There is no nonzero zero-eigenvalue solution.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.4 The Helmholtz Equation with Applications to the Poisson, Heat, and Wave Equations.md
title: Orthogonality and norms of spherical Dirichlet modes in a ball
body:
> [!theorem|b5a977f6-80ae-5e5d-893a-641f2e6133da.local at=d53f3db2-ed96-5b4d-a721-171b5604e268] Orthogonality and norms of spherical Dirichlet modes in a ball
> Let $a>0$. Use spherical coordinates with colatitude $\theta$, azimuth $\phi$, and volume measure $dV=r^2\sin\theta\,dr\,d\theta\,d\phi$. Write $Y_{n,m}$ for the standard unit-sphere orthonormal complex spherical harmonics and $j_n$ for the spherical Bessel function of the first kind. Let $\alpha_{n+1/2,j}$ be the $j$th positive zero of the ordinary Bessel function $J_{n+1/2}$, and set $\lambda_{n,j}=\alpha_{n+1/2,j}/a$ and
> $$
> \Psi_{jnm}(r,\theta,\phi)=j_n(\lambda_{n,j}r)Y_{n,m}(\theta,\phi),
> \qquad j\ge1,\ n\ge0,\ -n\le m\le n.
> $$
>
> These modes are orthogonal for the volume inner product:
> $$
> \int_{r<a}\Psi_{jnm}\overline{\Psi_{j'n'm'}}\,dV=0\quad\text{if }(j,n,m)\ne(j',n',m'),
> $$
> and
> $$
> \int_{r<a}|\Psi_{jnm}|^2\,dV=\frac{a^3}2j_{n+1}(\alpha_{n+1/2,j})^2.
> $$

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.4 The Helmholtz Equation with Applications to the Poisson, Heat, and Wave Equations.md
title: Mean-square expansion in spherical Dirichlet eigenfunctions inside a ball
body:
> [!theorem|8916bd16-dbad-5696-87d2-ac7d7eb4e660.local at=17efe8e4-cb89-5128-9528-308d98f0a88f] Mean-square expansion in spherical Dirichlet eigenfunctions inside a ball
> Let $a>0$. Use spherical coordinates with colatitude $\theta$, azimuth $\phi$, and volume measure $dV=r^2\sin\theta\,dr\,d\theta\,d\phi$. Write $Y_{n,m}$ for the standard unit-sphere orthonormal complex spherical harmonics and $j_n$ for the spherical Bessel function of the first kind. Let $\alpha_{n+1/2,j}$ be the $j$th positive zero of the ordinary Bessel function $J_{n+1/2}$, and set $\lambda_{n,j}=\alpha_{n+1/2,j}/a$ and
> $$
> \Psi_{jnm}(r,\theta,\phi)=j_n(\lambda_{n,j}r)Y_{n,m}(\theta,\phi),
> \qquad j\ge1,\ n\ge0,\ -n\le m\le n.
> $$
>
> For every $f\in L^2(\{r<a\},dV)$,
> $$
> f=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{m=-n}^{n}A_{jnm}\Psi_{jnm},
> \qquad
> A_{jnm}=\frac{2}{a^3j_{n+1}(\alpha_{n+1/2,j})^2}\int_{r<a}f\overline{\Psi_{jnm}}\,dV,
> $$
> with convergence in the $L^2$ norm. This statement does not by itself guarantee pointwise convergence.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.4 The Helmholtz Equation with Applications to the Poisson, Heat, and Wave Equations.md
title: Poisson–Dirichlet solution in a ball by harmonic lifting and eigenfunction expansion
body:
> [!theorem|8342a5a1-aa39-5e98-a879-b986f22aa73e.local at=60829fdd-9adc-5374-bc5a-69b98ee6c344] Poisson–Dirichlet solution in a ball by harmonic lifting and eigenfunction expansion
> Let $a>0$. Use spherical coordinates with colatitude $\theta$, azimuth $\phi$, and volume measure $dV=r^2\sin\theta\,dr\,d\theta\,d\phi$. Write $Y_{n,m}$ for the standard unit-sphere orthonormal complex spherical harmonics and $j_n$ for the spherical Bessel function of the first kind. Let $\alpha_{n+1/2,j}$ be the $j$th positive zero of the ordinary Bessel function $J_{n+1/2}$, and set $\lambda_{n,j}=\alpha_{n+1/2,j}/a$ and
> $$
> \Psi_{jnm}(r,\theta,\phi)=j_n(\lambda_{n,j}r)Y_{n,m}(\theta,\phi),
> \qquad j\ge1,\ n\ge0,\ -n\le m\le n.
> $$
>
> Consider $\Delta u=f$ in $r<a$, with $u=g$ at $r=a$. For $f\in L^2$ and continuous boundary data $g$, let $v$ be the harmonic extension of $g$. Set
> $$
> F_{jnm}=\frac{\int_{r<a}f\overline{\Psi_{jnm}}\,dV}{\int_{r<a}|\Psi_{jnm}|^2\,dV}.
> $$
> Then the solution is
> $$
> u=v-\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{m=-n}^{n}\frac{F_{jnm}}{\lambda_{n,j}^2}\Psi_{jnm}.
> $$
> The sum gives the weak zero-Dirichlet correction; smooth data yield the corresponding classical solution. The harmonic term $v$ supplies the prescribed boundary values.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.4 The Helmholtz Equation with Applications to the Poisson, Heat, and Wave Equations.md
title: Zero-Dirichlet wave evolution in a ball by spherical eigenmodes
body:
> [!theorem|34973adc-a87d-5d10-8d23-6589cf30567c.local at=b867b412-21bd-5e92-924e-4f5d556c8059] Zero-Dirichlet wave evolution in a ball by spherical eigenmodes
> Let $a>0$. Use spherical coordinates with colatitude $\theta$, azimuth $\phi$, and volume measure $dV=r^2\sin\theta\,dr\,d\theta\,d\phi$. Write $Y_{n,m}$ for the standard unit-sphere orthonormal complex spherical harmonics and $j_n$ for the spherical Bessel function of the first kind. Let $\alpha_{n+1/2,j}$ be the $j$th positive zero of the ordinary Bessel function $J_{n+1/2}$, and set $\lambda_{n,j}=\alpha_{n+1/2,j}/a$ and
> $$
> \Psi_{jnm}(r,\theta,\phi)=j_n(\lambda_{n,j}r)Y_{n,m}(\theta,\phi),
> \qquad j\ge1,\ n\ge0,\ -n\le m\le n.
> $$
>
> Let $c>0$. For $u_{tt}=c^2\Delta u$ in $r<a$, zero boundary displacement at $r=a$, and initial data $u(\cdot,0)=f$, $u_t(\cdot,0)=g$, define
> $$
> F_{jnm}=\frac{\int_{r<a}f\overline{\Psi_{jnm}}\,dV}{\int_{r<a}|\Psi_{jnm}|^2\,dV},\qquad
> G_{jnm}=\frac{\int_{r<a}g\overline{\Psi_{jnm}}\,dV}{\int_{r<a}|\Psi_{jnm}|^2\,dV}.
> $$
> The modal solution is
> $$
> u(r,\theta,\phi,t)=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{m=-n}^{n}\Psi_{jnm}(r,\theta,\phi)
> \left[F_{jnm}\cos(c\lambda_{n,j}t)+\frac{G_{jnm}}{c\lambda_{n,j}}\sin(c\lambda_{n,j}t)\right].
> $$
> For $f\in H_0^1$ and $g\in L^2$ this is the energy solution; smooth compatible data give a classical solution. Here $H_0^1$ denotes square-integrable functions with square-integrable first derivatives and zero boundary trace.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.5 Legendre's Differential Equation.md
title: Legendre polynomial with the normalization at one
body:
> [!definition|e429f6d7-0540-5e28-9e61-221696326ae9.local at=41c415fa-9568-515f-b55a-fd8b0d556215] Legendre polynomial with the normalization at one
> For a nonnegative integer $n$, the Legendre polynomial $P_n$ is the degree-$n$ polynomial solution of
> $$
> (1-x^2)y''-2xy'+n(n+1)y=0
> $$
> normalized by $P_n(1)=1$. Equivalently, its leading coefficient is $(2n)!/[2^n(n!)^2]$, and
> $$
> P_n(x)=\frac1{2^n}\sum_{m=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}(-1)^m\frac{(2n-2m)!}{m!(n-m)!(n-2m)!}x^{n-2m}.
> $$

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.5 Legendre's Differential Equation.md
title: General solution of Legendre’s equation of integer degree
body:
> [!equation|b18296d0-620e-5825-a4de-838c8ec5f642.local at=ab1df737-5909-567a-863a-e8af3166a93f] General solution of Legendre’s equation of integer degree
> For a fixed integer $n\ge0$, the general solution of
> $$
> (1-x^2)y''-2xy'+n(n+1)y=0,\qquad -1<x<1,
> $$
> is
> $$
> y(x)=c_1P_n(x)+c_2Q_n(x),
> $$
> where $P_n$ is the Legendre polynomial normalized by $P_n(1)=1$, $Q_n$ is the real Legendre function of the second kind on $(-1,1)$, and $c_1,c_2$ are arbitrary constants. The function $P_n$ is bounded at both endpoints, whereas $Q_n$ is unbounded there.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.5 Legendre's Differential Equation.md
title: Parity, endpoint values, bounds and zeros of Legendre polynomials
body:
> [!property|82caf074-b664-5cfc-ae3f-b233b751fd0d.local at=0a04882c-d6f2-52b0-93ba-d9f678235427] Parity, endpoint values, bounds and zeros of Legendre polynomials
> For integers $n\ge0$, let $P_n$ be the Legendre polynomial normalized by $P_n(1)=1$. Then
> $$
> P_n(-x)=(-1)^nP_n(x),\qquad P_n(-1)=(-1)^n,
> $$
> and $|P_n(x)|\le1$ for $-1\le x\le1$. For $n\ge1$, $P_n$ has exactly $n$ distinct zeros in $(-1,1)$, and all its relative extrema lie in $[-1,1]$. The constant polynomial $P_0=1$ is excluded from the extrema-location assertion.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.6 Legendre Polynomials and Legendre Series Expansions.md
title: Rodrigues’ formula for Legendre polynomials
body:
> [!identity|fb2e5281-924b-5151-a932-01eef37eb124.local at=b9818235-2688-508c-bd89-af0c22d81da8] Rodrigues’ formula for Legendre polynomials
> For every nonnegative integer $n$, the Legendre polynomial normalized by $P_n(1)=1$ satisfies
> $$
> P_n(x)=\frac1{2^n n!}\frac{d^n}{dx^n}(x^2-1)^n.
> $$

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.6 Legendre Polynomials and Legendre Series Expansions.md
title: Bonnet’s three-term recurrence for Legendre polynomials
body:
> [!identity|3812d1e6-7ecb-530a-a502-6d0f0a70d31f.local at=dbe9fd0e-5c32-5aa3-a0b2-b81c57582e0a] Bonnet’s three-term recurrence for Legendre polynomials
> For integers $n\ge1$, the Legendre polynomials normalized by $P_k(1)=1$ satisfy
> $$
> (n+1)P_{n+1}(x)+nP_{n-1}(x)=(2n+1)xP_n(x).
> $$

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.6 Legendre Polynomials and Legendre Series Expansions.md
title: Orthogonality and squared norms of Legendre polynomials
body:
> [!theorem|f402a21f-6687-5549-88bf-1527db76b6fc.local at=50b109e5-0896-5f49-b976-0d98ef1a9fe0] Orthogonality and squared norms of Legendre polynomials
> For nonnegative integers $m,n$, let $P_m,P_n$ be the Legendre polynomials normalized by $P_k(1)=1$. Then
> $$
> \int_{-1}^1P_m(x)P_n(x)\,dx=
> \begin{cases}0,&m\ne n,\\[2pt]\dfrac2{2n+1},&m=n.\end{cases}
> $$

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.6 Legendre Polynomials and Legendre Series Expansions.md
title: Pointwise convergence and coefficients of a Legendre series
body:
> [!theorem|5a845fe2-5dc9-55dd-b849-8dd528c0aef7.local at=0ce2435d-4e30-5b6a-9f67-51d5d3ec6ed2] Pointwise convergence and coefficients of a Legendre series
> Let $f$ be piecewise smooth on $[-1,1]$, with finitely many continuously differentiable pieces and finite one-sided limits of $f$ and $f'$ at their endpoints. For the Legendre polynomials $P_j$ normalized by $P_j(1)=1$, set
> $$
> A_j=\frac{2j+1}{2}\int_{-1}^1f(t)P_j(t)\,dt.
> $$
> At each $-1<x<1$,
> $$
> \sum_{j=0}^{\infty}A_jP_j(x)=\frac{f(x+)+f(x-)}2.
> $$
> At continuity points this equals $f(x)$. This statement makes no endpoint-convergence assertion.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.7 Associated Legendre Functions and Series Expansions.md
title: Associated Legendre functions of integer degree and nonnegative order
body:
> [!definition|e9be7f8c-6b27-5520-8b51-89b4ef5bb0a1.local at=d9a40629-4938-5adb-a3cb-945f71ab068c] Associated Legendre functions of integer degree and nonnegative order
> Let $n\ge0$ and $0\le m\le n$ be integers, and let $P_n$ be the Legendre polynomial with $P_n(1)=1$. On $-1<x<1$, define
> $$
> P_n^m(x)=(-1)^m(1-x^2)^{m/2}\frac{d^mP_n(x)}{dx^m}.
> $$
> The factor $(-1)^m$ specifies the Condon–Shortley phase convention. Values at $x=\pm1$ are defined by continuous extension. The degree is $n$ and the order is $m$.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.7 Associated Legendre Functions and Series Expansions.md
title: Negative-order associated Legendre functions with the Condon–Shortley phase
body:
> [!convention|219dd4b7-1248-54fb-9a76-50bb1fa8d7c2.local at=0de7a522-0a76-5af5-bd79-6b53cbc83052] Negative-order associated Legendre functions with the Condon–Shortley phase
> For integers $n\ge0$ and $1\le m\le n$, extend the associated Legendre functions by
> $$
> P_n^{-m}(x)=(-1)^m\frac{(n-m)!}{(n+m)!}P_n^m(x),\qquad -1\le x\le1,
> $$
> where positive orders use $P_n^m(x)=(-1)^m(1-x^2)^{m/2}d^mP_n(x)/dx^m$ and $P_n(1)=1$.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.7 Associated Legendre Functions and Series Expansions.md
title: Associated Legendre differential equation for integer degree and order
body:
> [!equation|319b9013-8b17-5eb7-8f78-3c37630e1bbe.local at=25be9b09-5c3c-542d-9b79-be7c91c589ac] Associated Legendre differential equation for integer degree and order
> For integers $n\ge0$ and $|m|\le n$, the associated Legendre function $P_n^m$ satisfies
> $$
> (1-x^2)y''-2xy'+\left(n(n+1)-\frac{m^2}{1-x^2}\right)y=0,\qquad -1<x<1.
> $$
> For nonnegative order, $P_n^m=(-1)^m(1-x^2)^{m/2}d^mP_n/dx^m$, where $P_n$ is the Legendre polynomial; negative orders are proportional to the corresponding positive orders.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.7 Associated Legendre Functions and Series Expansions.md
title: Orthogonality and norms of associated Legendre functions at fixed order
body:
> [!theorem|46143ca3-2007-5076-af3f-e74922744345.local at=afd136f1-6507-5601-9dfd-278ca930709b] Orthogonality and norms of associated Legendre functions at fixed order
> Fix an integer order $m$. For degrees $k,n\ge |m|$, use associated Legendre functions with the Condon–Shortley phase and the negative-order convention $P_n^{-q}=(-1)^q(n-q)!P_n^q/(n+q)!$. Then
> $$
> \int_{-1}^1P_k^m(x)P_n^m(x)\,dx=0\quad(k\ne n),
> $$
> and
> $$
> \int_{-1}^1[P_n^m(x)]^2\,dx=\frac2{2n+1}\frac{(n+m)!}{(n-m)!}.
> $$
> The underlying Legendre polynomials are normalized by $P_n(1)=1$.

path: Chapter 13 Partial Differential Equations in Spherical Coordinates/13.7 Associated Legendre Functions and Series Expansions.md
title: Pointwise convergence of an associated Legendre series at fixed nonnegative order
body:
> [!theorem|02e0ff4e-38c8-58ec-85b4-8ec243ddc266.local at=95d4c4f4-1f58-5179-b769-a7ad14f862d9] Pointwise convergence of an associated Legendre series at fixed nonnegative order
> Fix an integer $m\ge0$. Suppose $f$ is piecewise smooth on $[-1,1]$, with finitely many continuously differentiable pieces and finite one-sided limits of $f$ and $f'$ at their endpoints. Let
> $$
> P_n^m(x)=(-1)^m(1-x^2)^{m/2}\frac{d^mP_n(x)}{dx^m},\qquad n\ge m,
> $$
> where $P_n(1)=1$. Define
> $$
> A_n=\frac{2n+1}{2}\frac{(n-m)!}{(n+m)!}\int_{-1}^1f(t)P_n^m(t)\,dt.
> $$
> Then, for $-1<x<1$,
> $$
> \sum_{n=m}^{\infty}A_nP_n^m(x)=\frac{f(x+)+f(x-)}2.
> $$
> This equals $f(x)$ at continuity points. Endpoint convergence is not asserted.

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.1 Orthogonal Functions.md
title: Inner Product and Norm of Square-Integrable Functions
body:
> [!definition] Inner Product and Norm of Square-Integrable Functions
> Let $I=(a,b)$, allowing infinite endpoints. For real or complex functions $f,g\in L^2(I)$, define
>
> $$
> (f,g)=\int_a^b f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx,
> \qquad \|f\|_2=\left(\int_a^b |f(x)|^2\,dx\right)^{1/2}.
> $$
>
> For real functions the conjugate can be omitted. The inner product is linear in its first argument. Functions equal almost everywhere represent the same element of $L^2(I)$.

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.1 Orthogonal Functions.md
title: Orthogonal and Orthonormal Systems of Functions
body:
> [!definition] Orthogonal and Orthonormal Systems of Functions
> In $L^2(I)$ with inner product $(f,g)=\int_I f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, two functions are orthogonal when $(f,g)=0$. A system $\{f_n\}$ is orthogonal when $\|f_n\|_2>0$ for every $n$ and $(f_n,f_m)=0$ whenever $n\ne m$. It is orthonormal when, in addition, $\|f_n\|_2=1$ for every $n$. Dividing each member of an orthogonal system by its norm produces an orthonormal system.

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.1 Orthogonal Functions.md
title: Coefficients of an Orthogonal Function Expansion
body:
> [!theorem] Coefficients of an Orthogonal Function Expansion
> Let $\{f_j\}_{j\ge1}$ be a nonzero orthogonal system in $L^2(I)$, with $(f,g)=\int_I f\overline g\,dx$. If $f=\sum_{j=1}^\infty a_jf_j$ with convergence in $L^2(I)$, then
>
> $$
> a_j=\frac{(f,f_j)}{\|f_j\|_2^2},
> \qquad f=\sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{(f,f_j)}{\|f_j\|_2^2}f_j.
> $$
>
> The latter series is the generalized Fourier series of $f$ in this orthogonal system.

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.1 Orthogonal Functions.md
title: Completeness of an Orthogonal System in a Hilbert Space
body:
> [!definition] Completeness of an Orthogonal System in a Hilbert Space
> An orthogonal system $\{f_j\}$ in a Hilbert space $H$ is complete if the only element orthogonal to every $f_j$ is the zero element. Equivalently, the closure of its linear span is $H$. For $H=L^2(I)$, the zero element means a function that vanishes almost everywhere.

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.1 Orthogonal Functions.md
title: Weighted Inner Product, Norm, and Orthogonality of Functions
body:
> [!definition] Weighted Inner Product, Norm, and Orthogonality of Functions
> Let $w\ge0$ be a measurable weight on an interval $I$, and consider functions with $\int_I|f|^2w\,dx<\infty$. In $L^2(I,w\,dx)$, functions equal almost everywhere with respect to the measure $w\,dx$ are identified. Define
>
> $$
> (f,g)_w=\int_I f(x)\overline{g(x)}w(x)\,dx,
> \qquad \|f\|_w=\left(\int_I|f(x)|^2w(x)\,dx\right)^{1/2}.
> $$
>
> Functions $f,g$ are orthogonal with respect to $w$ if $(f,g)_w=0$. An orthogonal system has nonzero norm for each member and mutually orthogonal distinct members. It is orthonormal if every member has norm one.

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.1 Orthogonal Functions.md
title: Coefficients of a Weighted Orthogonal Function Expansion
body:
> [!theorem] Coefficients of a Weighted Orthogonal Function Expansion
> Let $\{f_j\}_{j\ge1}$ be a nonzero orthogonal system in $L^2(I,w\,dx)$ for a nonnegative weight $w$. Write $(f,g)_w=\int_I f\overline g\,w\,dx$ and $\|f\|_w^2=(f,f)_w$. If $f=\sum_{j=1}^\infty a_jf_j$ with convergence in this weighted norm, then
>
> $$
> a_j=\frac{(f,f_j)_w}{\|f_j\|_w^2},
> \qquad f=\sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{(f,f_j)_w}{\|f_j\|_w^2}f_j.
> $$

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.1 Orthogonal Functions.md
title: Parseval Identity for a Complete Weighted Orthogonal System
body:
> [!theorem] Parseval Identity for a Complete Weighted Orthogonal System
> Let $\{f_j\}_{j\ge1}$ be a complete nonzero orthogonal system in $L^2(I,w\,dx)$, where $w\ge0$. With $(f,g)_w=\int_I f\overline g\,w\,dx$ and $\|f\|_w^2=(f,f)_w$, every $f\in L^2(I,w\,dx)$ satisfies
>
> $$
> \int_I|f(x)|^2w(x)\,dx
> =\sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{|(f,f_j)_w|^2}{\|f_j\|_w^2}.
> $$

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.2 Sturm-Liouville Theory.md
title: Regular Sturm–Liouville Problem with Separated Boundary Conditions
body:
> [!definition|805bda36-235a-5169-9a2a-98b17eeb0c50.local at=8918ebfe-774e-5419-b917-6a9b41241c57] Regular Sturm–Liouville Problem with Separated Boundary Conditions
> Let $a<b$ be finite, $p\in C^1[a,b]$, and $q,r\in C[a,b]$ be real, with $p>0$ and $r>0$. Consider
>
> $$
> (py')'+(q+\lambda r)y=0,\qquad
> c_1y(a)+c_2y'(a)=0,\quad d_1y(b)+d_2y'(b)=0,
> $$
>
> where the boundary coefficients are real, $(c_1,c_2)\ne(0,0)$, and $(d_1,d_2)\ne(0,0)$.
>
> This boundary value problem is a regular Sturm–Liouville problem. A value of $\lambda$ admitting a nonzero solution is an eigenvalue, and such a solution is an eigenfunction.

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.2 Sturm-Liouville Theory.md
title: Singular Sturm–Liouville Problem
body:
> [!definition|56de0eb2-bd59-5c60-bcac-93664c7073f9.local at=f989c2af-ea26-5bc3-9ccf-f756a65490e0] Singular Sturm–Liouville Problem
> Consider $(py')'+(q+\lambda r)y=0$ on an interval $(a,b)$, with real coefficients, $p\in C^1(a,b)$, $q,r\in C(a,b)$, and $p,r>0$ in the interior. The problem is singular if an endpoint is infinite or the regular endpoint conditions on the coefficients fail. Appropriate boundary or endpoint admissibility conditions, such as boundedness, are part of the problem and depend on the singular endpoint.

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.2 Sturm-Liouville Theory.md
title: Real Discrete Spectrum of a Regular Separated Sturm–Liouville Problem
body:
> [!theorem|61c35791-6311-5925-97b4-7fa5400e592a.local at=f895caa3-0a82-5476-a777-7964874444e1] Real Discrete Spectrum of a Regular Separated Sturm–Liouville Problem
> Let $a<b$ be finite, $p\in C^1[a,b]$, and $q,r\in C[a,b]$ be real, with $p>0$ and $r>0$. Consider
>
> $$
> (py')'+(q+\lambda r)y=0,\qquad
> c_1y(a)+c_2y'(a)=0,\quad d_1y(b)+d_2y'(b)=0,
> $$
>
> where the boundary coefficients are real, $(c_1,c_2)\ne(0,0)$, and $(d_1,d_2)\ne(0,0)$.
>
> Its eigenvalues are real and can be ordered as a strictly increasing sequence $\lambda_1<\lambda_2<\cdots$ with $\lambda_j\to+\infty$.

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.2 Sturm-Liouville Theory.md
title: Vanishing Boundary Form and Sturm–Liouville Orthogonality
body:
> [!property|9d63ccb8-773a-5f08-9aac-aef50c8976b2.local at=abc50dbe-ec5f-50e5-b5c6-79eeb9d6d04e] Vanishing Boundary Form and Sturm–Liouville Orthogonality
> Let real functions $y_1,y_2$ solve $(py_j')'+(q+\lambda_jr)y_j=0$ on $(a,b)$ for distinct real parameters $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$, where $p\in C^1$, $q,r$ are continuous and real, and $p,r>0$ in the interior. Assume $y_1,y_2\in L^2((a,b),r\,dx)$ and the endpoint limits below exist. If
>
> $$
> \lim_{x\uparrow b}p(x)(y_1y_2'-y_2y_1')
> -\lim_{x\downarrow a}p(x)(y_1y_2'-y_2y_1')=0,
> $$
>
> then $\int_a^b y_1(x)y_2(x)r(x)\,dx=0$.

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.2 Sturm-Liouville Theory.md
title: Simplicity and Orthogonality for Regular Separated Sturm–Liouville Problems
body:
> [!theorem|d47be7bf-422c-5bf2-adb7-8da618a5954a.local at=6572f4b5-3e07-592c-be0b-5f9a7b965356] Simplicity and Orthogonality for Regular Separated Sturm–Liouville Problems
> Let $a<b$ be finite, $p\in C^1[a,b]$, and $q,r\in C[a,b]$ be real, with $p>0$ and $r>0$. Consider
>
> $$
> (py')'+(q+\lambda r)y=0,\qquad
> c_1y(a)+c_2y'(a)=0,\quad d_1y(b)+d_2y'(b)=0,
> $$
>
> where the boundary coefficients are real, $(c_1,c_2)\ne(0,0)$, and $(d_1,d_2)\ne(0,0)$.
>
> Each eigenvalue has a one-dimensional eigenspace. Eigenfunctions for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal in $L^2((a,b),r\,dx)$:
>
> $$
> \int_a^b y_j(x)\overline{y_k(x)}r(x)\,dx=0\qquad(\lambda_j\ne\lambda_k).
> $$

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.2 Sturm-Liouville Theory.md
title: Eigenfunction Expansion for a Regular Separated Sturm–Liouville Problem
body:
> [!theorem|9fd91445-18fe-55d1-9aaa-1205e1e63c0d.local at=3a24cf97-788d-544f-8042-dca7da7b4f8f] Eigenfunction Expansion for a Regular Separated Sturm–Liouville Problem
> Let $a<b$ be finite, $p\in C^1[a,b]$, and $q,r\in C[a,b]$ be real, with $p>0$ and $r>0$. Consider
>
> $$
> (py')'+(q+\lambda r)y=0,\qquad
> c_1y(a)+c_2y'(a)=0,\quad d_1y(b)+d_2y'(b)=0,
> $$
>
> where the boundary coefficients are real, $(c_1,c_2)\ne(0,0)$, and $(d_1,d_2)\ne(0,0)$.
>
> Choose one real nonzero eigenfunction $y_j$ for each eigenvalue, in increasing eigenvalue order. These eigenfunctions form a complete orthogonal system in $L^2((a,b),r\,dx)$. For $f$ in that space, its expansion converges in the weighted $L^2$ norm and has coefficients
>
> $$
> f=\sum_{j=1}^\infty A_jy_j,\qquad
> A_j=\frac{\int_a^b f(x)y_j(x)r(x)\,dx}{\int_a^b y_j(x)^2r(x)\,dx}.
> $$
>
> If $f$ is piecewise smooth on $[a,b]$, the series converges at each interior point to $[f(x+)+f(x-)]/2$, and hence to $f(x)$ at every interior point of continuity.

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.3 The Hanging Chain.md
title: Orthogonality and Norms of Hanging-Chain Bessel Modes
body:
> [!property|863a398f-f0e7-5916-be05-fdab2ed15b2f.local at=b61880c9-2b7e-57fa-8d6a-a871183f4339] Orthogonality and Norms of Hanging-Chain Bessel Modes
> Let $L>0$ and let $\alpha_j$ be the $j$th positive zero of the Bessel function $J_0$. Define $X_j(x)=J_0(\alpha_j\sqrt{x/L})$ for $0\le x\le L$. Then
>
> $$
> \int_0^L X_j(x)X_k(x)\,dx=0\quad(j\ne k),\qquad
> \int_0^L X_j(x)^2\,dx=LJ_1(\alpha_j)^2.
> $$

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.6 The Biharmonic Operator.md
title: Biharmonic Operator and Biharmonic Functions
body:
> [!definition|76835f9d-28d6-5f69-8417-b4f9e1169841.local at=1be6cc23-0b90-5b50-91a0-067c983cefa0] Biharmonic Operator and Biharmonic Functions
> For $u\in C^4(\Omega)$ on an open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$, the biharmonic operator is the iterated Laplacian,
>
> $$
> \nabla^4u=\nabla^2(\nabla^2u)=u_{xxxx}+2u_{xxyy}+u_{yyyy}.
> $$
>
> The function $u$ is biharmonic on $\Omega$ if $\nabla^4u=0$ there.

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.6 The Biharmonic Operator.md
title: Biharmonic Dirichlet Problem on a Disk via Two Harmonic Extensions
body:
> [!theorem|370f36f3-d8bc-5f47-90f8-c6b10700f5fe.local at=5369b0e0-c11b-5a65-b241-3e717de98fa2] Biharmonic Dirichlet Problem on a Disk via Two Harmonic Extensions
> Let $a>0$ and prescribe smooth $2\pi$-periodic functions $f,g$ on the boundary of the disk $D_a=\{r<a\}$. Let $w$ and then $v$ be the regular harmonic functions in the disk with boundary data
>
> $$
> w(a,\theta)=f(\theta),\qquad
> v(a,\theta)=\frac{w_r(a,\theta)-g(\theta)}{2a}.
> $$
>
> Then the unique smooth biharmonic solution of
>
> $$
> \nabla^4u=0\ \text{in }D_a,\qquad
> u(a,\theta)=f(\theta),\quad u_r(a,\theta)=g(\theta)
> $$
>
> is $u(r,\theta)=(a^2-r^2)v(r,\theta)+w(r,\theta)$.

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.7 Vibrations of Circular Plates.md
title: Radial Scaling of Solutions of the Laplace Eigenvalue Equation
body:
> [!proposition] Radial Scaling of Solutions of the Laplace Eigenvalue Equation
> Suppose $\phi(r,\theta)$ satisfies $\nabla^2\phi=\lambda\phi$ on a planar domain. For a positive real dilation $\alpha$ and a nonzero constant $A$, define $\psi(r,\theta)=A\phi(\alpha r,\theta)$ on the correspondingly rescaled domain. Then $\nabla^2\psi=\alpha^2\lambda\psi$. This is a statement about the differential equation; boundary conditions must also be rescaled.
>
> The same algebra applies to a complex value of $\alpha$ when the radial factor has an analytic continuation to the required complex arguments, as for integer-order Bessel functions.

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.7 Vibrations of Circular Plates.md
title: Clamped Circular-Plate Eigenfunctions from Bessel Functions
body:
> [!theorem] Clamped Circular-Plate Eigenfunctions from Bessel Functions
> Let $a>0$. For each integer $m\ge0$, let $k_{mn}$, $n=1,2,\ldots$, be the positive roots in increasing order of
>
> $$
> J_m(ka)I_m'(ka)-I_m(ka)J_m'(ka)=0,
> $$
>
> where $J_m$ and $I_m$ are the Bessel and modified Bessel functions of order $m$, and primes denote derivatives of their arguments. Define
>
> $$
> R_{mn}(r)=I_m(k_{mn}a)J_m(k_{mn}r)-J_m(k_{mn}a)I_m(k_{mn}r).
> $$
>
> The nonzero modes $R_{mn}(r)\cos(m\theta)$ for $m\ge0$, and $R_{mn}(r)\sin(m\theta)$ for $m\ge1$, are smooth at the center and satisfy
>
> $$
> \nabla^4\phi=k_{mn}^4\phi\quad(r<a),\qquad
> \phi(a,\theta)=\phi_r(a,\theta)=0.
> $$

path: Chapter 14 Sturm-Liouville Theory with Engineering Applications/14.7 Vibrations of Circular Plates.md
title: Integrals of Products of Order-Zero Bessel and Modified Bessel Functions
body:
> [!identity] Integrals of Products of Order-Zero Bessel and Modified Bessel Functions
> For a nonzero real constant $\lambda$, with $J_\nu$ and $I_\nu$ denoting Bessel and modified Bessel functions,
>
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> \int xJ_0(\lambda x)^2\,dx
> &=\frac{x^2}{2}\left[J_0(\lambda x)^2+J_1(\lambda x)^2\right]+C,\\
> \int xI_0(\lambda x)^2\,dx
> &=\frac{x^2}{2}\left[I_0(\lambda x)^2-I_1(\lambda x)^2\right]+C,\\
> \int xI_0(\lambda x)J_0(\lambda x)\,dx
> &=\frac{x}{2\lambda}\left[I_1(\lambda x)J_0(\lambda x)+I_0(\lambda x)J_1(\lambda x)\right]+C.
> \end{aligned}
> $$

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.1 Schrödinger's Equation.md
title: Born Position Probability Rule for a Normalized Wave Function
body:
> [!equation|54a28dfd-30da-5523-99ec-ce9d48ef36e8.local at=bdd72c66-8c3e-5f08-bbd0-143fc071b740] Born Position Probability Rule for a Normalized Wave Function
> For a normalized wave function $\psi\in L^2(\Omega)$, the position probability density is $\rho(\mathbf x)=|\psi(\mathbf x)|^2$, with $\int_\Omega|\psi|^2\,dV=1$. The probability of finding the particle in a measurable region $D\subseteq\Omega$ is
>
> $$
> \Pr(\mathbf x\in D)=\int_D|\psi(\mathbf x)|^2\,dV.
> $$

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.1 Schrödinger's Equation.md
title: Time-Dependent Schrödinger Equation for a Particle in a Scalar Potential
body:
> [!equation|badc4a50-c499-55b4-bff5-9b6b456cc60e.local at=176aa5f0-d7dc-5812-9efb-664ab086a528] Time-Dependent Schrödinger Equation for a Particle in a Scalar Potential
> For a nonrelativistic spin-free particle of mass $\mu>0$ in a time-independent real scalar potential $V(\mathbf x)$, with no magnetic vector potential,
>
> $$
> i\hbar\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t}
> =-\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu}\nabla^2\psi+V(\mathbf x)\psi.
> $$
>
> Here $\hbar=h/(2\pi)$ is the reduced Planck constant, $\psi$ is the wave function, and the Laplacian acts on the spatial variables. The equation is supplied with the physical domain, boundary conditions, and initial state.

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.1 Schrödinger's Equation.md
title: Normalizable and Normalized Quantum Wave Functions
body:
> [!definition|45879971-2f63-545d-9561-b7cd14586826.local at=f4ad4499-052e-5d10-8351-85c6e2652dfd] Normalizable and Normalized Quantum Wave Functions
> A nonzero wave function $u$ on a configuration domain $\Omega$ is normalizable if $\int_\Omega|u|^2\,dV<\infty$. It is normalized if that integral equals one. A normalizable wave function becomes normalized after division by its $L^2$ norm. Pointwise decay at infinity is not part of the abstract $L^2$ definition; the bound-state solutions considered here also decay.

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.1 Schrödinger's Equation.md
title: Stationary State of a Time-Independent Schrödinger Hamiltonian
body:
> [!definition|f702ef12-9c84-51b6-8698-798a3021c25a.local at=cc04c61e-0f04-52c0-a04f-9c109182fe94] Stationary State of a Time-Independent Schrödinger Hamiltonian
> For a particle of mass $\mu>0$ with a time-independent real potential $V$, let $H=-\hbar^2\nabla^2/(2\mu)+V$ be the self-adjoint Hamiltonian with the prescribed domain and boundary conditions. If $Hu=Eu$, $E\in\mathbb R$, and $u$ is a normalized eigenfunction, then
>
> $$
> \psi(\mathbf x,t)=e^{-iEt/\hbar}u(\mathbf x)
> $$
>
> is a stationary state of energy $E$. Its position probability density is $|u(\mathbf x)|^2$, independent of time.

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.2 The Hydrogen Atom.md
title: Bound-State Energies and Degeneracy of the Spin-Free Hydrogen Atom
body:
> [!theorem] Bound-State Energies and Degeneracy of the Spin-Free Hydrogen Atom
> Consider the nonrelativistic, spin-free hydrogen Coulomb Hamiltonian $H=-\hbar^2\nabla^2/(2\mu)-\epsilon^2/r$ with a fixed nucleus, electron mass $\mu>0$, and the usual regular physical domain at the origin. Here $\epsilon^2$ is the Coulomb coupling (in SI, $e^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$), $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant, and $a=\hbar^2/(\mu\epsilon^2)$.
>
> Write $\nu=1,2,\ldots$, $n=0,\ldots,\nu-1$, and $m=-n,\ldots,n$. Let $Y_{n,m}$ be orthonormal spherical harmonics and $L_j^\alpha$ the generalized Laguerre polynomials. Define
>
> $$
> R_{\nu n}(r)=e^{-r/(\nu a)}\left(\frac{2r}{\nu a}\right)^n L_{\nu-n-1}^{2n+1}\left(\frac{2r}{\nu a}\right).
> $$
>
> The bound-state energies and a basis of their spatial eigenspaces are
>
> $$
> E_\nu=-\frac{\mu\epsilon^4}{2\hbar^2\nu^2},\qquad
> u_{\nu nm}(r,\theta,\phi)=R_{\nu n}(r)Y_{n,m}(\theta,\phi).
> $$
>
> The eigenspace at $E_\nu$ has dimension $\nu^2$ before spin is included. Arbitrary linear combinations within that eigenspace are also states of the same energy.

title: Parseval Identity for the Unitary Fourier Transform

> Use the unitary angular-frequency Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-i\omega x}f(x)\,dx$, extended from integrable square-integrable functions to all of $L^2(\mathbb R)$ by $L^2$ limits.
>
> For $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb R)$,
>
> $$
> \int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx
> =\int_{\mathbb R}\widehat f(\omega)\overline{\widehat g(\omega)}\,d\omega.
> $$
