title: Plancherel Norm Identity for the Unitary Fourier Transform
body:
> [!theorem|53a7cbce-e8ac-580f-adec-f211d6ebcd85.local at=751cc718-f630-584d-b54b-90e3afaf91fa] Plancherel Norm Identity for the Unitary Fourier Transform
> Use the unitary angular-frequency Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-i\omega x}f(x)\,dx$, extended from integrable square-integrable functions to all of $L^2(\mathbb R)$ by $L^2$ limits.
>
> Every $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ satisfies
>
> $$
> \int_{\mathbb R}|f(x)|^2\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}|\widehat f(\omega)|^2\,d\omega.
> $$

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.3 Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle.md
title: Mean-Square Spread of a Square-Integrable Function About a Point
body:
> [!definition|ed5fa2e1-80e1-5e31-a743-ccf855acdb28.local at=b0d75f5e-b823-50cd-b9ea-1d50e814fd40] Mean-Square Spread of a Square-Integrable Function About a Point
> For a nonzero $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ and $a\in\mathbb R$, define
>
> $$
> \Delta_af=\frac{\int_{\mathbb R}(x-a)^2|f(x)|^2\,dx}{\int_{\mathbb R}|f(x)|^2\,dx}.
> $$
>
> This quantity can be infinite. When $a$ is the mean of the normalized density $|f|^2/\|f\|_2^2$, it is the variance; its square root is the standard deviation. The symbol $\Delta_a$ here denotes mean-square spread, not standard deviation.

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.3 Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle.md
title: Heisenberg Uncertainty Inequality for the Unitary Fourier Transform
body:
> [!theorem|b2853fb2-4b61-5ff1-ae4b-2f9b2f1f032d.local at=a8920430-5d02-57d7-9ac0-111b097ee555] Heisenberg Uncertainty Inequality for the Unitary Fourier Transform
> Use the unitary angular-frequency Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-i\omega x}f(x)\,dx$, extended from integrable square-integrable functions to all of $L^2(\mathbb R)$ by $L^2$ limits.
>
> Let $f\ne0$ in $L^2(\mathbb R)$ and $a,\alpha\in\mathbb R$. Define
>
> $$
> \Delta_af=\frac{\int_{\mathbb R}(x-a)^2|f(x)|^2\,dx}{\|f\|_2^2},\qquad
> \Delta_\alpha\widehat f=\frac{\int_{\mathbb R}(\omega-\alpha)^2|\widehat f(\omega)|^2\,d\omega}{\|\widehat f\|_2^2}.
> $$
>
> If both moments are finite, then $\Delta_af\,\Delta_\alpha\widehat f\ge1/4$. If either is infinite, the inequality holds in the extended sense. At the respective means this is the standard-deviation inequality $\sigma_x\sigma_\omega\ge1/2$.

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.4 Hermite and Laguerre Polynomials.md
title: Physicists’ Hermite Polynomials
body:
> [!definition|19ed3268-923a-5175-b0b7-34d2c9d04b09.local at=fb11acdf-ab67-52df-9d3c-2ac218191a5b] Physicists’ Hermite Polynomials
> The physicists' Hermite polynomial $H_n$ is the polynomial solution of $H_n''-2xH_n'+2nH_n=0$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, for $n=0,1,2,\ldots$.
>
> $$
> H_{n}(x)=n!\sum_{j=0}^{M} \frac{(-1)^{j}(2 x)^{n-2 j}}{j!(n-2 j)!},
> $$
>
> where $M=\frac{n}{2}$ if $n$ is even or $M=\frac{n-1}{2}$ if $n$ is odd.

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.4 Hermite and Laguerre Polynomials.md
title: Weighted Orthogonality and Norms of Physicists’ Hermite Polynomials
body:
> [!theorem|6e32b0f4-a134-52da-92b5-4ff791421141.local at=ae4809c8-09c9-592d-b0d6-b8498aa02cc1] Weighted Orthogonality and Norms of Physicists’ Hermite Polynomials
> The physicists' Hermite polynomial $H_n$ is the polynomial solution of $H_n''-2xH_n'+2nH_n=0$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, for $n=0,1,2,\ldots$.
>
> $$
> \int_{-\infty}^\infty H_m(x)H_n(x)e^{-x^2}\,dx
> =\begin{cases}0,&m\ne n,\\2^nn!\sqrt\pi,&m=n.\end{cases}
> $$

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.4 Hermite and Laguerre Polynomials.md
title: Hermite Series Expansion with Gaussian Weight
body:
> [!theorem|51b8cc9b-4f9a-524f-93ba-008d2df464c2.local at=6e3b54e0-9c0e-5578-be0f-a15e118f660f] Hermite Series Expansion with Gaussian Weight
> The physicists' Hermite polynomial $H_n$ is the polynomial solution of $H_n''-2xH_n'+2nH_n=0$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, for $n=0,1,2,\ldots$.
>
> For $f\in L^2(\mathbb R,e^{-x^2}dx)$, its Hermite expansion converges in that weighted norm and is
>
> $$
> f=\sum_{j=0}^\infty A_jH_j,\qquad
> A_j=\frac{1}{2^jj!\sqrt\pi}\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)H_j(x)e^{-x^2}\,dx.
> $$
>
> If $f$ is also piecewise smooth, the series converges at each finite $x$ to $[f(x+)+f(x-)]/2$, and hence to $f(x)$ at continuity points.

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.4 Hermite and Laguerre Polynomials.md
title: Laguerre Polynomials
body:
> [!definition|a8eee23b-bc7f-58a2-9654-ab9573067743.local at=2392cb69-ba1a-59ad-966e-88a08887f6ea] Laguerre Polynomials
> The Laguerre polynomial $L_n$ solves $xL_n''+(1-x)L_n'+nL_n=0$ and has leading coefficient $(-1)^n/n!$, for $n=0,1,2,\ldots$.
>
> $$
> L_{n}(x)=n!\sum_{j=0}^{n} \frac{(-1)^{j}}{(j!)^{2}(n-j)!} x^{j} .
> $$

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.4 Hermite and Laguerre Polynomials.md
title: Weighted Orthogonality and Unit Norms of Laguerre Polynomials
body:
> [!theorem|67be6b7a-d430-5516-a261-a7c3b3d0d1ee.local at=9a8d7693-19cf-5127-9bf4-bf77f65b0960] Weighted Orthogonality and Unit Norms of Laguerre Polynomials
> The Laguerre polynomial $L_n$ solves $xL_n''+(1-x)L_n'+nL_n=0$ and has leading coefficient $(-1)^n/n!$, for $n=0,1,2,\ldots$.
>
> $$
> \int_0^\infty L_m(x)L_n(x)e^{-x}\,dx
> =\begin{cases}0,&m\ne n,\\1,&m=n.\end{cases}
> $$

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.4 Hermite and Laguerre Polynomials.md
title: Laguerre Series Expansion with Exponential Weight
body:
> [!theorem|a4e31473-2fcb-525c-958f-476f80490a1a.local at=0ce9b992-9e38-556e-b4d2-89da4eebc5e9] Laguerre Series Expansion with Exponential Weight
> The Laguerre polynomial $L_n$ solves $xL_n''+(1-x)L_n'+nL_n=0$ and has leading coefficient $(-1)^n/n!$, for $n=0,1,2,\ldots$.
>
> For $f\in L^2((0,\infty),e^{-x}dx)$, its Laguerre expansion converges in that weighted norm and is
>
> $$
> f=\sum_{j=0}^\infty A_jL_j,\qquad A_j=\int_0^\infty f(x)L_j(x)e^{-x}\,dx.
> $$
>
> If $f$ is also piecewise smooth on $[0,\infty)$, the series converges at every $x>0$ to $[f(x+)+f(x-)]/2$, and hence to $f(x)$ at continuity points.

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.4 Hermite and Laguerre Polynomials.md
title: Generalized Laguerre Polynomials
body:
> [!definition|50e2ccf1-9203-5933-852e-3bb14c6eb7f5.local at=45f48f09-f412-5152-b6a3-e437fb9ad12c] Generalized Laguerre Polynomials
> For $\alpha>-1$ and integers $n\ge0$, let $L_n^\alpha$ denote the generalized Laguerre polynomial solving $xy''+(\alpha+1-x)y'+ny=0$ with leading coefficient $(-1)^n/n!$.
>
> $$
> L_{n}^{\alpha}(x)=\Gamma(\alpha+n+1) \sum_{j=0}^{n} \frac{(-1)^{j}}{j!(n-j)!\Gamma(\alpha+j+1)} x^{j}
> $$
>
> Here $\Gamma$ is the gamma function.

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.4 Hermite and Laguerre Polynomials.md
title: Weighted Orthogonality and Norms of Generalized Laguerre Polynomials
body:
> [!theorem|7f66db87-1a71-5e78-99e1-964dc08b0749.local at=b5fa0093-3e56-57e1-9f10-12b71ab4dfc1] Weighted Orthogonality and Norms of Generalized Laguerre Polynomials
> For $\alpha>-1$ and integers $n\ge0$, let $L_n^\alpha$ denote the generalized Laguerre polynomial solving $xy''+(\alpha+1-x)y'+ny=0$ with leading coefficient $(-1)^n/n!$.
>
> $$
> \int_0^\infty L_m^\alpha(x)L_n^\alpha(x)x^\alpha e^{-x}\,dx
> =\begin{cases}0,&m\ne n,\\\Gamma(n+\alpha+1)/n!,&m=n.\end{cases}
> $$

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.4 Hermite and Laguerre Polynomials.md
title: Generalized Laguerre Series Expansion with Gamma Weight
body:
> [!theorem|af060bf3-e630-597f-9052-f92a4f18ff42.local at=ce33c97d-86a8-525e-8c2a-af2f045154fb] Generalized Laguerre Series Expansion with Gamma Weight
> For $\alpha>-1$ and integers $n\ge0$, let $L_n^\alpha$ denote the generalized Laguerre polynomial solving $xy''+(\alpha+1-x)y'+ny=0$ with leading coefficient $(-1)^n/n!$.
>
> For $f\in L^2((0,\infty),x^\alpha e^{-x}dx)$, the generalized Laguerre expansion converges in that weighted norm and is
>
> $$
> f=\sum_{j=0}^\infty A_jL_j^\alpha,\qquad
> A_j=\frac{j!}{\Gamma(j+\alpha+1)}\int_0^\infty f(x)L_j^\alpha(x)x^\alpha e^{-x}\,dx.
> $$
>
> If $f$ is also piecewise smooth on $[0,\infty)$, the series converges for $x>0$ to $[f(x+)+f(x-)]/2$, and hence to $f(x)$ at continuity points.

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.4 Hermite and Laguerre Polynomials.md
title: Rodrigues Formula for Generalized Laguerre Polynomials
body:
> [!identity|2430145a-7223-50a5-b679-46a23ce39b8e.local at=a91d59ee-a8c3-5b47-bbf6-936ac6d4461c] Rodrigues Formula for Generalized Laguerre Polynomials
> For $\alpha>-1$ and integers $n\ge0$, let $L_n^\alpha$ denote the generalized Laguerre polynomial solving $xy''+(\alpha+1-x)y'+ny=0$ with leading coefficient $(-1)^n/n!$.
>
> For $x>0$,
>
> $$
> L_n^\alpha(x)=\frac{x^{-\alpha}e^x}{n!}\frac{d^n}{dx^n}\left(x^{n+\alpha}e^{-x}\right).
> $$
>
> The right side extends to the polynomial at $x=0$.

path: Chapter 15 An Introduction to Quantum Mechanics/15.4 Hermite and Laguerre Polynomials.md
title: Derivative and Three-Term Recurrences for Generalized Laguerre Polynomials
body:
> [!theorem|3d2d887f-90dc-5099-a66f-293a73c26db4.local at=889768a9-4bc1-5575-b0e4-0b909f6c744c] Derivative and Three-Term Recurrences for Generalized Laguerre Polynomials
> For $\alpha>-1$ and integers $n\ge0$, let $L_n^\alpha$ denote the generalized Laguerre polynomial solving $xy''+(\alpha+1-x)y'+ny=0$ with leading coefficient $(-1)^n/n!$.
>
> For integers $n\ge1$,
>
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> (L_n^\alpha)'&=-L_{n-1}^{\alpha+1},\\
> L_n^\alpha&=\frac{x}{n}(L_{n-1}^\alpha)'+\left(1+\frac{\alpha}{n}-\frac{x}{n}\right)L_{n-1}^\alpha,\\
> (L_n^\alpha)'&=(L_{n-1}^\alpha)'-L_{n-1}^\alpha,\\
> (n+1)L_{n+1}^\alpha&=(2n+\alpha+1-x)L_n^\alpha-(n+\alpha)L_{n-1}^\alpha.
> \end{aligned}
> $$

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.1 Green's Theorem and Identities.md
title: Simple Closed Plane Curve (Jordan Curve)
body:
> [!definition] Simple Closed Plane Curve (Jordan Curve)
> A simple closed plane curve (Jordan curve) is the image of a continuous parametrization $C:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^2$ with $a<b$, $C(a)=C(b)$, and no other repeated points: if $a\le t_1<t_2\le b$ and $C(t_1)=C(t_2)$, then $t_1=a$ and $t_2=b$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.1 Green's Theorem and Identities.md
title: Positive Orientation of a Simple Closed Plane Curve
body:
> [!convention] Positive Orientation of a Simple Closed Plane Curve
> Orientation. Jordan's theorem allows us to define the orientation of a simple curve $C$. You are moving in the positive direction along $C$ if the interior region is to your left; otherwise. you are moving in the negative direction of $C$. We denote by $-C$ the reverse of $C$. It is the curve that is traversed in the opposite direction as $C$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.1 Green's Theorem and Identities.md
title: Open Sets and Connected Regions in the Plane
body:
> [!definition] Open Sets and Connected Regions in the Plane
> Open Sets and Regions. A subset $U$ of the plane is open if for every $\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right)$ in $U$ there is an open disk $D$ centered at ( $x_{0}, y_{0}$ ) and contained entirely in $U$. In other words, $U$ is open if every point in $U$ is an interior point. Consequently, if $U$ is open, then it cannot contain any of its boundary points, since boundary points are not interior points. An open subset $S$ of the plane is connected if and only if any two points ( $x_{0}, y_{0}$ ) and ( $x_{1}, y_{1}$ ) in $S$ can be joined by a polygonal line that is entirely contained in $S$. (By a polygonal line we mean a curve formed by finitely many line segments joined end to end.) A nonempty open connected subset of the plane is called a region.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.1 Green's Theorem and Identities.md
title: Simply Connected and Multiply Connected Plane Regions
body:
> [!definition] Simply Connected and Multiply Connected Plane Regions
> An open connected plane region $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is simply connected if the bounded interior of every simple closed curve lying in $D$ is also contained in $D$. A region that is not simply connected is called multiply connected. Geometrically, a simply connected plane region has no holes.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.1 Green's Theorem and Identities.md
title: Line Integrals Along Piecewise Smooth Plane Curves
body:
> [!definition] Line Integrals Along Piecewise Smooth Plane Curves
> Line Integral. If $C$ is a continuous, piecewise continuously differentiable curve parametrized by $(x(t), y(t)), a \leq t \leq b$, and $f(x, y)$ is a continuous function on $C$, we define the line integral of $f$ over $C$ to be
>
> $$
> \int_{C} f(x, y) d s=\int_{a}^{b} f(x(t), y(t)) \sqrt{\left[x^{\prime}(t)\right]^{2}+\left[y^{\prime}(t)\right]^{2}} d t
> $$
>
> Two other integrals will be of interest:
>
> $$
> \int_{C} f(x, y) d x=\int_{a}^{b} f(x(t), y(t)) x^{\prime}(t) d t
> $$
>
> $$
> \int_C f(x,y)\,dy=\int_a^b f(x(t),y(t))y'(t)\,dt.
> $$

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.1 Green's Theorem and Identities.md
title: Green’s Theorem for a Simply Connected Plane Region
body:
> [!theorem] Green’s Theorem for a Simply Connected Plane Region
> Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise smooth simple closed plane curve, and let $D$ be its bounded interior. If $M,N$ are real functions of class $C^1$ on a neighborhood of $\overline D$, then
>
> $$
> \int_{C}(M(x, y) d x+N(x, y) d y)=\iint_{D}\left(\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}\right) d x d y
> $$

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.1 Green's Theorem and Identities.md
title: Green’s Theorem for a Multiply Connected Plane Region
body:
> [!theorem] Green’s Theorem for a Multiply Connected Plane Region
> Let $\Omega$ be a bounded plane region whose boundary $\Gamma$ consists of finitely many disjoint piecewise smooth simple closed curves. Orient the outer curve counterclockwise and the inner curves clockwise, so $\Omega$ is on the left. If $M,N\in C^1$ on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$, then
>
> $$
> \int_{\Gamma} M(x, y) d x+N(x, y) d y=\iint_{\Omega}\left(\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}\right) d x d y
> $$

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.1 Green's Theorem and Identities.md
title: Green’s First and Second Identities in the Plane
body:
> [!theorem] Green’s First and Second Identities in the Plane
> Let $\Omega$ be a bounded plane region with a boundary $\Gamma$ consisting of finitely many disjoint piecewise smooth simple closed curves. Let $n$ be the outward unit normal, $ds$ arc length, and $u,v$ real $C^2$ functions on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$. Write $\nabla^2=\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2$ and $\partial_n u=\nabla u\cdot n$. Then we have Green's first identity
>
> $$
> \iint_{\Omega}\left(u \nabla^{2} v+\nabla u \cdot \nabla v\right) d x d y=\int_{\Gamma} u \frac{\partial v}{\partial n} d s
> $$
>
> and Green's second identity
>
> $$
> \iint_{\Omega}\left(u \nabla^{2} v-v \nabla^{2} u\right) d x d y=\int_{\Gamma}\left(u \frac{\partial v}{\partial n}-v \frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\right) d s
> $$

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.1 Green's Theorem and Identities.md
title: Zero Gradient Implies Constancy on a Connected Region
body:
> [!proposition] Zero Gradient Implies Constancy on a Connected Region
> If $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ is open and connected and $u\in C^1(\Omega)$ satisfies $u_x=u_y=0$ throughout $\Omega$, then $u$ is constant on $\Omega$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.1 Green's Theorem and Identities.md
title: Uniqueness of the Classical Dirichlet Solution for Laplace’s Equation
body:
> [!theorem] Uniqueness of the Classical Dirichlet Solution for Laplace’s Equation
> Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded connected region with piecewise smooth boundary $\Gamma$. Suppose $u_1,u_2$ are real $C^2$ functions near $\overline\Omega$, harmonic in $\Omega$, and $u_1=u_2$ on $\Gamma$. Then $u_1=u_2$ throughout $\Omega$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.1 Green's Theorem and Identities.md
title: Uniqueness up to a Constant for the Classical Neumann Problem
body:
> [!theorem] Uniqueness up to a Constant for the Classical Neumann Problem
> Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded connected region with piecewise smooth boundary $\Gamma$ and outward unit normal $n$. If real functions $u_1,u_2\in C^2$ near $\overline\Omega$ are harmonic in $\Omega$ and $\partial_n u_1=\partial_n u_2$ on the smooth pieces of $\Gamma$, then $u_1-u_2$ is constant throughout $\Omega$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.2 Harmonic Functions and Green's Identities.md
title: Outward Normal Derivative of the Planar Logarithmic Potential
body:
> [!proposition] Outward Normal Derivative of the Planar Logarithmic Potential
> Fix $p=(x_0,y_0)\in\mathbb R^2$, let $v(x,y)=\log\sqrt{(x-x_0)^2+(y-y_0)^2}$ for $(x,y)\ne p$, and let $C_r$ be the circle centered at $p$ with radius $r>0$. With $n$ directed outward from the disk bounded by $C_r$,
>
> $$
> \frac{\partial v}{\partial n}(x,y)=\frac1r\qquad ((x,y)\in C_r).
> $$

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.2 Harmonic Functions and Green's Identities.md
title: Harmonicity of the Planar Logarithmic Potential Away from Its Pole
body:
> [!proposition] Harmonicity of the Planar Logarithmic Potential Away from Its Pole
> Fix $(x_0,y_0)\in\mathbb R^2$. The function $v(x,y)=\frac{1}{2} \ln \left(\left(x-x_{0}\right)^{2}+\left(y-y_{0}\right)^{2}\right)$ is harmonic at all points $(x, y) \neq\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right)$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.2 Harmonic Functions and Green's Identities.md
title: Gauss’s Circle Mean Value Property for Harmonic Functions
body:
> [!theorem] Gauss’s Circle Mean Value Property for Harmonic Functions
> Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be open and let $u\in C^2(\Omega)$ satisfy $u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0$. Let $\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right)$ be any point in $\Omega$ and $r>0$ be any real number such that the closed disk of radius $r>0$ centered at ( $x_{0}, y_{0}$ ) is contained in $\Omega$. Then
>
> $$
> u\left(x_0,y_0\right)=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} u\left(x_{0}+r \cos t, y_{0}+r \sin t\right) d t
> $$

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.2 Harmonic Functions and Green's Identities.md
title: Strong Maximum and Minimum Principles for Real Harmonic Functions
body:
> [!theorem] Strong Maximum and Minimum Principles for Real Harmonic Functions
> Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be an open connected region and $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be harmonic. If $u$ attains a maximum or a minimum over $\Omega$ at an interior point, then $u$ is constant throughout $\Omega$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.2 Harmonic Functions and Green's Identities.md
title: Boundary Extrema of a Real Harmonic Function on a Bounded Region
body:
> [!corollary] Boundary Extrema of a Real Harmonic Function on a Bounded Region
> Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be bounded, open, and connected. If $u:\overline\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and harmonic in $\Omega$, its maximum $M$ and minimum $m$ on $\overline\Omega$ are attained on $\partial\Omega$. Either $u$ is constant or $m<u(x,y)<M$ at every point of $\Omega$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.3 Green's Functions.md
title: Boundary Representation of a Harmonic Function by the Logarithmic Potential
body:
> [!theorem|a384e142-071f-55c9-9e2c-1bdedc32d8e9.local at=857e12bf-aded-561d-91f8-323224d3d026] Boundary Representation of a Harmonic Function by the Logarithmic Potential
> Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded region with piecewise smooth boundary $\Gamma$, consisting of finitely many disjoint simple closed curves, and let $n$ be the outward unit normal. Boundary integrals use arc length $ds$, with normal derivatives taken in the boundary variable $q=(x,y)$.
>
> If $u$ is harmonic in $\Omega$ and $C^2$ near $\overline\Omega$, then, for every $p=(x_0,y_0)\in\Omega$, with $v(q)=\log|q-p|$,
>
> $$
> u(p)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_\Gamma\left(u\frac{\partial v}{\partial n}-v\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\right)ds.
> $$

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.3 Green's Functions.md
title: Dirichlet Green Function for the Planar Laplacian with Positive Logarithmic Singularity
body:
> [!definition|741d9777-c712-540a-80fe-756acbd4dced.local at=52fc8526-8d1a-5adc-a68b-20f8c28b20fa] Dirichlet Green Function for the Planar Laplacian with Positive Logarithmic Singularity
> Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded region with piecewise smooth boundary $\Gamma$, consisting of finitely many disjoint simple closed curves, and let $n$ be the outward unit normal. Boundary integrals use arc length $ds$, with normal derivatives taken in the boundary variable $q=(x,y)$.
>
> For a pole $p=(x_0,y_0)\in\Omega$, use the normalization $G(q,p)=\log|q-p|+h(q,p)$, where $h(\cdot,p)$ is harmonic in $\Omega$ and continuous on $\overline\Omega$, with $h(q,p)=-\log|q-p|$ on $\Gamma$. Thus $G=0$ on the boundary. This is the Green function for $\Delta=\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2$ with logarithmic coefficient $+1$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.3 Green's Functions.md
title: Dirichlet Boundary Representation Using a Planar Green Function
body:
> [!theorem|59691839-c6be-57a1-9e75-19d859e2170f.local at=ecd1d0b6-7014-52f1-b4aa-f1aa6d594d63] Dirichlet Boundary Representation Using a Planar Green Function
> Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded region with piecewise smooth boundary $\Gamma$, consisting of finitely many disjoint simple closed curves, and let $n$ be the outward unit normal. Boundary integrals use arc length $ds$, with normal derivatives taken in the boundary variable $q=(x,y)$.
>
> For a pole $p=(x_0,y_0)\in\Omega$, use the normalization $G(q,p)=\log|q-p|+h(q,p)$, where $h(\cdot,p)$ is harmonic in $\Omega$ and continuous on $\overline\Omega$, with $h(q,p)=-\log|q-p|$ on $\Gamma$. Thus $G=0$ on the boundary. This is the Green function for $\Delta=\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2$ with logarithmic coefficient $+1$.
>
> If $u$ is harmonic in $\Omega$ and $C^2$ near $\overline\Omega$, then
>
> $$
> u(p)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_\Gamma u(q)\,\partial_{n_q}G(q,p)\,ds_q,\qquad p\in\Omega.
> $$
>
> The same representation extends to continuous boundary data and their continuous harmonic extension on a regular domain, with the boundary integral interpreted via the Poisson kernel.

title: Harmonicity, Boundary Values, Sign, Uniqueness, and Symmetry of a Planar Dirichlet Green Function
body:
> [!theorem|4fe9c616-91e8-5363-b3cb-caddd3fc1715.local at=3eedc89b-aebd-598c-a0d4-921df1967707] Harmonicity, Boundary Values, Sign, Uniqueness, and Symmetry of a Planar Dirichlet Green Function
> Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded region with piecewise smooth boundary $\Gamma$, consisting of finitely many disjoint simple closed curves, and let $n$ be the outward unit normal. Boundary integrals use arc length $ds$, with normal derivatives taken in the boundary variable $q=(x,y)$.
>
> For a pole $p=(x_0,y_0)\in\Omega$, use the normalization $G(q,p)=\log|q-p|+h(q,p)$, where $h(\cdot,p)$ is harmonic in $\Omega$ and continuous on $\overline\Omega$, with $h(q,p)=-\log|q-p|$ on $\Gamma$. Thus $G=0$ on the boundary. This is the Green function for $\Delta=\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2$ with logarithmic coefficient $+1$.
>
> For distinct $p,q\in\Omega$, $G(\cdot,p)$ is harmonic away from $p$, $G(q,p)\le0$, and $G(q,p)=G(p,q)$. It vanishes on $\Gamma$ and is uniquely determined by the region and this logarithmic normalization. At the pole it has a logarithmic singularity tending to $-\infty$.

Thus $G=0$ on the boundary. This is the Green function for $\Delta=\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2$ with logarithmic coefficient $+1$.
>

title: Distributional Poisson Equation for a Planar Dirichlet Green Function
body:
> [!theorem|a833de56-a04f-5be0-970e-55ea484b3bba.local at=bed2b6f0-4287-5286-9d61-9500aa2d5986] Distributional Poisson Equation for a Planar Dirichlet Green Function
> Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded region with piecewise smooth boundary $\Gamma$, consisting of finitely many disjoint simple closed curves, and let $n$ be the outward unit normal. Boundary integrals use arc length $ds$, with normal derivatives taken in the boundary variable $q=(x,y)$.
>
> For a pole $p=(x_0,y_0)\in\Omega$, use the normalization $G(q,p)=\log|q-p|+h(q,p)$, where $h(\cdot,p)$ is harmonic in $\Omega$ and continuous on $\overline\Omega$, with $h(q,p)=-\log|q-p|$ on $\Gamma$. Thus $G=0$ on the boundary. This is the Green function for $\Delta=\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2$ with logarithmic coefficient $+1$.
>
> For a fixed $p\in\Omega$, the locally integrable function $U(q)=G(q,p)/(2\pi)$ satisfies $\Delta_qU=\delta_p$ in distributions and $U=0$ on $\Gamma$. Equivalently, for every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$,
>
> $$
> \frac1{2\pi}\iint_\Omega G(q,p)\Delta\phi(q)\,dA_q=\phi(p).
> $$
>
> Here $\delta_p$ is the unit point mass, defined by $\langle\delta_p,\phi\rangle=\phi(p)$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.4 Green's Functions for the Disk and the Upper Half-Plane.md
title: Distance Ratio for Inversion in a Circle
body:
> [!proposition|7112982e-ecb6-51c2-8bb5-2b1e4132df24.local at=cf51912a-e210-5bfc-9215-22d31a88f591] Distance Ratio for Inversion in a Circle
> Let $R>0$ and $A\in\mathbb R^2$ satisfy $0<|A|<R$. Its inverse in the circle $|P|=R$ is $A^*=R^2A/|A|^2$, lying on the same ray from the origin. For every $P$ on that circle,
>
> $$
> |A-P|=\frac{|A|}{R}|A^*-P|.
> $$
>
> Thus the proportionality constant is $k=|A|/R$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.4 Green's Functions for the Disk and the Upper Half-Plane.md
title: Poisson Equation on a Disk with Zero Dirichlet Boundary Data
body:
> [!theorem|7824230a-489f-518c-90b8-6dd44c9aee12.local at=d3d55a19-d8a9-5aa3-a991-c3c51a850555] Poisson Equation on a Disk with Zero Dirichlet Boundary Data
> Let $D_R=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2<R^2\}$ with $R>0$. If $u\in C^2$ near $\overline{D_R}$ satisfies $\Delta u=f$ in $D_R$ and $u=0$ on its boundary, then at $0\le r_0<R$,
>
> $$
> u(r_0,\phi)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^R f(r,\theta)\log\left[R^2\frac{r^2+r_0^2-2rr_0\cos(\theta-\phi)}{r^2r_0^2+R^4-2rr_0R^2\cos(\theta-\phi)}\right]r\,dr\,d\theta.
> $$
>
> The integral uses polar area measure; the logarithmic singularity at the evaluation point is integrable.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.4 Green's Functions for the Disk and the Upper Half-Plane.md
title: Poisson Integral Formula for the Dirichlet Problem on a Disk
body:
> [!theorem|085c8b9c-2da6-5374-b4d0-8218f2dab441.local at=a48455fd-1410-59da-9551-f52b6081645b] Poisson Integral Formula for the Dirichlet Problem on a Disk
> Let $R>0$ and let $f$ be a continuous $2\pi$-periodic real function. The unique function harmonic on $D_R=\{x^2+y^2<R^2\}$ and continuous on $\overline{D_R}$ with boundary values $u(R,\theta)=f(\theta)$ is
>
> $$
> u(r,\phi)=\frac{R^2-r^2}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{f(\theta)}{R^2+r^2-2rR\cos(\theta-\phi)}\,d\theta,\qquad0\le r<R.
> $$

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.4 Green's Functions for the Disk and the Upper Half-Plane.md
title: Poisson Kernel for a Disk in Angular Coordinates
body:
> [!definition|7dcff161-bc01-5934-8a51-69019c6630a7.local at=7d1c341b-fafe-5cc7-acd6-016d3f373b95] Poisson Kernel for a Disk in Angular Coordinates
> For a disk of radius $R>0$, define the angular Poisson kernel by
>
> $$
> P_R(r,\alpha)=\frac{R^2-r^2}{R^2+r^2-2rR\cos\alpha},\qquad0\le r<R,\quad\alpha\in\mathbb R.
> $$
>
> In the boundary integral with measure $d\theta/(2\pi)$, the angular difference is $\alpha=\theta-\phi$, where $(r,\phi)$ is the interior evaluation point.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.4 Green's Functions for the Disk and the Upper Half-Plane.md
title: Green Potential for the Poisson Equation in the Upper Half-Plane
body:
> [!theorem|1be9f76d-35f8-5d7b-a140-6dc2ab962fd5.local at=9542d3ef-da00-5ce7-9529-328e4ee86e35] Green Potential for the Poisson Equation in the Upper Half-Plane
> Let $H=\{(x,y):y>0\}$ and let $f$ be Hölder continuous with compact support in $H$. The bounded solution of $\Delta u=f$ in $H$ with continuous zero boundary values on $y=0$ is
>
> $$
> u(x_0,y_0)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_0^\infty\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x,y)\log\frac{(x-x_0)^2+(y-y_0)^2}{(x-x_0)^2+(y+y_0)^2}\,dx\,dy,\qquad y_0>0.
> $$
>
> It tends to zero at infinity. Without a boundedness or growth condition, zero boundary values alone do not guarantee uniqueness on this unbounded domain.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.4 Green's Functions for the Disk and the Upper Half-Plane.md
title: Poisson Integral Formula for Bounded Harmonic Functions in the Upper Half-Plane
body:
> [!theorem|80e9f0c0-0701-5904-a9df-a6cb291067a3.local at=394f2488-c1fc-59a1-9c13-a06dacf708fe] Poisson Integral Formula for Bounded Harmonic Functions in the Upper Half-Plane
> If $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is bounded and continuous, the unique bounded harmonic function on $H=\{(x,y):y>0\}$ that extends continuously to $u(x,0)=f(x)$ is
>
> $$
> u(x_0,y)=\frac y\pi\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{f(x)}{(x-x_0)^2+y^2}\,dx,\qquad x_0\in\mathbb R,\ y>0.
> $$

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.5 Analytic Functions.md
title: Complex Differentiability and Analyticity
body:
> [!definition|7a3918ec-b8ce-5fb6-afb3-3fa188f9f22a.local at=a45fda6d-881f-5946-8622-f57e69eefd7e] Complex Differentiability and Analyticity
> Let $f$ be defined on an open subset of $\mathbb C$. We say that $f(z)$ is differentiable at $z$ if its derivative $f^{\prime}(z)$, or $\frac{d}{d z} f(z)$, exists and is finite at $z$, where
>
> $$
> f^{\prime}(z)=\lim _{\zeta \rightarrow z} \frac{f(\zeta)-f(z)}{\zeta-z}
> $$
>
> If $S$ is an open set in the complex plane we say that $f$ is analytic on $S$ if $f$ is differentiable at all points $z$ in $S$. A function is analytic at one point $z_{0}$ if it is analytic on an open set that contains $z_{0}$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.5 Analytic Functions.md
title: Cauchy–Riemann Characterization and Derivative of an Analytic Function
body:
> [!theorem|144da62d-4427-57b4-ac3a-8afa8fc7b053.local at=0803b93e-4117-5d9d-9123-298a06c10d2d] Cauchy–Riemann Characterization and Derivative of an Analytic Function
> The function $f(z)=u(x, y)+i v(x, y)$ is analytic in an open set $S$ if and only if the partial derivatives of $u$ and $v$ are continuous and satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann equations
>
> $$
> u_{x}=v_{y} \quad \text { and } \quad u_{y}=-v_{x} .
> $$
>
> Furthermore, if $f$ is analytic, then the derivative $f^{\prime}(z)$ is given as either of
>
> $$
> f^{\prime}(z)=u_{x}(x, y)+i v_{x}(x, y) \text { or } f^{\prime}(z)=v_{y}(x, y)-i u_{y}(x, y) .
> $$

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.5 Analytic Functions.md
title: Entire Function
body:
> [!definition|88c531a0-86d5-5f63-ac74-4b12f49c99bf.local at=6f435288-03a3-5ea8-a345-b33c2c859469] Entire Function
> A function $f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ is entire if it is analytic at every point of the complex plane.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.5 Analytic Functions.md
title: Linear Combination, Product, Quotient, and Chain Rules for Analytic Functions
body:
> [!theorem|52a6a037-84b9-5823-bda1-5ba137365ab9.local at=f28a0cb1-e92f-5908-b201-1cad8e00aa98] Linear Combination, Product, Quotient, and Chain Rules for Analytic Functions
> Suppose that $f$ and $g$ are analytic on an open set $S$ and $c_{1}, c_{2}$ are complex constants. Then $c_{1} f+c_{2} g$ and $f g$ are analytic on $S$ with
>
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
> \left(c_{1} f+c_{2} g\right)^{\prime}(z) & =c_{1} f^{\prime}(z)+c_{2} g^{\prime}(z) \text { and } \\
> (f g)^{\prime}(z) & =f^{\prime}(z) g(z)+f(z) g^{\prime}(z) .
> \end{aligned}
> $$
>
> Also, $\frac{f}{g}$ is analytic on $S$ minus the points where $g=0$, and
>
> $$
> \left(\frac{f}{g}\right)^{\prime}(z)=\frac{f^{\prime}(z) g(z)-f(z) g^{\prime}(z)}{(g(z))^{2}} \quad(g(z) \neq 0) .
> $$
>
> If $g$ is analytic at $z_{0}$ and $f$ is analytic at $g\left(z_{0}\right)$, then the composition $(f \circ g)(z)$ is analytic at $z_{0}$ and we have the chain rule
>
> $$
> (f \circ g)^{\prime}\left(z_{0}\right)=f^{\prime}\left(g\left(z_{0}\right)\right) g^{\prime}\left(z_0\right)
> $$

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.5 Analytic Functions.md
title: Real and Imaginary Parts of an Analytic Function Are Harmonic
body:
> [!theorem|b7a06797-f906-50ff-8bce-f74fe316c00c.local at=23d4e2e9-dc45-5f38-a0ef-c7277625cf49] Real and Imaginary Parts of an Analytic Function Are Harmonic
> Suppose that $f=u+i v$ is analytic on an open set $S$. Then its real and imaginary parts, $u(x, y)$ and $v(x, y)$, are harmonic on $S$; that is, $u$ and $v$ satisfy Laplace's equation $\nabla^{2} \phi=0$ on $S$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.5 Analytic Functions.md
title: Harmonic Conjugate of a Real Harmonic Function
body:
> [!definition|715fe8a9-cd33-5925-878f-de84255bbee7.local at=11b37645-96d6-5666-b4b8-bef8bba1ed00] Harmonic Conjugate of a Real Harmonic Function
> Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb C$ be open and let $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be harmonic. A real harmonic function $v$ on $\Omega$ is a harmonic conjugate of $u$ if $f=u+iv$ is analytic on $\Omega$; equivalently, $u_x=v_y$ and $u_y=-v_x$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.5 Analytic Functions.md
title: Simply Connected Plane Regions and Global Harmonic Conjugates
body:
> [!theorem|d0d34a97-7afe-5050-b4d6-aa73417469ef.local at=9952bf75-89e2-556b-83d0-c2a3b533e215] Simply Connected Plane Regions and Global Harmonic Conjugates
> For an open connected set $\Omega\subset\mathbb C$, every real harmonic function $u$ on $\Omega$ has a single-valued harmonic conjugate on $\Omega$ if and only if $\Omega$ is simply connected. The assertion concerns every harmonic function; a particular one may have a conjugate on a multiply connected region.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.5 Analytic Functions.md
title: Orthogonality of Regular Level Curves of Harmonic Conjugates
body:
> [!theorem|504a572f-b3e7-5934-a665-bc458cbe57bb.local at=cae4b1cb-c767-50df-aeee-fa994f060043] Orthogonality of Regular Level Curves of Harmonic Conjugates
> Let $u+iv$ be analytic on an open subset of $\mathbb C$. At every point where its complex derivative is nonzero, the level curves of $u$ and $v$ through that point are regular and meet at right angles. Equivalently, $
abla u\cdot
abla v=0$ and $|
abla u|=|
abla v|>0$ there. Critical points require separate treatment.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.6 Solving Dirichlet Problems with Conformal Mappings.md
title: Conformal Analytic Map on a Plane Region
body:
> [!definition|4aa8335e-21b9-5f2e-93c5-c935f2b04dea.local at=0cee039e-d4de-5f5b-874d-29151c937050] Conformal Analytic Map on a Plane Region
> An analytic function $f$ on an open plane region $\Omega$ is locally conformal if $f'(z)\ne0$ at every point. Such a map preserves angles and their orientation locally. A one-to-one analytic map between regions is a conformal bijection; local conformality alone does not imply global injectivity.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.6 Solving Dirichlet Problems with Conformal Mappings.md
title: Harmonicity Is Preserved by Composition with an Analytic Map
body:
> [!theorem|c84549ac-ef3c-5ab7-b968-312ffecb93d3.local at=9e8c0cf0-b21d-56d4-99b4-62ae71e38eba] Harmonicity Is Preserved by Composition with an Analytic Map
> Let $\Omega,\Omega'\subset\mathbb C$ be open regions, let $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ be analytic, and let $U$ be real harmonic on $\Omega'$. Then $\phi(z)=U(\operatorname{Re}f(z),\operatorname{Im}f(z))$ is harmonic on $\Omega$. Injectivity and nonvanishing of $f'$ are not required for this direction.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.6 Solving Dirichlet Problems with Conformal Mappings.md
title: Transferring a Dirichlet Problem by a Conformal Bijection
body:
> [!procedure|5ca97458-3567-5fc0-9544-1f86491b4179.local at=b2fd3be1-e2a9-5be5-82f0-3b596fa0d5bb] Transferring a Dirichlet Problem by a Conformal Bijection
> Let $\phi$ be sought with $\Delta\phi=0$ on a plane region $\Omega$ and boundary values $b$ on $\Gamma$. Use a conformal bijection $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ with a homeomorphic extension between the relevant boundary pieces $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$. Fix a boundedness or growth class when uniqueness on an unbounded region is needed.
>
> Step 1: Describe clearly the region $\Omega^{\prime}=f[\Omega]$ and its boundary $\Gamma^{\prime}=f[\Gamma]$ in the $w$-plane.
> Step 2: Since $f$ is one-to-one, we have an inverse function $f^{-1}$ defined on $\Omega^{\prime}$ and $\Gamma^{\prime}$. For $w$ on $\Gamma^{\prime}, f^{-1}(w)$ is on $\Gamma$ and so we can define the function $b \circ f^{-1}(w)$ for all $w$ on $\Gamma^{\prime}$. This determines the boundary values on $\Gamma^{\prime}$.
> Step 3: Set up and solve the Dirichlet problem on $\Omega^{\prime}$ consisting of Laplace's equation $\nabla^{2} U(w)=0$ for all $w$ in $\Omega^{\prime}$ and $U(w)=b \circ f^{-1}(w)$ for all $w$ on $\Gamma^{\prime}$. (This is our transformed Dirichlet problem.)
> Step 4: Let $\phi(z)=U\circ f(z)$ for all $z$ in $\Omega$. Then $\phi(z)$ is a solution of our original Dirichlet problem on $\Omega$. Indeed, $\phi$ is harmonic on $\Omega$. For $z$ on $\Gamma, f(z)$ belongs to $\Gamma^{\prime}$, and $\phi(z)=U \circ f(z)=b \circ f^{-1}(f(z))=b(z)$. Hence $\phi$ satisfies the desired boundary condition.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.7 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings.md
title: Planar Green Function from a Disk Map Sending Its Pole to the Origin
body:
> [!theorem] Planar Green Function from a Disk Map Sending Its Pole to the Origin
> Let $\Omega\subsetneq\mathbb C$ be simply connected and let $z_0\in\Omega$. Suppose $\phi(\cdot,z_0)$ is a conformal bijection onto the unit disk with $\phi(z_0,z_0)=0$. Assume the boundary correspondence used here extends to the relevant boundary points with $|\phi|=1$. Use the planar Dirichlet Green function normalized by $G(z,z_0)=\log|z-z_0|+h(z,z_0)$, with $h(\cdot,z_0)$ harmonic and $G=0$ on the boundary; this corresponds to $\Delta_zG=2\pi\delta_{z_0}$.
>
> Then, for $z\in\Omega\setminus\{z_0\}$,
>
> $$
> G(z,z_0)=\log|\phi(z,z_0)|.
> $$

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.7 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings.md
title: Linear Fractional (Möbius) Transformation
body:
> [!definition] Linear Fractional (Möbius) Transformation
> Let $a, b, c$, and $d$ be complex numbers with $a d-b c \neq 0$. The function
>
> $$
> f(z)=\frac{a z+b}{c z+d}
> $$
>
> is called a linear fractional transformation or Möbius transformation. It acts on the extended complex plane $\widehat{\mathbb C}$, assigning the pole to $\infty$ and using the limiting value at $\infty$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.7 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings.md
title: Injectivity, Composition, and Inverse of Möbius Transformations
body:
> [!proposition] Injectivity, Composition, and Inverse of Möbius Transformations
> Let $f(z)=(az+b)/(cz+d)$ with complex coefficients satisfying $ad-bc\ne0$, regarded as a map of the extended complex plane.
>
> (i) A linear fractional transformation is one-to-one.
> (ii) The composition of any two linear fractional transformations is another linear fractional transformation.
> (iii) The inverse of the linear fractional transformation $f$ is the linear fractional transformation
>
> $$
> f^{-1}(z)=\frac{d z-b}{-c z+a}
> $$

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.7 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings.md
title: Möbius Automorphisms of the Unit Disk
body:
> [!theorem] Möbius Automorphisms of the Unit Disk
> Let $z_{0}$ be a complex number in $D=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<1\}$ (thus $|z_0|<1$ ). Consider the linear fractional transformation
>
> $$
> f_{z_{0}}(z)=\frac{z-z_{0}}{1-\overline{z_{0}} z} .
> $$
>
> Then (i) $f_{z_{0}}$ is analytic on $D$;
> (ii) $f_{z_{0}}$ maps $D$ one-to-one onto $D$;
> (iii) $f_{z_{0}}$ maps the unit circle onto the unit circle;
> (iv) $f_{z_{0}}\left(z_{0}\right)=0$. Every conformal bijection of the unit disk onto itself has the form $e^{i\theta}f_{z_0}(z)$ for some real $\theta$ and some $z_0\in D$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.7 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings.md
title: Planar Green Function from an Arbitrary Conformal Map to the Unit Disk
body:
> [!theorem] Planar Green Function from an Arbitrary Conformal Map to the Unit Disk
> Let $\Omega\subsetneq\mathbb C$ be simply connected and $\phi:\Omega\to D$ a conformal bijection onto the unit disk, with the assumed boundary correspondence. Use the planar Dirichlet Green function normalized by $G(z,z_0)=\log|z-z_0|+h(z,z_0)$, with $h(\cdot,z_0)$ harmonic and $G=0$ on the boundary; this corresponds to $\Delta_zG=2\pi\delta_{z_0}$.
>
> For distinct $z,z_0\in\Omega$,
>
> $$
> G(z,z_0)=\log\left|\frac{\phi(z)-\phi(z_0)}{1-\overline{\phi(z_0)}\phi(z)}\right|.
> $$

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.7 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings.md
title: Planar Green Function from a Conformal Map to the Upper Half-Plane
body:
> [!theorem] Planar Green Function from a Conformal Map to the Upper Half-Plane
> Let $\Omega\subsetneq\mathbb C$ be simply connected and $\phi:\Omega\to\{w:\operatorname{Im}w>0\}$ a conformal bijection, with boundary correspondence to the extended real axis. Use the planar Dirichlet Green function normalized by $G(z,z_0)=\log|z-z_0|+h(z,z_0)$, with $h(\cdot,z_0)$ harmonic and $G=0$ on the boundary; this corresponds to $\Delta_zG=2\pi\delta_{z_0}$.
>
> For distinct $z,z_0\in\Omega$,
>
> $$
> G(z,z_0)=\log\left|\frac{\phi(z)-\phi(z_0)}{\phi(z)-\overline{\phi(z_0)}}\right|.
> $$

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.7 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings.md
title: Conformal Invariance of the Planar Dirichlet Green Function
body:
> [!theorem] Conformal Invariance of the Planar Dirichlet Green Function
> Let $\Omega,\Omega'\subsetneq\mathbb C$ be simply connected regions and $\phi:\Omega\to\Omega'$ a conformal bijection with the required boundary correspondence. Suppose $g(w,w_0)$ is the Dirichlet Green function on $\Omega'$ normalized by $g(w,w_0)=\log|w-w_0|+$ a function harmonic at $w_0$. Then the Green function on $\Omega$ with the same normalization is
>
> $$
> G(z,z_0)=g\bigl(\phi(z),\phi(z_0)\bigr),\qquad z,z_0\in\Omega,\ z\ne z_0.
> $$

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.8 Neumann Functions and the Solution of Neumann Problems.md
title: Planar Neumann Function with Positive Logarithmic Singularity
body:
> [!definition|e7c59d8b-44bd-5b15-99f3-dedc446a016f.local at=0ad9873a-c103-53c8-bcbb-90a90c293734] Planar Neumann Function with Positive Logarithmic Singularity
> Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a simply connected plane region with piecewise smooth boundary $\Gamma$ and outward unit normal $n$. For each pole $p\in\Omega$, a Neumann function in this convention satisfies:
>
> (i) $N(\cdot,p)$ is harmonic on $\Omega\setminus\{p\}$.
> (ii) $\partial_{n_z}N(z,p)=C$ on smooth pieces of $\Gamma$, for a constant independent of the boundary point and pole.
> (iii) $N(z,p)=\log|z-p|+H(z,p)$, where $H(\cdot,p)$ is harmonic throughout $\Omega$.
>
> For bounded $\Omega$ of boundary length $L$, necessarily $C=2\pi/L$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.8 Neumann Functions and the Solution of Neumann Problems.md
title: Boundary Flux Constant of a Neumann Function on a Bounded Plane Region
body:
> [!proposition|70dd256e-9be0-5f33-a04f-bcb34c2af2a7.local at=0f329697-663d-5fc2-abf1-7cdad681ab09] Boundary Flux Constant of a Neumann Function on a Bounded Plane Region
> Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be bounded, simply connected, and have piecewise smooth boundary $\Gamma$ of length $L>0$, with outward unit normal $n$. Write $z=x+iy$ and $p=x_0+iy_0\in\Omega$.
>
> If $N(z,p)=\log|z-p|+H(z,p)$ with $H$ harmonic in $\Omega$ and regular enough up to $\Gamma$ for Green’s identity, and $\partial_{n_z}N=C$ on $\Gamma$, then $CL=2\pi$ and therefore $C=2\pi/L$.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.8 Neumann Functions and the Solution of Neumann Problems.md
title: Neumann Boundary Representation for Harmonic Functions on a Bounded Plane Region
body:
> [!theorem|d00d8502-4689-5ddc-a0cc-bd3046064426.local at=cfac0fd2-3132-553e-b16f-7565120e5820] Neumann Boundary Representation for Harmonic Functions on a Bounded Plane Region
> Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be bounded, simply connected, and have piecewise smooth boundary $\Gamma$ of length $L>0$, with outward unit normal $n$. Write $z=x+iy$ and $p=x_0+iy_0\in\Omega$.
>
> A Neumann function in the positive-logarithmic convention has the form $N(z,p)=\log|z-p|+H(z,p)$, where $H(\cdot,p)$ is harmonic throughout $\Omega$, and satisfies $\partial_{n_z}N(z,p)=2\pi/L$ on the smooth boundary pieces.
>
> If a real $C^2$ function $u$ near $\overline\Omega$ is harmonic in $\Omega$ and satisfies $\partial_n u=f$ on $\Gamma$, then $\int_\Gamma f\,ds=0$ and
>
> $$
> u(p)=A-\frac1{2\pi}\int_\Gamma N(z,p)f(z)\,ds_z,\qquad A=\frac1L\int_\Gamma u\,ds.
> $$
>
> Thus the representation determines the solution up to an additive constant.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.8 Neumann Functions and the Solution of Neumann Problems.md
title: Zero-Flux Neumann Kernel Obtained from a Conformal Half-Plane Map
body:
> [!theorem|615861ea-6882-597e-8521-eb95d663fba0.local at=c0635cfb-c82f-5b89-a930-5a2e089b91b7] Zero-Flux Neumann Kernel Obtained from a Conformal Half-Plane Map
> Let $\phi$ be a conformal bijection from an unbounded simply connected plane region $\Omega$ onto the upper half-plane. Assume it extends smoothly with nonzero derivative on the boundary arcs under consideration and takes them to the real axis. For distinct $z,p\in\Omega$,
>
> $$
> N(z,p)=\log|\phi(z)-\phi(p)|+\log|\phi(z)-\overline{\phi(p)}|
> $$
>
> is harmonic away from $p$, has singular part $\log|z-p|$, and satisfies $\partial_{n_z}N=0$ on those arcs. Behavior at boundary corners, exceptional points, and infinity must be checked for the intended boundary-value representation.

path: Chapter 16 Green's Functions and Conformal Mappings/16.8 Neumann Functions and the Solution of Neumann Problems.md
title: Neumann Function Representation for the Poisson–Neumann Problem on a Bounded Plane Region
body:
> [!theorem|52cbf0f8-4130-52e9-9a70-64404837c141.local at=2e3bcc5d-117a-58a4-816b-ef77d1fc988a] Neumann Function Representation for the Poisson–Neumann Problem on a Bounded Plane Region
> Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be bounded, simply connected, and have piecewise smooth boundary $\Gamma$ of length $L>0$, with outward unit normal $n$. Write $z=x+iy$ and $p=x_0+iy_0\in\Omega$.
>
> A Neumann function in the positive-logarithmic convention has the form $N(z,p)=\log|z-p|+H(z,p)$, where $H(\cdot,p)$ is harmonic throughout $\Omega$, and satisfies $\partial_{n_z}N(z,p)=2\pi/L$ on the smooth boundary pieces.
>
> If $u\in C^2$ near $\overline\Omega$ satisfies $\Delta u=h$ in $\Omega$ and $\partial_n u=f$ on $\Gamma$, then $\iint_\Omega h\,dA=\int_\Gamma f\,ds$ and
>
> $$
> u(p)=A+\frac1{2\pi}\iint_\Omega h(z)N(z,p)\,dA_z-\frac1{2\pi}\int_\Gamma N(z,p)f(z)\,ds_z,
> \qquad A=\frac1L\int_\Gamma u\,ds.
> $$
>
> In particular, the solution is determined up to an additive constant.

path: Chapter 17 Sampling and Discrete Fourier Analysis with Applications to Partial Differential Equations/17.1 The Sampling Theorem.md
title: Band-Limited Function and Angular-Frequency Bandwidth
body:
> [!definition|94784048-1192-5e9e-b02c-2d7eaca6456a.local at=f9ae5be4-de0f-5a32-a04e-92d01c8c3b79] Band-Limited Function and Angular-Frequency Bandwidth
> Use the unitary angular-frequency Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$, interpreted by its $L^2$ extension when necessary. A function $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ is band-limited if $\widehat f=0$ almost everywhere outside a bounded interval. Any $W>0$ such that $\widehat f(\omega)=0$ for almost every $|\omega|>W$ is a bandwidth in this centered angular-frequency convention. For sampling, use the continuous representative given by Fourier inversion.

path: Chapter 17 Sampling and Discrete Fourier Analysis with Applications to Partial Differential Equations/17.1 The Sampling Theorem.md
title: Bandwidth under Linear Combination, Translation, and Convolution
body:
> [!theorem|93e36581-6bd4-580b-893f-5867d2ff424e.local at=f9baee9f-8a8a-50e7-8fd6-9f6fc239de92] Bandwidth under Linear Combination, Translation, and Convolution
> Use the unitary angular-frequency Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$, interpreted by its $L^2$ extension when necessary.
>
> Let $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ be band-limited with bandwidths $W_1,W_2$ and let $a,b\in\mathbb C$.
>
> (a) $af+bg$ has bandwidth at most $\max(W_1,W_2)$.
> (b) For real $c$, $f(x-c)$ has the same admissible bandwidth $W_1$.
> (c) If $f$ has bandwidth $W_1$ and $g\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, their normalized convolution
>
> $$
> (f*g)(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x-t)g(t)\,dt
> $$
>
> belongs to $L^2$ and has bandwidth at most $W_1$. The analogous statement holds with the two factors interchanged.

path: Chapter 17 Sampling and Discrete Fourier Analysis with Applications to Partial Differential Equations/17.1 The Sampling Theorem.md
title: Shannon Sampling Theorem for Square-Integrable Band-Limited Functions
body:
> [!theorem|4c40236c-e418-5e99-be39-e1e862ca0aef.local at=611d5282-f241-5d09-a91b-d1153d1fb2c6] Shannon Sampling Theorem for Square-Integrable Band-Limited Functions
> Use the unitary angular-frequency Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$, interpreted by its $L^2$ extension when necessary.
>
> Let $W>0$ and let $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ have Fourier transform supported almost everywhere in $[-W,W]$. Take its continuous inverse-Fourier representative. Then
>
> $$
> f(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}f\left(\frac{n\pi}{W}\right)\frac{\sin(Wx-n\pi)}{Wx-n\pi},\qquad x\in\mathbb R,
> $$
>
> where $\sin t/t$ is assigned its limiting value one at $t=0$. Symmetric partial sums converge in $L^2(\mathbb R)$ and uniformly on $\mathbb R$. Thus the samples at spacing $\pi/W$ determine $f$ uniquely in this class.

path: Chapter 17 Sampling and Discrete Fourier Analysis with Applications to Partial Differential Equations/17.1 The Sampling Theorem.md
title: Sinc Reconstruction of the Fourier Transform of a Time-Limited Function
body:
> [!theorem|0ba04e44-1ab8-5055-833d-981e6b78ac38.local at=fd80a014-c3b6-5572-820f-05ea40b5203e] Sinc Reconstruction of the Fourier Transform of a Time-Limited Function
> Use the unitary angular-frequency Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$, interpreted by its $L^2$ extension when necessary.
>
> If $T>0$ and $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ vanishes almost everywhere outside $[-T,T]$, then its continuous Fourier transform satisfies
>
> $$
> \widehat f(\omega)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}\widehat f\left(\frac{n\pi}{T}\right)\frac{\sin(T\omega-n\pi)}{T\omega-n\pi}.
> $$
>
> Use the limiting value one for each removable sinc quotient. Symmetric partial sums converge in $L^2$ and uniformly; samples at spacing $\pi/T$ determine the transform.

path: Chapter 17 Sampling and Discrete Fourier Analysis with Applications to Partial Differential Equations/17.1 The Sampling Theorem.md
title: Fourier Transform from Uniform Samples of a Band-Limited Function
body:
> [!theorem|28e15c10-8e5e-5408-9023-68331e83e99d.local at=4cab5303-52d5-57aa-9fab-a568e58418c6] Fourier Transform from Uniform Samples of a Band-Limited Function
> Use the unitary angular-frequency Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$, interpreted by its $L^2$ extension when necessary. Let $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ have spectrum supported in $[-W,W]$, $W>0$, and take its continuous representative. Let $\chi_{[-W,W]}$ denote the indicator of that frequency interval; endpoint values do not affect the $L^2$ transform.
>
> $$
> \widehat f(\omega)=\frac1W\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,\chi_{[-W,W]}(\omega)\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}f\left(\frac{n\pi}{W}\right)e^{-in\pi\omega/W}.
> $$
>
> The series converges in $L^2([-W,W])$. Additional regularity supplies the usual pointwise Fourier-series conclusions.

path: Chapter 17 Sampling and Discrete Fourier Analysis with Applications to Partial Differential Equations/17.1 The Sampling Theorem.md
title: Cosine-Series Reconstruction of the Fourier Transform from Even Band-Limited Samples
body:
> [!theorem|7cd918f2-1c69-5f69-b560-22cbaa862aba.local at=0b2c5c7b-2101-5733-961a-862277cca5ae] Cosine-Series Reconstruction of the Fourier Transform from Even Band-Limited Samples
> Use the unitary angular-frequency Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$, interpreted by its $L^2$ extension when necessary. Let $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ have spectrum supported in $[-W,W]$, $W>0$, and take its continuous representative. Let $\chi_{[-W,W]}$ denote the indicator of that frequency interval; endpoint values do not affect the $L^2$ transform. Assume also that $f(-x)=f(x)$. Then, with convergence in $L^2([-W,W])$,
>
> $$
> \widehat f(\omega)=\frac1W\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,\chi_{[-W,W]}(\omega)\left[f(0)+2\sum_{n=1}^\infty f\left(\frac{n\pi}{W}\right)\cos\left(\frac{n\pi\omega}{W}\right)\right].
> $$

path: Chapter 17 Sampling and Discrete Fourier Analysis with Applications to Partial Differential Equations/17.2 Partial Differential Equations and the Sampling Theorem.md
title: Heat Equation Solution from Uniform Samples of Band-Limited Initial Data
body:
> [!equation] Heat Equation Solution from Uniform Samples of Band-Limited Initial Data
> Let $c,W>0$, let $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ have unitary Fourier transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$ supported in $[-W,W]$, and use the continuous representative of $f$. The heat evolution $u_t=c^2u_{xx}$ on $\mathbb R$, with $u(\cdot,t)\to f$ in $L^2$ as $t\downarrow0$, is, for $t>0$,
>
> $$
> u(x, t)=\frac{1}{W} \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} f\left(\frac{n \pi}{W}\right) \int_{0}^{W} e^{-c^{2} \omega^{2} t} \cos \left(\omega\left(x-n \frac{\pi}{W}\right)\right) d \omega
> $$
>
> Interpret the series as the limit of symmetric partial sums.

path: Chapter 17 Sampling and Discrete Fourier Analysis with Applications to Partial Differential Equations/17.3 The Discrete and Fast Fourier Transforms.md
title: Unitary Discrete Fourier Transform with Positive Exponential Convention
body:
> [!definition] Unitary Discrete Fourier Transform with Positive Exponential Convention
> Let $N\ge1$ be an integer and $x=(x(0),\ldots,x(N-1))\in\mathbb C^N$. The unitary discrete Fourier transform with positive exponential convention is the sequence $X=\mathcal F_Nx$ defined by
>
> $$
> X(k)=\frac1{\sqrt N}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}x(j)e^{2\pi ijk/N},\qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1.
> $$
>
> The sign and normalization are part of this convention.

path: Chapter 17 Sampling and Discrete Fourier Analysis with Applications to Partial Differential Equations/17.3 The Discrete and Fast Fourier Transforms.md
title: Inverse of the Unitary Positive-Exponent Discrete Fourier Transform
body:
> [!definition] Inverse of the Unitary Positive-Exponent Discrete Fourier Transform
> For an integer $N\ge1$ and $X\in\mathbb C^N$, define
>
> $$
> (\mathcal F_N^{-1}X)(k)=\frac1{\sqrt N}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}X(j)e^{-2\pi ijk/N},\qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1.
> $$
>
> This is the negative-exponent unitary transform, inverse to $(\mathcal F_Nx)(k)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}x(j)e^{2\pi ijk/N}$.

path: Chapter 17 Sampling and Discrete Fourier Analysis with Applications to Partial Differential Equations/17.3 The Discrete and Fast Fourier Transforms.md
title: Inversion and Uniqueness of the Unitary Discrete Fourier Transform
body:
> [!theorem] Inversion and Uniqueness of the Unitary Discrete Fourier Transform
> For an integer $N\ge1$, define $(\mathcal F_Nx)(k)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}x(j)e^{2\pi ijk/N}$ and $(\mathcal F_N^{-1}X)(k)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}X(j)e^{-2\pi ijk/N}$ for $k=0,\ldots,N-1$. Then every $x\in\mathbb C^N$ satisfies
>
> $$
> \mathcal F_N^{-1}(\mathcal F_Nx)=x.
> $$
>
> Consequently, $\mathcal F_Nx=\mathcal F_Ny$ implies $x=y$.

path: Chapter 17 Sampling and Discrete Fourier Analysis with Applications to Partial Differential Equations/17.3 The Discrete and Fast Fourier Transforms.md
title: Normalized Cyclic Convolution of Finite Complex Sequences
body:
> [!definition] Normalized Cyclic Convolution of Finite Complex Sequences
> Let $N\ge1$ be an integer and $x,y\in\mathbb C^N$, extended to all integer indices with period $N$. Their normalized cyclic convolution is
>
> $$
> (x*y)(k)=\frac1{\sqrt N}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}x(j)y(k-j),\qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1.
> $$
>
> The index $k-j$ is taken modulo $N$.

path: Chapter 17 Sampling and Discrete Fourier Analysis with Applications to Partial Differential Equations/17.3 The Discrete and Fast Fourier Transforms.md
title: Convolution Theorem for the Unitary Positive-Exponent Discrete Fourier Transform
body:
> [!theorem] Convolution Theorem for the Unitary Positive-Exponent Discrete Fourier Transform
> For an integer $N\ge1$, let $x,y\in\mathbb C^N$ have $N$-periodic extensions, define
>
> $$
> (\mathcal F_Nx)(k)=\frac1{\sqrt N}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}x(j)e^{2\pi ijk/N},\qquad
> (x*y)(k)=\frac1{\sqrt N}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}x(j)y(k-j),
> $$
>
> and put $X=\mathcal F_Nx$, $Y=\mathcal F_Ny$. Then
>
> $$
> \mathcal F_N(x*y)=XY,\qquad \mathcal F_N^{-1}(XY)=x*y,
> $$
>
> where $XY$ is pointwise multiplication and $(\mathcal F_N^{-1}Z)(k)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}Z(j)e^{-2\pi ijk/N}$.

path: Chapter 17 Sampling and Discrete Fourier Analysis with Applications to Partial Differential Equations/17.4 The Fourier and Discrete Fourier Transforms.md
title: Approximate a Continuous Fourier Transform Using a Unitary IDFT
body:
> [!procedure] Approximate a Continuous Fourier Transform Using a Unitary IDFT
> Use the continuous transform $\widehat f(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-i\omega x}\,dx$. Suppose $f$ is integrable and sufficiently regular for the sampled quadrature below.
>
> 1. Choose a window length $M>0$ so the tails outside $[-M/2,M/2]$ are acceptably small, and an even sample count $N$. A power of two is convenient for a radix-two FFT. Set $h=M/N$.
> 2. Form the wrapped samples $a_j=f(jh)$ for $0\le j<N/2$ and $a_j=f(jh-M)$ for $N/2\le j<N$.
> 3. Compute the negative-exponent unitary transform
>
> $$
> b_k=\frac1{\sqrt N}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}a_j e^{-2\pi ijk/N},\qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1.
> $$
>
> 4. Set $q_k=k$ for $0\le k<N/2$ and $q_k=k-N$ for $N/2\le k<N$. Then use
>
> $$
> \widehat f\left(\frac{2\pi q_k}{M}\right)\approx\frac{M}{\sqrt{2\pi N}}b_k.
> $$
>
> The Nyquist bin is assigned to the negative endpoint here; it is one bin, not two independent endpoint values.
> 5. Check convergence by enlarging the window and reducing the sample spacing. Increasing $M$ at fixed $N$ also coarsens the samples, so it need not improve the total error. Control both truncation and quadrature/aliasing errors.

path: Chapter 18 Finite Difference Numerical Methods/18.1 The Finite Difference Method for the Heat Equation.md
title: Forward Difference Approximation of a First Time Derivative
body:
> [!equation|8be3d570-9f65-54d8-8ad4-5bd3d976df08.local at=cc1356ee-b017-5db7-8a9a-4b6f9d19b50a] Forward Difference Approximation of a First Time Derivative
> For a sufficiently smooth function $u(x,t)$ sampled on the uniform grid $(ih,jk)$, $k>0$, put $u_{ij}=u(ih,jk)$. Then
>
> $$
> u_t(ih,jk)\approx\frac{u_{i,j+1}-u_{ij}}{k}.
> $$
>
> The local derivative error is $O(k)$ if $u_{tt}$ is bounded near the sample.

path: Chapter 18 Finite Difference Numerical Methods/18.1 The Finite Difference Method for the Heat Equation.md
title: Centered Second Difference Approximation of a Spatial Second Derivative
body:
> [!equation|8de3a8f9-9e94-5b61-91ca-4ae204cd2319.local at=3be280a4-58ca-5492-82c5-b9ac2e3cc78b] Centered Second Difference Approximation of a Spatial Second Derivative
> For a sufficiently smooth function $u(x,t)$ sampled on the uniform grid $(ih,jk)$, $h>0$, put $u_{ij}=u(ih,jk)$. Then
>
> $$
> u_{xx}(ih,jk)\approx\frac{u_{i+1,j}-2u_{ij}+u_{i-1,j}}{h^2}.
> $$
>
> The local derivative error is $O(h^2)$ if the fourth spatial derivative is bounded near the sample.

path: Chapter 18 Finite Difference Numerical Methods/18.1 The Finite Difference Method for the Heat Equation.md
title: Explicit Forward-Time Centered-Space Scheme for the One-Dimensional Heat Equation
body:
> [!equation|e650f2d0-28fd-5ccc-bcca-8fb1cddee1e1.local at=b41cfc86-b4d2-5447-8c65-fa44ba1fdd40] Explicit Forward-Time Centered-Space Scheme for the One-Dimensional Heat Equation
> For $u_t=c^2u_{xx}$, $c>0$, use spatial step $h>0$, time step $k>0$, and approximations $U_i^j\approx u(ih,jk)$. The explicit finite-difference update is
>
> $$
> U_i^{j+1}=(1-2s)U_i^j+s(U_{i+1}^j+U_{i-1}^j),\qquad s=\frac{c^2k}{h^2}.
> $$
>
> Supply initial samples and the prescribed boundary values at each step. The usual grid-independent stability restriction is $0<s\le\tfrac12$. For smooth solutions the differential-equation truncation error is $O(k+h^2)$.

path: Chapter 18 Finite Difference Numerical Methods/18.2 The Finite Difference Method for the Wave Equation.md
title: Centered Finite-Difference Scheme for the One-Dimensional Wave Equation
body:
> [!equation] Centered Finite-Difference Scheme for the One-Dimensional Wave Equation
> For $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ with $c>0$, spatial step $h>0$, and time step $k>0$, let $U_i^j\approx u(ih,jk)$ and $s=(ck/h)^2$. The centered update is
>
> $$
> U_i^{j+1}=2(1-s)U_i^j+s(U_{i+1}^j+U_{i-1}^j)-U_i^{j-1}.
> $$
>
> For initial displacement $f$ and velocity $g$, initialize the interior grid by
>
> $$
> U_i^0=f(ih),\qquad U_i^1=f(ih)+kg(ih)+\frac s2\bigl(f((i+1)h)-2f(ih)+f((i-1)h)\bigr).
> $$
>
> Enforce the prescribed boundary data at every time level. The usual mesh-independent CFL condition is $0<ck/h\le1$; for smooth solutions and compatible initial/boundary data this centered scheme is second-order accurate in space and time.

path: Chapter 18 Finite Difference Numerical Methods/18.3 The Finite Difference Method for Laplace's Equation.md
title: Five-Point Finite-Difference Laplace Equation on a Uniform Square Grid
body:
> [!equation|933cc6a7-5662-5579-a1a8-dd5c8a9c42d3.local at=b29b3ea2-f5b9-5f74-858b-2fe2edf8d504] Five-Point Finite-Difference Laplace Equation on a Uniform Square Grid
> Let $U_{ij}$ approximate a harmonic function $u$ on a square grid $(ih,jh)$ of spacing $h>0$. The centered finite-difference Laplace equation at an interior gridpoint is
>
> $$
> \frac{U_{i+1,j}+U_{i-1,j}+U_{i,j+1}+U_{i,j-1}-4U_{ij}}{h^2}=0,
> $$
>
> or equivalently
>
> $$
> U_{ij}=\frac14(U_{i+1,j}+U_{i-1,j}+U_{i,j+1}+U_{i,j-1}).
> $$
>
> Each interior value is the average of its four nearest grid neighbors. Boundary values must be supplied to determine the discrete Dirichlet solution.

path: Chapter 18 Finite Difference Numerical Methods/18.4 Iteration Methods for Laplace's Equation.md
title: Jacobi Iteration for the Five-Point Discrete Dirichlet Problem
body:
> [!algorithm|002ac32b-92bb-57fe-abc4-77f42e3fed38.local at=c7086cd6-d3bf-5a51-89ad-4b8565f4bce5] Jacobi Iteration for the Five-Point Discrete Dirichlet Problem
> On a finite rectangular square grid, hold all prescribed boundary values fixed and initialize the interior values $U_{ij}^{0}$. For each sweep $r=0,1,\ldots$, update every interior gridpoint using only the preceding sweep:
>
> $$
> U_{ij}^{r+1}=\frac14\left(U_{i+1,j}^{r}+U_{i-1,j}^{r}+U_{i,j+1}^{r}+U_{i,j-1}^{r}\right).
> $$
>
> Use a separate array for the new sweep. The iterates converge to the unique discrete Dirichlet solution. Monitor the residual $4U_{ij}-U_{i+1,j}-U_{i-1,j}-U_{i,j+1}-U_{i,j-1}$ against a chosen tolerance; a small change between sweeps alone is not an error bound for the continuous PDE.

path: Chapter 18 Finite Difference Numerical Methods/18.4 Iteration Methods for Laplace's Equation.md
title: Gauss–Seidel Iteration for the Five-Point Discrete Dirichlet Problem
body:
> [!algorithm|6ec9c20f-5bbe-5a87-86db-c80b32aa6f90.local at=11278057-f5f0-5f3e-bf1e-a0ed52b858dd] Gauss–Seidel Iteration for the Five-Point Discrete Dirichlet Problem
> On a finite rectangular square grid, hold prescribed boundary values fixed. Starting from an interior guess, sweep rows from bottom to top and within each row from left to right. At sweep $r+1$, set
>
> $$
> U_{ij}^{r+1}=\frac14\left(U_{i+1,j}^{r}+U_{i-1,j}^{r+1}+U_{i,j+1}^{r}+U_{i,j-1}^{r+1}\right).
> $$
>
> Thus the left and lower neighbors use their newly updated values, and the right and upper neighbors use their preceding-sweep values. These iterates converge to the discrete Dirichlet solution. Check the discrete residual against the chosen stopping tolerance.

title: Successive Overrelaxation for the Five-Point Discrete Dirichlet Problem
body:
> [!algorithm|e9513713-9e35-5148-9699-d188ed5ec318.local at=f99704ca-8ed0-58fc-9dfc-69cfd82438bc] Successive Overrelaxation for the Five-Point Discrete Dirichlet Problem
> On a finite rectangular square grid with fixed Dirichlet boundary data, choose $0<\omega<2$ and an initial guess for the interior values. Sweep rows bottom to top and entries left to right, updating by
>
> $$
> U_{ij}^{r+1}=(1-\omega)U_{ij}^{r}+\frac\omega4\left(U_{i+1,j}^{r}+U_{i-1,j}^{r+1}+U_{i,j+1}^{r}+U_{i,j-1}^{r+1}\right).
> $$
>
> This iteration converges to the discrete Dirichlet solution. The case $\omega=1$ is Gauss–Seidel; $1<\omega<2$ is overrelaxation and $0<\omega<1$ is underrelaxation. Equivalently, write $s=\omega/4$, so $0<s<1/2$. Select the parameter and stopping tolerance with reference to the residual and convergence behavior.
